The degree helps with the analytical side of things, understanding data and stuff. Though honestly, half the time I feel like I’m just putting out fires. Fires, eh? Sounds stressful. You work too hard, you do. You need to take more holidays. That young man of yours, Daniel… is he still working all hours at that tech company? Pretty much. He's a software engineer, and they’re always pushing for deadlines. He's good at it, though. Really good. He's talking about maybe trying to negotiate a four-day week. It’s becoming more common, apparently. A four-day week? Now  that's  an idea. Imagine having three days off! What would you do with yourself? Sleep, probably. Honestly, I don’t know.

… honestly, I still can’t believe how much they’re charging for a pint of bitter ‘ere. Eight euros! Eight! Back ‘ome in Doncaster, you’d get change from a fiver, easily. It’s daylight robbery, it is. Oh, you’re such a Yorkshire tightwad, aren't you, Liv? It  is  expensive, I’ll grant you that, but we’re in France, things are different. Think of it as… contributing to the local economy. Contributing to their fancy holidays, more like! And it doesn’t taste any better, mind. It's all frothy and…wrong. Anyway, how’s the dissertation going? Still stuck on the methodology section? You looked proper stressed last night. Don't remind me. It's a nightmare. Professor Davies is insistent on a completely quantitative approach, even though it just doesn't  fit  the subject. I'm trying to explain that qualitative data would give a much richer insight into consumer behaviour, but she just keeps waving her hands and talking about statistical significance. Honestly, it's like talking to a brick wall. Quantitative, qualitative… sounds like proper science babble to me. I barely scraped through biology A-Level, remember? All those titrations and…things. I’m just glad I picked English Lit. Essays all the way. Much less pressure to prove anything scientifically. Easy for you to say! You're dissecting metaphors, I'm trying to justify why interviews are a valid research method. It’s infuriating. I think I need to re-read Popper. Remind me what  falsification  actually means again? My brain feels like mush. Falsification…? Right, isn't that the thing about being able to  disprove  a theory, rather than just proving it? Summat like that. My little brother's doing A-Level Physics, he'd know. He's a proper brainbox, that one. Been going on about string theory all week. Drives our mum mental. That's it! Thanks. Okay, so I need to frame my argument around how qualitative data can  challenge  existing assumptions, rather than 'prove' anything definitively. It's a subtle difference, but Davies seems to hang on every word. Did you catch that football match last night? Man United were dreadful. Oh, don’t even  start  me on football. Absolutely shocking. Erik ten Hag needs to be sacked, honestly. They were playing like they’d never kicked a ball before. And don't get me started on the refereeing decisions.

… honestly, it was  huge . I mean, genuinely the size of my hand. And right in the bathroom. You’d think I'd be used to it living near the countryside, but no. It just… appeared. Ooh, nasty. I ‘ate spiders, I do. Proper jumpy, I am. Luckily, we don't get ‘em that big in town, not usually. Mostly little ‘uns, scuttlin’ about. Though Mrs. Higgins down the road, she ‘ad a right infestation last year. Said they were comin’ through the letterbox! Good heavens! Through the letterbox? That  is  unsettling. I tried the usual, you know, cup and card trick. But this one… it just wasn’t having it. It kept sort of edging around the rim, lookin’ at me like  I  was the one being unreasonable. Eventually, my husband had to dispatch it. Typical, innit? Men and spiders. Always ‘ave to be the hero. I tend to scream and get my son, Mark, to deal with ‘em. He's got a bit of a thing for reptiles and stuff, so spiders don’t bother him. Though he did bring ‘ome a gecko once… nearly gave my mum a ‘eart attack. A gecko! Oh, my goodness. That's a step up from a spider, isn't it? We had a mouse problem a few years back. That was… distressing. Not so much the mouse itself – though it did nibble on the biscuit tin – but the  sound . Scratching in the walls at night. Drove me to distraction. Mice are worse, I reckon. Spiders, you see ‘em. Mice, you don’t, not until they’ve made a right mess of things. We ‘ad ‘em in the old house, before we moved to the flats. Used to find little droppings everywhere. And they’d get into the cupboards, ruin all the food. Horrible. Exactly! It’s the unseen damage, isn’t it? Makes you feel… invaded. Though, oddly enough, I’m much more tolerant of birds. We get robins nesting in the hawthorn bush every year. Birds are lovely. Always ‘ave liked birds. My nan used to ‘ave a bird feeder, and I’d spend hours watchin’ ‘em. Blue tits, robins, all sorts. We don't get many where I live now, just pigeons mostly. They’re more trouble than they’re worth, honestly. Dirty birds. Pigeons  are  rather… assertive. But the robins, they're quite charming. They seem to recognise me now, even.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of names on Great-Grandad Thomas’ side is just bewildering. I’ve got this spreadsheet, you see, trying to untangle it all. He apparently had  seven  children, and tracing their lines…it's a proper rabbit hole. Did your grandmother, Bronwen, ever mention anything about the Davies family connecting to anyone in Dorset, by any chance? I’m grasping at straws here, but… Oh, Dorset! That’s a long way from the Valleys, love. Bronwen wouldn’t have known Dorset from Denmark, I reckon. She was very much a ‘stay put’ sort of woman. Bristol born and bred, she was, even though her parents were up from near Swansea. No, family trips weren’t really…a thing. She’d talk about her father, though. Old Man Davies, a miner he was. Tough as nails, she said. But not much beyond that. Family tree talk wasn’t her forte. More interested in the price of tea and what the neighbours were up to, bless her. Miners, right. That explains the strong Welsh connection then. So, quite different to my side – mostly agricultural labourers and a few… well, a rather dubious solicitor, according to family lore. It’s fascinating, though isn’t it? Trying to piece it all together. It makes you feel so connected, and yet… also incredibly small. It does. And it's a comforting thought, isn’t it? Knowing where you come from. Though, honestly, having spent thirty years in a classroom, I preferred the present tense with children. History's all well and good, but I found dealing with  current  dramas rather enough! How long have you been teaching, dear? Twenty years now. Secondary English. It's…rewarding, most of the time. Though lately, it's felt increasingly like herding cats. Different pressures, you know? And a lot more paperwork. It’s funny, isn't it? We both ended up in schools, just… different generations. What did you teach? Primary. Reception and Year One, mostly. Little ones. Oh, the joy of teaching a child to read! That's a feeling you don't forget. I retired early, you see. Shortly after… after I lost Margaret. Oh, I am so sorry. I didn’t realise… Auntie Carol just mentioned you were retired. I’m truly sorry for your loss. It was six years ago now. Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease. Horrible, horrible thing. It took her quickly, thankfully, but the decline… it was devastating to watch.

… honestly, seeing that balloon drift so low over Farmer Giles’ field was a bit startling. It looked like it was going to land  in  the barley. Did you see how the dog went absolutely mental? Poor Winston thought it was some kind of giant, colourful predator. He does have a dramatic flair, that one. Yes, I saw. He was practically trying to burrow into your legs. Giles probably wasn't thrilled, though. He's pretty protective of his barley. Though, to be fair, a hot air balloon landing isn’t exactly ideal for a harvest. No, it really wasn't. I felt awful. I hope they managed to get it up again okay. It’s just… magical, isn't it? Seeing them float across the Norfolk skies. It’s one of the few things that makes braving these muddy paths worthwhile. Absolutely. Especially on a day like this. Although, even the mud can’t detract from the sheer volume of wildlife at the moment. Did you see that kestrel hovering by the hedgerow earlier? It was brilliant. We're incredibly lucky to have this on our doorstep. I did! Such a beautiful bird. It makes me think we should finally get round to that camping trip we’ve been talking about for ages. Just…properly, away from everything. Maybe somewhere a bit further afield, without those dreadful power lines crisscrossing the landscape. They really ruin the view, don’t they? They do. It’s a constant visual reminder of… well, everything connected to modern life. Camping sounds wonderful. Though, we need to be realistic. "Further afield" translates to "significantly more expensive," doesn’t it? We need to actually  plan  it, not just dream about it. You’re right, of course. Practicality reigns supreme. It's always the money, isn't it? We could rough it, I suppose. Just a tent and a stove. Although, Winston wouldn’t be terribly impressed with minimal comforts. He expects a certain standard, that dog. He absolutely does. He's convinced he's royalty. We could look at Breydon Water maybe? It's not  wild , wild, but it’s close enough, and the birdwatching is fantastic. Less chance of a rogue hot air balloon scaring him senseless, too. That’s a good shout, actually. And probably kinder on the bank account. We could even try that new Dutch oven recipe I found. Imagine, stew cooked over an open fire… Now  that  sounds tempting.

…and honestly, the humidity is just  suffocating . It’s not even proper heat, it’s just…sticky. Makes concentrating on lesson planning a nightmare. You wouldn't believe the grammatical errors that creep in when you're constantly fanning yourself! Aye, you're tellin' me. My joints ache somethin' fierce in this weather. Feels like I’m livin’ in a greenhouse sometimes. Though, t'be fair, it’s better than last winter, wasn’t it? That was a proper sodden one. Remember February? Non-stop rain. Don’t remind me. I had a student practically learning English  through  meteorological reports. "Persistent precipitation," "low-pressure systems"... it all became vocabulary. It was…efficient, I suppose. How are things at the gyms? Still battling to get everyone motivated in the heat? Oh, you bet. Folks are more interested in ice cream than incline trainers, I reckon. Had a member complainin’ the other day that the air con wasn’t powerful enough. Honestly! Like I control the weather. It's always somethin'. Keeps me busy though, runnin’ between the Solihull and Birmingham branches. Lot of travelling. That sounds exhausting. I’m quite happy tucked away with my books and teenagers mostly. Though “happy” is a strong word some days. I’m reading a fascinating thing at the moment, actually, a biography of Samuel Johnson. Samuel Johnson? Now that's a name. Wasn't he one o' them dictionary fellas? He  was  the dictionary fella, essentially! And a brilliant writer. It’s making me think a lot about the evolution of language, obviously, given what I do. It’s humbling, you know? To think about how much effort went into establishing ‘correct’ English. And then I have to explain the difference between “affect” and “effect” for the fifteenth time this week. Sounds like a thankless task sometimes. I never understood half the rules at school, to be honest. Preferred playin' rugby. Didn’t need grammar for a good tackle! It’s a different skill set, definitely. Although, a good coach needs communication skills, doesn't he? It's not just about shouting instructions. Spot on. That's where I've learned the most in recent years, actually. It’s not about bein’ a sergeant major, it's about understandin’ what motivates each person. I've been doin’ a bit of coaching training myself, surprisingly enough. Learning about different learning styles, mirroring body language... it's all a bit psychological, really.

…and honestly, lad, I don’t know  why  they keep changing the marking schemes. It’s a nightmare! Last year it was all about ‘showing working’, this year it’s ‘elegant solutions’. What  is  an elegant solution to a simultaneous equation for a fifteen-year-old, eh? It’s just maths, not a blooming art competition! Sounds stressful, Mrs. Harrison. Is it making you drink more tea? You’ve had three cups since they arrived. Aye, she gets like that when the papers come. Used to be the same with my knitting patterns, always changing the stitches. Not as much money in it though, marking papers. She’s a clever woman, our Brenda. Always did have a head for numbers. Clever indeed. Reminds me of old Mr. Grimshaw down the docks. Could calculate the weight of a cod in his head, just by lookin’ at it. Used to fleece the tourists, he did. Oh, don't start with the dock stories, Arthur. Not again. And it’s not about the money, it’s about consistency! They want us to reward creativity, but then penalise them if they don’t stick to a specific method. Honestly! Right, so like, if I solved something a different way, but got the right answer, I could still lose marks? Potentially, yes. That's the frustrating part. It depends on the examiner, and the level of 'deviation' from the expected solution. Which is why there’s a standardisation process… ugh, it’s all just… administrative fluff. Standardisation? Sounds a bit posh for all that, doesn't it? Back in my day, you just marked what was right and what was wrong. Simple as that. Aye. No fancy rules then. Just common sense. Though, mind you, try tellin’ a teenager  that . Hey! I’m not  that  bad. Although… History's killin’ me. Mr. Davies keeps asking about 'historiographical interpretations'…what even  is  that? Oh dear. It means how historians look at things, love. Different perspectives, questioning sources... It’s good they’re teaching you that, actually. It’s important to think critically. Though, at your age, I understand it sounding bonkers. Critical thinking? Sounds like a fancy way of saying 'arguin’ back'. A little bit, maybe, Elsie! Now, Arthur, are you sure you’ve remembered your medicine? And Elsie, would you like another biscuit? I made some shortbread earlier. Shortbread, you say? Never refuse a bit of shortbread from our Brenda.

… honestly, I still think we should’ve gone through Richmond. This A66 is just relentless. Trucks, lorries, all going flat out. It’s giving me the willies. Now, now, Brenda. It's a direct route, isn’t it? And we want to get to that gig at the Holmfirth Picturedrome, remember? No time for scenic routes today. Besides, Richmond's lovely, but it adds at least forty minutes. Forty minutes of  peaceful  driving, mind you. Less chance of being overtaken by something the size of a house. Did you see that one back there? Nearly blew us into the hedge! Honestly, modern drivers… no spatial awareness. Not like my dad, he could judge a gap a mile off. Your dad could judge a good pint a mile off, more like. Remember him trying to parallel park his Morris Minor in Keswick? Took him a good twenty minutes and half a bottle of bitter. Oh, don’t remind me! The whole street lined up to watch. He called it “careful maneuvering.” Honestly. Anyway, is that satnav still working alright? It's been a bit funny lately. Kept telling us we were in a field near Penrith last week. It's fine, it's fine. Just needs updating, I think. I’ll get around to it. It's just… I’m starting to distrust them, those things. Remember Old Man Hemmings? Swore his satnav led him straight into a duck pond. Said the ducks weren't impressed. Oh, Percy Hemmings. A proper character. Always had a story. Speaking of stories, Sarah’s wedding is next month, isn’t it? Have you finished writing your poem for them? Nearly. I’ve got the first draft down. It's proving tricky, trying to capture both her and Ben. They're such a…a  pair . But in a good way, obviously. It needs a bit more…oomph, I think. Maybe a dash of Wordsworth. Wordsworth, eh? A bit grand for a wedding, isn't it? Although, a ceilidh  would  be nice. They’re having one, aren’t they? I love a good ceilidh. Makes a change from all this indie music you drag me to. Drag you? I thought you enjoyed seeing me struggle through a Gay Gordons! Remember that one in Hawes? You were practically howling with laughter. Well, you  were  a sight! All elbows and apologies. It's the music I like, really. Something a bit lively.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of beige in that kitchen was offensive. Beige tiles, beige countertops, even the bloody spice rack was beige! It just sucked all the life out of the space. Remember what Mr. Harrison used to say at uni? “Architecture is frozen music!” Beige is…frozen silence. Harsh, Liv, harsh. But fair. Though I'm pretty sure Mr. Harrison mostly just wanted to sound profound. Did you manage to get photos of that ridiculous window placement? I need ammunition for the meeting on Monday. Oh,  loads . It’s like they actively tried to block out any natural light. Photos are on the shared drive, labeled “Beige Apocalypse.” Speaking of ammunition, did you hear back from Ben? He sounded utterly wretched on the phone yesterday. Yeah, just a quick text. Still getting chewed out by old man Davies. Apparently, he submitted the preliminary designs for the extension, and Davies basically ripped them to shreds. Said they lacked… ‘vision’. Can you  believe  that? Ben’s designs are always technically brilliant. Ugh, Davies. He’s such a dinosaur. All style over substance, that one. Poor Ben. He’s putting in such long hours. We should probably drag him out for a pint later this week. Maybe force-feed him some actual, inspiring architecture. Definitely. Honestly, sometimes I think he takes Davies' criticism to heart. He's too good for that negativity. Right, breakfast? I’m starving. Thinking full English. Need serious protein after wading through that building. You? Ooh, tempting. But I'm feeling lighter. Just a croissant and a latte, I think. Gotta maintain some semblance of architectural figure, you know? Can’t be fueling the beige with bacon grease. Architectural figure? You and your principles. So, back to the university brief… are you still leaning towards the communal living concept? I’m still wrestling with it. It feels… overly idealistic. I am. I think there's real potential. We've talked about the housing crisis, the loneliness epidemic… a well-designed communal space could actually  address  those issues. It’s not just about shared kitchens and laundry rooms, it's about fostering a sense of community. I was reading this article about co-housing in Denmark, and they've had amazing results. Plus, it gives us a chance to be really creative with the interior spaces. Think layered privacy, adaptable modules… That’s the bit I'm struggling with – the practicality.

… honestly, it was  chaos  getting back from Manchester yesterday. Absolute gridlock on the M6. I swear, people just forget how to merge. It’s like they think lanes just… appear out of nowhere. Oh, Mum, you and your driving stories. Sounds stressful, though. Was it really bad? I was lucky, I just got the train. Much more civilised. Civilised is one word for it. Expensive is another! Honestly, I think I aged about five years in that traffic. People were trying to overtake on the hard shoulder! On the  hard shoulder , Lily! Where has common sense gone? Right? It’s just… selfishness, isn't it? Everyone thinking they’re more important. Did you at least have some good music? Music helped. Bit of Florence + the Machine. But even Florence couldn’t drown out the sound of angry horns. Anyway, enough about my motorway misery. How was your weekend? Did you manage to see Chloe and Ben? It was good, actually. Yeah, I went over to Chloe’s on Saturday. We just chilled, ordered a takeaway, watched awful reality TV. Ben was there too, he's properly into that baking show now, which is hilarious. He tried to make macarons last week… it was a disaster. Oh, Ben. Bless him. He’s a good lad. You two seem to be spending a lot of time with them lately. That’s lovely. It’s good you have such a solid group of friends. It is. They're really supportive. It's just… nice to have people who  get  it, you know? Work’s been a bit hectic, all the new policy changes, and they just… listen without judgement. Absolutely. Good friends are invaluable. I was thinking… next Saturday, would you be free for dinner? I was going to try that new Italian place, ‘Bella Notte’, down by the river. I've heard really good things. We could have a proper catch-up, just the two of us. No motorway stories, I promise. Ooh, Bella Notte! I've seen pictures, it looks really nice. Next Saturday sounds good, Mum. I might need rescuing from some spreadsheets beforehand, though. This new project is draining the life out of me. Spreadsheets? Oh dear. Well, rescued you will be. And we can formulate a plan to conquer those spreadsheets over pasta and wine. Speaking of rescuing… have you heard from Sarah? I haven’t seen her for ages.

…and honestly, the ‘demonstrated ability to thrive under pressure’ bit feels  so  cliché. Like, who  doesn’t  say that? It’s just…empty. I’ve rewritten it three times now. Aye, it is a bit of a bore, isn't it? Right, let's have a look. You sent me the draft, didn’t you? Hold on… …Right, here we are. "Proven ability to manage multiple projects simultaneously, consistently meeting deadlines…" See? Textbook. You need to  show  them you thrive under pressure, not just  tell  them. Exactly! That's what I was thinking. But how? I don’t want to waffle on about accidentally setting off the fire alarm in Year 7. Though that  was  a pressured situation… No, definitely don’t mention the fire alarm! Think about a specific instance at the school. Remember that time the Ofsted inspection was sprung on you all with barely any notice, and you had to pull together those displays and sort out the student feedback forms? Oh god,  that  was awful. Absolute chaos. Mrs. Higgins nearly had a breakdown. There you go! "Successfully navigated an unexpected Ofsted inspection, rapidly adapting plans and collaborating with colleagues to ensure a positive outcome, despite extremely limited preparation time." See? Specific, shows initiative, teamwork,  and  that you don’t crumble when things get hectic. Much better than ‘thrive’. You're brilliant, honestly. I get so stuck in my head trying to sound…professional. It feels so artificial. You’re so good at making things sound natural, probably because of the radio. You’re used to crafting things for an audience. It's a habit, I suppose. And years of interviews, both giving and taking! This job sounds right up your street, though. Digital content producer for BBC Birmingham? That's perfect for someone with your language skills and your understanding of…well, everything. It is, it really is. It’s just… a bit intimidating. It’s a step up from teaching, isn't it? I mean, I love teaching, but it's…safe. Predictable. This feels…exposed. It  is  a different beast. But you’re more than capable. You’ve always been a fantastic communicator. And you've got that analytical brain from your Masters. They’ll see that. What are you worried about with the interview itself? Just the usual, I think. The ‘tell me about yourself’ question. It always throws me. It feels so…vain. Right.

…so, honestly, the thought of another quarterly report just… drains me, alright? It's not the  work  exactly, it's the pointless, endless cycle of it all. Pushing numbers around for shareholders who wouldn’t know a good product if it bit them. I get it. Absolutely. You’ve been saying similar things for a while now, haven’t you? It’s a relief, in a way, to actually voice it properly, instead of just grumbling over breakfast. Though, swapping a high-powered marketing job for… well, for miniature succulents feels a bit drastic, doesn’t it? Drastic, maybe. But fulfilling. Look, remember that little stall we saw at the markets in Byron Bay last week? The woman was making a killing selling these tiny cacti and succulents. She said she started it as a hobby, and now it’s her full-time gig. No stress, fresh air, and people genuinely  happy  to give her money. Sounds a lot better than explaining ROI to Barry from accounting. Barry  is  a special case. But starting a business, even a small one, isn’t all sunshine and succulents, you know. There’s the website, the sourcing, the propagating… the potential for root rot! And honestly, financially, are you sure about this? We’ve got a comfortable life, a mortgage… That’s where the planning comes in. And why I’m bouncing it off you, of course. I've been doing a bit of research. Online sales are the main thing, obviously. Etsy, maybe a simple Shopify store. I reckon I can start small, build it up over six months, maybe a year,  while  still doing some freelance marketing work – a couple of hours a week, just to keep the bills paid. I’ve already found a wholesaler in Melbourne who does excellent prices on pots and soil. Okay, that sounds… more sensible. Freelance to ease the transition, definitely. And Melbourne's good for sourcing. But the marketing side – you’d still need to focus on  that  for the business, right? Social media, photos, descriptions? It's not just sticking plants in pots. Exactly! Which is why  you  are a lifesaver. Your photography is fantastic, and you have a knack for writing engaging descriptions. You could really help with the branding and the whole aesthetic. Plus, you’re excellent at dealing with people, which will be crucial for customer service. Oh, stop it. You’re buttering me up.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of Deliveroo boxes piling up is embarrassing. It's not sustainable, is it? I mean, we're eating like kings and queens, but at what cost? And mostly beige food, let's be honest. Little Leo here is practically fuelled by chicken nuggets. Nuggy! More nuggy! Och, now, don’t be so hard on yourself, dear. You’ve got a wee one to look after. It's easy to fall into convenience. When my lot were small, it was fish fingers and beans, and we all survived. Though, I do recall my daughter going through a phase of only eating orange things… carrots, cheese puffs, even insisted her mashed potatoes were orange! Orange potatoes. Remarkable. Reminds me of a rather eccentric author I published, believed he could improve the flavour of everything with a dash of saffron. Drove the poor kitchen staff mad. Though, back to this 'Deliveroo mountain,' is it worth saving the time, really? You used to be such a whiz in the kitchen, Penelope. I  was , Geoffrey! Before Leo arrived and my brain turned to mush. And truthfully, it’s not just the cooking. It's…everything. Trying to juggle a toddler and feeling useful. My sister keeps saying I should get a part-time job now Leo’s a little older, but where would I even  start ? Everything seems to require a degree these days. Nonsense, Penelope. You've got a wealth of life experience. Plenty of places would value that. Though, I’ll admit, the schooling situation is a worry. Heard Mrs. Henderson down the street is practically beside herself; little Jamie’s on a waiting list for every primary school within a five-mile radius. The housing shortage feeds into it, you know. Too many people, not enough space. And now, with all the…well, all the new arrivals. Good people, of course, the Poles and others coming over. Hard workers. But it puts a strain on everything – schools, the NHS… Don't start with the ‘new arrivals’, Geoffrey. That's a slippery slope. Leo’s nursery has a lovely Polish girl in his class, she’s brilliant with him. And the NHS is struggling because of  underfunding , not because of hardworking immigrants. It's completely different. Although, trying to get a doctor’s appointment these days… it's frankly ridiculous. I tried claiming for Leo’s cough medicine last week and was on hold for forty-five minutes!

…and honestly, the whole thing with the car park passes at the doctors is just ridiculous, isn’t it? They’re saying you need a pass now, even just to  drop  someone off. It’s creating chaos. I spent twenty minutes circling yesterday trying to find somewhere to let Mum out! Oh, don't even get me started on that! I heard Mrs. Higgins was practically in tears trying to get a pass. She just wanted to take her husband for his check-up. It's meant to make things easier, they said. Easier for  who  though? It’s just another way to make life difficult. Honestly, sometimes I think they just invent these rules to feel important. Exactly! And the council, they’re just… well, you know the council. Anyway, enough about that, it’s giving me a headache. How’s your knee been? Did you manage that walk with Sarah last weekend? It's alright, thank you. Still a bit twingey, to be honest. I  did  go with Sarah, but it was more of a potter, really. She's training for that half marathon, bless her, so she practically dragged me around. I felt like an old woman! Remember when we used to run around like teenagers? Before kids and knees giving way? Oh, absolutely! Sixth form was a whirlwind. Do you ever think about…Old Mr. Davies? The history teacher? Mr. Davies! Goodness me, yes! What a character. Always smelled faintly of pipe tobacco and mothballs. He really believed in us, didn’t he? Even when we were being right little horrors. He did. He was the one who convinced me to apply to Uni. I was all set to go straight into a secretarial role. Said I had a ‘facility with language’ – which basically meant I was good at spotting typos, I think. Which, ironically, is what I do now! Marketing and proofing, all these years later. How’s work going? Still battling with those difficult customers? Oh, you know, the usual. Some days are good, some are… challenging. Had one woman yesterday who wanted a discount because the weather was ‘depressing’. Honestly! But lunchtime supervisions are alright, keeps me active. Speaking of active, are you still doing those Pilates classes? I am! Though I missed a couple last month. Been a bit under the weather, just a nasty cold, nothing serious. Felt completely wiped out, though.

…aye, but that’s the thing, right? It’s nae just about retweetin’ funny memes, though God knows I’m guilty o’ that enough. For the comms team at the council, Twitter’s become… essential, almost. We had that wee kerfuffle last week wi’ the bin collections, and it was Twitter that sorted it. Folk were properly fuming, messages floodin’ in, but we managed to get ahead of it, explain the delays, redirect folks to the website for specific info… calmed things doon remarkably quick.      Aye, I can imagine. Bin collections. A national crisis in Scotland, it seems. Seriously though, that's good work. You're turning a potential PR disaster into a managed response. I’m still trying to convince some of the more… established academics here that Twitter isn’t just for self-promotion and shouting into the void.      Shoutin’ intae the void is half the fun, isn’t it? But ye’re right. It’s a mindset shift for some. They see it as… frivolous. Like it detracts from the ‘serious’ work. Bit like how my da used to look at email, remember? “Letters are proper communication, son!”      Oh, I remember your da well! Sticking to his principles. Same here. Professor MacIntyre, bless his soul, still submits handwritten drafts for everything. But even  he  acknowledges the reach now. I’m trying to get the department to use it more to publicise research, connect wi’ potential students, even just show folk what we're actually  doing  here. It’s all a bit ‘ivory tower’ as it stands.      Exactly! It’s about demystifying things. Showin' folk the human side. We’ve started doin’ wee “a day in the life” threads on the council account. Sounds daft, but folk actually  engage  wi' it. They like seeing the folk behind the uniforms, y’know? It makes them feel like they’re being listened to.      Smart. I’ve been experimenting with short video clips - little explainers about specific research projects. Had a student do the editing, thankfully. My technical skills peak at sending an email. The engagement's been decent, surprisingly. Though I did get one comment calling me “a digital charlatan.”      A digital charlatan! Oh, that’s brilliant. Ye cannae win, can ye? There’ll always be someone takin’ exception to somethin’. Did ye reply?      I did. Politely pointed out that I was actively trying to make academic research more accessible to the public.

… honestly, the sheer  volume  of washing up after brunch was criminal. Like, six people, everyone contributing, and it still looked like a bomb had gone off. Did you even  see  the state of the hob? Sounds about right for a Saturday with that lot. Luckily, I escaped to a quiet shift at the hospital. Relatively quiet, anyway. Old Mrs. Higgins decided she was marrying Ryan Reynolds. Again. Oh, bless her. She's a character. Still, I’m exhausted. Between that and trying to explain to Mark  again  that “casual” doesn’t mean texting every five minutes, my brain feels fried. Mark, huh? Still at it? You told him pretty clearly last week, didn’t you? What’s the latest? Apparently, a lack of texts equates to a lack of interest. Honestly, it's like dealing with a teenager. I sent him a meme about clingy barnacles, hoping he'd get the hint. Oh, brilliant. Passive-aggressive meme warfare. Classic. Though, maybe not the most direct approach? Bit of a British thing, though, isn’t it? Indirect communication? I know, I know. It’s just… confronting things feels awful. Plus, he’s nice, genuinely. Just… intense. Honestly, sometimes I think he finds my perfectly reasonable boundaries deeply offensive. Boundaries are  important , Liv. Especially with people who seem to struggle with them. You need to protect your energy. You've been working flat-out with this new project at work, haven’t you? How’s that going, actually? The one with the community garden? It's… a lot. The council are being incredibly slow with permissions, and old Mr. Peterson keeps complaining about potential noise. He's convinced we're going to host rave parties amongst the marrows. Marrow raves. Now  that's  an image. Seriously though, that's frustrating. Bureaucracy at its finest. Least you're doing something worthwhile. It's way more fulfilling than dealing with marital delusions involving Hollywood actors. True. Though a Hollywood actor offering me a quiet weekend might be pretty fulfilling right now. This pasta sauce smells amazing, by the way. What is it? Just a simple tomato and basil. Needed something comforting after a twelve-hour shift. Thought we could just have a chill night in? Maybe watch that ridiculous dating show you’re obsessed with? Oh,  yes . Absolutely. And wine. Definitely wine. Speaking of chill… you wouldn’t happen to know someone who’s very good at setting boundaries for other people, would you?

… honestly, I still think it’s a bit much, isn’t it? Him wanting to stay a  week . A week! Last time he came, it was three days and I was knackered for a fortnight afterwards. Not that he noticed, mind you. Just sailed off back to… well, wherever it is he’s flitting about these days. Dad, you say that, but you secretly love it when he visits. You spend hours showing him old photos and reminiscing about childhood. Don’t pretend you don’t. Reminiscing is one thing, love. Being  worn down  is another. He’s like a whirlwind, your Uncle George is. Always has been. And at our age… well, a week feels a bit… ambitious. Now, now, George isn’t  that  bad. A bit chaotic, granted. But he’s good company, and it’ll be lovely to have him. Think of it as a proper family get-together. And he  does  genuinely want to see you, Arthur. He called me just yesterday asking about your health. He asks about my health because he feels guilty he doesn’t ring more often. It’s performative concern, believe me. Still, a week… What even  is  he doing these days anyway? Still “consulting”? Apparently, he's doing some work with a start-up in Bristol. Something to do with… sustainable seaweed farming? Honestly, even  I  struggled to understand it. Seaweed farming? Good Lord. Honestly. Well, as long as he’s keeping busy. Right, logistics then. He's driving, is he? Because if he’s flying into Exeter, someone’s going to have to meet him. He’s driving, yes. Said he wanted to see the countryside. Which is nice, I suppose. I can pick him up from the motorway junction, no problem. That’s on his route, isn’t it? Sounds good, Mum. That saves Dad having to navigate the back lanes. Speaking of navigating, did you get used to the new car, Dad? I know you were a bit apprehensive about all the technology. Apprehensive is an understatement! It's like flying the space shuttle. All these beeping noises and flashing lights. But… I’m getting there. Still haven’t figured out how to connect my phone to the bloody thing, though. It's all Bluetooth and widgets and… honestly. It’s alright for you young ‘uns who’ve grown up with it. It takes time, Arthur. You’ll get the hang of it.

… honestly, Arthur, I’m tellin’ ya, this Spanish is a right pickle. I thought French was bad enough back in school, but this… the verbs! They just  shift  around like quicksand. I’ve been at Duolingo for six weeks now, religiously, and I still can’t confidently order a coffee without sounding like a right plum. Six weeks, eh? That's nothin’, love. Nothin’ at all. I tried it a few years back, Rosetta Stone, the fancy one. Cost a fortune. Thought immersion was the way to go – just pictures, no explainin’. Utterly useless. I ended up more confused than when I started. It’s just… the sounds, isn’t it? They roll off the tongue so differently. Exactly! That ‘r’ sound! It’s like a tiny motor running in the back of your throat. And the subjunctive… don't even  start  me on the subjunctive. Old Mrs. Higgins, one of my students, she’s fluent - lived in Spain for twenty years. She tried to explain it to me and I stared at her like a cod. See, that's the problem with these apps, and Rosetta Stone was the same. No proper explanation of the  why  behind things. It's all repetition. You gotta understand the grammar, the structure. I used to think, being a quantity surveyor, I was good with detail, with patterns. Thought that'd help. It didn’t. Not with Spanish. Well, you weren’t having to conjugate verbs in the preterite, were ya? It's a different ball game altogether. I've started lookin' at some actual textbooks. Old-school, I know. But I need somethin' that  tells  me what's happening, not just flashes pictures of apples and asks me to say "la manzana." Sensible, that. Textbooks and a good teacher, that’s what you need. Though finding a good one… that’s the rub, isn't it? It's interesting though, isn't it, how easily some people pick up languages? I was reading about Catalonia the other day. They all speak Catalan  and  Castillian. Proper bilinguals. Imagine that. Aye, it's amazin'. And Belgium, isn't it? Flemish and French. My cousin’s wife, she's Belgian. Says she flicks between 'em without even thinkin'. It's ingrained. I wonder if it's easier when you're younger. Probably is. Young brains are more plastic, they say. Though I reckon it's a bit of a myth, to be honest.

… honestly, Dad, it’s just  mountains  of it. I thought you said you’d had a bit of a clear-out before I came down? I did, I did. But then you start looking, and suddenly it's all… important. Bills from 1998, you know? Can't just  chuck  that. Sentimental value, sort of. Plus, your mum always said… well, never mind. What are you doing with that pile? Those look like bank statements. Yeah, I’m trying to separate the stuff that needs shredding from the things we actually need to keep for tax or whatever. It’s a nightmare. This one’s from… 2007? Seriously? And it’s for like, £1.27 interest. You kept a statement for a pound twenty-seven? Well, it all adds up, doesn’t it? Besides, at the time, that was probably a decent cup of tea. Speaking of adding up, I was looking at flights to Malaga for October… they’ve gone up again. Ridiculous. Malaga? Oh, right. For your anniversary? Have you tried Skyscanner? Sometimes you can get a better deal if you’re flexible with the dates. I could have a quick look later if you like. I'm pretty good at finding cheap flights, it’s a skill. Almost like… corpus linguistics, spotting patterns. Corpus… what now? You and your fancy words since becoming a teacher. Just find me a cheap flight, that’s all I ask. I was reading an article about Kelly Brook, actually. Apparently she's opened a vegan restaurant. Kelly Brook and vegan food? That’s… an unexpected combination. But good for her, I suppose. Anything’s better than another dodgy reality TV show. Back to this paperwork, though. Have you seen your passport? I need to scan it for that visa application. Passport… somewhere in here, I reckon. Probably buried under old photos of your aunt Mildred. I’m terrible with keeping things tidy, you know that. Always have been. Your mum was the organised one. Everything in its place. I tried, honestly, but… it’s a losing battle. I know, I know. It’s alright, we'll find it. Speaking of losing battles – this recipe for shepherd's pie, it's completely illegible! Mum’s handwriting was getting pretty shaky towards the end. Do you remember how much lamb she used to put in? Oh, she never skimped on the lamb, that's for sure.

… honestly, it’s just the  principle  of it, innit? Three quid for AdBlue. Three quid! They’re robbing us blind, these petrol stations. Especially when you consider how little is actually  in  the bottle. Right, you’re on one about the AdBlue again. It’s a necessary evil, love. Keeps the car running, stops it from choking on its own emissions. Think of the planet. The planet? Don’t give me that. They’re exploiting the fact we  have  to have it. It’s like printer ink, remember? Used to be a fiver for a cartridge, now it’s… ridiculous. And the garage on the A19 was genuinely trying to upsell me windscreen wash  with  the AdBlue. Like I needed both at the same time. Classic. They always try to get one over. Though, to be fair, your windscreen  was  looking a bit grim. That’s beside the point! It’s the blatant profiteering. And the queues! Honestly, driving in this country is just…stressful. Especially around here. All those roundabouts. You’re getting worked up. We’re on a scenic route, remember? I thought you liked the countryside? I  do , when I'm not battling tractors and lorries. And don’t even get me started on the bikers. The bikers? What have the bikers done now? They just…weave, don't they? Just  weave  in and out of traffic. I saw one near Durham the other week, practically riding on the boot of a van. Gave me a right fright. It's just reckless. They're probably just enjoying the ride. It’s a beautiful day for it. You’ve got to admit, there’s a certain freedom to it. Freedom to endanger themselves and everyone else! My mam used to say they’re all mad. Properly, genuinely mad. She’s right, you know. And they make so much noise! I can hear 'em coming a mile off, then  whizz  past. They do like a bit of noise, I’ll give you that. But they're enthusiasts, y’know? It’s their hobby. Plus, you benefit from the taxes they pay on their bikes, contributing to road maintenance. Road maintenance that's full of potholes the size of craters! I swear, I nearly lost a tyre last month on that road near Houghton-le-Spring. It's a disgrace. Do you think they even  spend  the money from road tax on roads?

…and honestly, the way Murray used to grind out points, especially when he was younger, was just phenomenal. It wasn’t flashy, it wasn’t Federer-esque brilliance, but it was relentlessly effective. Did you watch any of his early Wimbledon runs, Leo? Uh, not really. Mum keeps putting them on when I’m trying to game. It’s, like, really long. And slow. He has a point, love. It  is  a different pace to the modern game. Everything’s about power now, aces, quick points. Murray was about making his opponent work for  every single one . Exactly! And that’s what I was trying to explain to Mark at the club this afternoon. He’s trying to get young Ethan to just bash everything, and it’s… well, it’s a bit misguided. Ethan’s got a good serve, but no consistency, and zero tactical awareness. Mark’s a bit shouty, isn’t he? He made me do fifty burpees last week because I missed a forehand. He’s enthusiastic. A bit too enthusiastic, perhaps. But that's why I’m glad  you’re  getting sessions with Sarah now. She’s much more nuanced. Remember what she said about your footwork? Yeah, something about split-stepping and being light on my feet. It's hard though. Feels weird. It  is  hard, son. Everything good in tennis takes practice. It’s not just hitting the ball hard. Look at Djokovic. Incredible athlete, yes, but it's his court coverage, his return of serve... that’s what sets him apart. He anticipates everything. And that comes from hours of drilling, and understanding the game. I was telling Mark, you need to build a foundation, Leo. Like, groundstrokes first, then consistency, then  then  you can start thinking about adding power. It's like building a house – you need good foundations or the whole thing comes tumbling down. So, I shouldn’t try and hit it as hard as I can all the time? No, darling. Not all the time. There's a time and a place for a flat-out winner, but if you’re constantly going for broke, you’re just going to make unforced errors. Think about placement, spin… variety. Remember when we watched Alcaraz at Wimbledon last year? Ah, that was a brilliant final. The drop shot he used against Djokovic… genius. He was good. Really fast. He is, isn’t he?

Right, so… these napkins. Seriously? Auntie Brenda’s gone a bit mad, hasn’t she? They genuinely look like… well, you know. Little white underpants.      Oh, don't start, Liam. She meant well. Brenda’s always been a bit…  eccentric  with the festive decorations. Remember the singing Santa last year? Nearly gave your Grandad a heart attack.      Eccentric is putting it mildly! Honestly, I showed a photo of these to my flatmates at uni and they were  dying . They've already nicknamed me 'Napkin Queen'.      It’s the thought that counts, love. Though, I have to admit, they  are  a bit… unfortunate. Speaking of thoughts, anyone got a plan for tackling the Christmas shopping still left? I’m dreading the Trafford Centre tomorrow.      I finished mine weeks ago, thank you very much. All online, of course. No fighting through crowds for this old girl. Besides, I’ve already started on the Christmas cake. It’s a good one this year, if I do say so myself. Lots of brandy.      Trafford Centre’s a nightmare, Dad. Absolute madness. Did anyone see how much a turkey costs this year? Robbery, I tell ya! Nearly needed a loan.      Don't I know it. I ended up going to the butcher in Marple. A bit more expensive, but at least the quality’s good. And he didn’t look at me like I’d asked him to single-handedly solve the energy crisis. So, Chloe, how did your friends spend Christmas Eve? Anything exciting?      Pretty chill, actually. A few of us went to a pub quiz. Pretty awful singing, I won’t lie. Someone tried to do Mariah Carey and… well, let's just say it was a crime against Christmas music.      Sounds about right. Speaking of music, has anyone been watching  Downton Abbey ? That soundtrack is beautiful! They use such lovely instrumentals.      Oh, I adore  Downton Abbey . The costumes are fabulous. Takes you back, doesn’t it? Though, I prefer a bit of Vera Lynn myself. Proper tunes.      Vera Lynn? Grandma, you’re well old school! No offence. But I’m more into… well, stuff my mates listen to. They were calling me ‘Stockport Slim’ when I told them I was coming home for Christmas. They’ve got weird nicknames for everyone, based on where they’re from.      “Stockport Slim”? That’s… creative. You haven't told them about your cousin Sarah’s trip to Florida yet, have you?

… honestly, the deadline for the Henderson report is just looming. It’s all spreadsheets and risk assessments. Not exactly stimulating, you know? I spent three hours yesterday just colour-coding things! Oh, bless you, darling. Sounds dreadful. Still, you’re good at that sort of thing. Always were, meticulous. Remember when you organised that entire school fete when you were, what, ten? Everything down to the ribbon colours on the stalls. Mum! Don’t remind me. I was a total control freak even then. It’s probably why I ended up in project coordination. Dad, are you even listening? You’re staring into space. Sorry, love. Just thinking about the price of fertiliser. Ridiculous, it is. Honestly, how are small farms supposed to cope? Anyway, what was that about school fetes? Sounds… energetic. She was amazing! It raised a fortune for the new library books. But back to your work, dear. Is it just the workload, or is there something else bothering you with this job? You sounded a bit…flat. It’s just…Mark. He’s being incredibly vague about his weekend. Said he was “catching up with mates,” but he’s been acting really weird all week. And he’s usually glued to his phone, but it’s been silent. It's just making me jump to conclusions, you know? Men are all the same, aren’t they? Always keeping things bottled up. It wouldn't hurt him to share a bit, would it? Though, I’ve learned over the years, sometimes it's best  not  to ask too many questions. It rarely ends well. Now, George, that’s a bit cynical! Lily, don’t listen to your father. Communication is key, always. Have you tried just asking him directly? Gently? I did, sort of. He just deflected. Said I was being paranoid. It’s just…we’ve been together two years. You’d think I’d be able to trust him. Two years isn’t a long time, in the grand scheme of things. Remember when your mother and I first got together? She thought I was courting the butcher’s daughter for weeks before she realised I was actually writing letters to  her ! Oh, George! Don’t dredge that up again. It was a misunderstanding! And perfectly innocent. You were terrible at expressing yourself back then. This is why I needed a family catch-up. I just needed to vent.

… honestly, the butternut squash risotto is just  never  quite right. I think I overcook the rice every single time. It’s supposed to be al dente, isn't it? Not… mush. Al dente, yes. Though you know, nobody’s ever complained. You're a bit of a perfectionist, love. It always tastes lovely. More importantly, how was your appraisal? You were sounding a bit fraught this morning. Ugh. Standard. Lots of “meets expectations,” a vague mention of “opportunities for growth,” and my manager, Susan, using the word “synergy” approximately seventeen times. It felt…pointless. And slightly condescending. Susan, eh? Always a fan of corporate buzzwords, that one. Did you at least manage to argue for a bit of training? You were talking about that transcription software course. I did, actually. Got it approved! Starts next month. Fingers crossed it’ll make things a bit less…tedious. Speaking of tedious, I saw they’ve finally opened that new Marks and Spencer down by the station. Oh, really? I hadn’t noticed. Is it any good? They do a rather good meal deal, don’t they? Useful for lunches. Apparently. I was mainly scoping out the food hall. They’ve got those little sourdough pizzas, the ones you can cook in the oven. Seemed rather tempting. Though I did eye up a particularly handsome looking piece of salmon. Thinking maybe that with roasted vegetables… Ooh, salmon sounds good. Better than mushy risotto, definitely. And speaking of Marks and Spencer, did you see that article about their new commitment to equine welfare? Apparently, they’re being really strict with their suppliers about horse meat traceability. Good. It’s a horrific thought, isn’t it? Absolutely dreadful. Honestly, some of the things people get away with… Right, I’m going to wrestle with this rice again. Distraction tactics clearly aren’t working. Have you done the crossword today? Just the cryptic clues. Stuck on 17 down. “Murky pool concealing head of state .” Any ideas? Hmm… sounds like…bog? With a 'R' for Rex? Bog… Rex… That’s brilliant! You’ve cracked it! Honestly, you're a crossword genius. You should be doing them for a living. Don't be silly. I'm already paid to listen to people ramble for eight hours a day. So, you remember that bottle of Rioja we got for our anniversary, fourteen years ago? I found it in the back of the cupboard.

… honestly, I just don’t  get  why everyone’s so obsessed with platform heels right now. Me ankles are screaming just thinkin’ about ‘em. Oh, come on, love! They’re dead glamorous! You gotta suffer for fashion, don’t ya? I got a pair of silver ones, proper sparkly. Wore 'em last week and felt like a queen, I did. I think it depends where you’re goin’. If you’re just poppin’ to the shops, flat shoes are sensible. Nobody wants a twisted ankle on a Saturday afternoon. But for a night out… yeah, a bit of a heel can make a difference. Aye, Liv’s right, they  are  a bit fab. Though I always end up takin’ mine off halfway through the night. Waste of a good outfit, innit? I got some black ones with a little ankle strap. Thought I was bein’ sensible, but still, murder on the feet. You’re tellin’ me! I tried ‘em once, proper tiny little heel, didn’t think it’d be too bad. Limped home. Absolutely limped. I’m more of a chunky boot girl, meself. Practical  and  stylish. See! Exactly! I’m with ya, Wakefield lass. Boots are life. And honestly, I'm already dreading tonight. I’ve nothin’ to wear. I thought I had a good black top, but then I remembered I spilled red wine down it last month. Proper mortified when I saw it. Oh, babe, that’s tragic! You always look gorgeous, though. Don’t stress! What about that blue dress you wore to Sarah’s? The one with the little flowers? Nah, washed it and it shrunk. It looks like somethin’ a doll would wear now. Plus, it’s freezin’ tonight. I'm considering wearing leggings under a dress, but that feels… desperate, doesn't it? Leggings under a dress is totally fine! Everyone does it. It’s practical. And layer up with a nice coat. You won't be lookin' desperate, you'll be lookin' sensible. Are we still meeting at The Lion’s Den? Aye, that’s the plan. I'm wearin' me new jeans and a sparkly top. Hopin’ I don't spill anythin’  on  me top, mind. I’m clumsy as owt. I’m also thinkin’ I might attempt the heels again. For the first hour, at least. You’ll regret that, trust me. Just stick to the boots, love. And honestly, don't worry too much about what you’re wearin’.

…Honestly, it's just  exhausting  being the one who remembers everything. Not just work stuff for Mr. Henderson, but birthdays, anniversaries, even when the boiler is due a service. It feels like I’m permanently holding the whole family together. You wouldn’t believe the state of his calendar sometimes.      You’ve always been organised, love. It’s one of the things I… well, one of the things I admire about you. Though, yes, I can see how it’d be draining. You're a proper earth mother, aren’t you? Grounded, practical. Unlike me, floating around in the clouds thinking about… I don’t know… Roman bathhouses.      Roman bathhouses? What on earth prompted  that ?      Just had a thought. Imagine throwing a party, a proper knees-up, but set in Hadrian’s Wall, during its heyday. Toilets would be a bit of an issue, admittedly, but think of the atmosphere! Legionnaires, philosophers, decent wine... you'd  have  to organise the catering, naturally.      You are incorrigible. A Roman themed party? That sounds… chaotic. And sticky. No, thank you. I’m quite happy with a simple barbecue if we ever manage to have one without it raining. Though, you know, sometimes I wonder if there’s someone out there who  gets  this need to organise, to care for things… a proper soulmate. Not just a companion, but someone who instinctively understands.      Hmm. Soulmates. I used to think it was all a load of old rubbish, frankly. But then I met you.      Oh, don't start with the romantic clichés! You were considerably charmed by my ability to make a decent shepherd’s pie, if memory serves.      That was a contributing factor, yes. But there was…a sense of rightness. Like two bits of a slightly wonky puzzle fitting together. Though, to be fair, you've always been far more… spiritually inclined than I am. Remember that weekend in Glastonbury? You were practically levitating by the Tor.      It wasn’t levitating! It was a strong connection to the land. I felt… something. And you were complaining about the mud and the overpriced crystals. Honestly, sometimes I think you’re deliberately resistant to anything remotely… unseen.      I’m a pragmatist, darling. I deal in bits and bytes, not auras. Though, I’ll admit, that woman reading palms at the festival was scarily accurate about my aunt Mildred’s bunions.      See! Even you have to acknowledge something!

…Honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork is ridiculous. They’re introducing  another  new system next quarter. Honestly, you’d think they’d focus on making the current ones work before inventing more! It’s all about appearances, isn't it? "Modernising," they call it.      Sounds stressful, Sarah. Is it impacting your team much? You always seem to take it all in your stride, but even  you  must have your limits.      It always does, doesn't it? Adds another layer of…well, frankly, pointless busywork. Though, to be fair, our department are being spared the worst of it this time. More aimed at Sales and Marketing, apparently. Which explains the glum look on your face!      Spare me the mercy, Angela! It's not the  doing  I mind, it's the constant upheaval. You get everyone trained, then  bam , a new process. And the training, oh the training! It’s all online modules now, too. Feels so impersonal. Still, at least it pays the bills. Speaking of which, Maisie, how's the little craft business going? Last I heard you were having trouble sourcing yarn.      It’s…okay. Slow. People are feeling the pinch, I think. Plus, everyone suddenly decided to knit during lockdown, so the market’s a bit saturated now. I’ve started doing custom orders, which helps, like little baby blankets and things. I'm thinking of offering workshops – teach people to knit, you know?      That's a really good idea, Maisie! Utilise your skills. It's far more satisfying than churning out endless scarves for nobody. Remember that awful purple acrylic I bought you for your 18th? Dreadful stuff.       Ugh , don't remind me! I think my nan still has some remnants of that nightmare. It's funny, isn't it, how different things are now? Everyone’s so…global. I was chatting to someone online about knitting patterns the other day, and she was from Japan. We were discussing the differences in stitch tension and yarn weights.      It's fascinating, the way culture influences even something like knitting. It's all about tradition, isn't it? Makes you wonder about language too. I was reading something about how certain cultures don't even  have  words for colours we readily identify.      That’s right! And the stereotyping that goes along with it all. People assuming things about you based on your accent, or where you’re from. I get ‘country bumpkin’ vibes  immediately  when I'm down in London.

… honestly, I just don’t get why Liam’s being so cagey about the house next year. He keeps saying “options are open” but ‘options open’ usually means he’s already secretly decided and doesn't want to tell us. Proper Northern passive-aggression, that is. Liam's always been a bit of a mystery, innit? Though, to be fair, house hunting in this place is a nightmare. Everything’s either falling apart or costs a fortune. Remember Sarah trying to find somewhere last year? The state of that kitchen she showed us… looked like a bomb had gone off. Oh god,  don’t  remind me. It was covered in, like, ancient baked-on something. I’m still having nightmares. And it was £120 a week! You’d think for that you'd get at least functioning appliances. So, where's he looking, do you know? Anywhere near town? 'Cos I really don’t fancy another year of bus journeys. He mumbled something about Abbey Road. Which is…miles out. Miles! I'd rather live back in Furness, honestly. At least I knew where the chippy was. And my mum would do me laundry. Abbey Road? Seriously? He'll be spending his whole student loan on transport. Listen, I booked that table at Nando’s for Friday, by the way. Celebrating finally finishing that dreadful essay on… what  was  that essay on again? Something about tax policies? My brain’s fried. The impact of quantitative easing on disposable income, if I remember correctly. Absolutely soul-destroying. I spent three hours just trying to understand ‘fiscal drag’. Sounds like something from a horror film, doesn’t it? Fiscal drag! That’s brilliant. Sounds like something you’d get stuck in quicksand doing. Right, Nando's is good. I'm starving. Talking of money, has anyone figured out how self-assessment actually  works ? I’m pretty sure I earned enough from that summer job to actually need to do one, and I have absolutely no idea where to start. Oh, man, don't even. I’ve been avoiding it. My older brother did mine last year, said it's a proper headache. Apparently, if you mess it up, HMRC come after you like vultures. He keeps going on about allowances and tax codes… it’s all Greek to me. I think the Uni does a free workshop on it next week. I saw a leaflet.

… honestly, the library's just a joke at the moment. Packed every single desk, you can't even  breathe  let alone concentrate. It's worse than the 505 bus at rush hour, and that's saying something, eh Mum? Oh, the 505. Don’t get me started. Remember when young Jamie here tried to sneak onto that bus without a ticket? Nearly had a heart attack, I did. And you wanting to go to uni… Bolton to… where was it again, Leeds? Is that still the plan, love? Yeah, Leeds. Still the plan. It’s just… stressful, trying to get the work done. And expensive! I saw someone with a genuinely amazing tattoo yesterday though, a full sleeve. Proper artistry. Thinking maybe I'll get something small when I finish my degree, as a reward. A tattoo? Really? Won’t Dad go mental? He still moans about me getting my ears pierced. Your father is… cautious. He worries. It's what dads do. A small tattoo won’t be the end of the world, Jamie. Though perhaps consider something tasteful. No skulls or dragons, eh? Speaking of stressful, I’ve just finished a project with a supermarket chain. Trying to optimise their delivery routes... Honestly, the logistics are insane. More complicated than a maternity ward, ironically. Oh, don’t I know it! That's a fair comparison, actually. Speaking of which, hospital's been mad busy. Had three inductions last night, all back to back. Exhausting. Though, a lovely young couple, expecting their first. Makes it all worthwhile. One of them was scrolling through Facebook the whole labour though. Said she was ‘live updating her mates’. Honestly! Seriously? While  in  labour? That’s… dedication, I suppose. Or madness. Sounds mad. Mrs. Peterson said Facebook is just people showing off. She said it's why everyone feels rubbish about their own lives. There’s some truth to that, young man. It’s curated reality. Anyway, this Istrian food is fantastic. It's a million miles away from the grey drizzle and supermarket sandwiches back home. Remember when we all used to go to that little Italian place on Bradshawgate, Mum? Before they closed it down? Oh, Luigi’s! That was a treat. Little gem it was. Best lasagne in Bolton, I swear. It’s a shame they didn’t last. So, Leeds, then? Have you looked at houses yet? Shared houses, I mean?

…and honestly, Doreen, the cream teas weren’t  that  good. All hype, I tell ya. Proper clotted cream's gotta be thick enough to stand a spoon up in, and theirs was… well, runny. Like double cream pretending. Oh, Arthur, you’re always a bit of a grumble-bum about the food, aren’t you? I thought they were lovely. Especially with a nice pot of Earl Grey. But it wasn’t the food I wanted to talk about, was it? It was about young Mark and that volunteering. Yeah, he really threw himself into it, didn't he? The YHA in St Ives. Said it was brilliant, even with the early starts helping with the breakfast rush. Met some right characters, apparently. St Ives. Lovely place. Went there years ago with your mother, Margaret did. Proper artist’s colony even then. Though it weren't half as crowded. Remember that little lighthouse? Tiny thing, hardly bigger than a shed. But the view… proper spectacular. Oh, the one on the island? Yes, I remember you showing me pictures. You were obsessed with lighthouses for a while, weren’t you, Arthur? Still am, mind you! They’re beacons of hope, they are. Literally and figuratively. Reminds me of… well, never you mind. Old history. Mark was talking about a cycling race they had nearby. “Yorkshire in a Day” he called it. Apparently it was bonkers – cyclists going up and down these incredible hills. He didn't participate, thankfully. Said he was happy enough cheering from the sidelines with a pasty. Sounds exhausting. He’s got energy for days though, that boy. It’s good to see him doing something worthwhile. You know, it’s a long way to cycle, but proper lovely countryside though, Yorkshire. We took little Emily there once, years ago. She was fascinated by the sheep. Sheep. Now there’s a topic. Spent an hour trying to explain to a tourist down in Cornwall the difference between a Suffolk and a Dorset. She just looked at me like I'd grown a second 'ead. People don't appreciate a good breed of sheep anymore. Sounds about right! He sent me some photos, by the way. Loads of them. Coastal paths, beaches, even a picture of him trying – and failing - to catch a crab. Oh, lovely! I must have a look. He's always been terrible at crab catching.

… honestly, I just think he expects me to  know  what he wants. Like, reading minds is part of the job description now, apparently. It’s exhausting, innit? He says he likes ‘adventure’ but then whinges if I suggest going to a new pub. Adventure to him is apparently ordering a different pint. Sounds… complicated. You’re better off with a good kebab, honestly. No ambiguity with a kebab. You know exactly what you’re getting. Donut meat and chips, sorted. None of this ‘emotional labour’ nonsense. Donut meat? Is that… are you even serious, Liam? Though, I get your point. Relationships are a minefield. Especially when people are rubbish at communicating. Chloe, you’ve only been seeing him a few months, right? Don’t bend over backwards trying to decipher his vague pronouncements. Aye, three months. Feels like three years at times. He’s alright, don’t get me wrong. Just… a bit dense, like. Back home, lads just  said  what they wanted. Going for a pint, going for a dance, going to steal someone’s garden gnome – you knew where you stood! This is all subtle hints and passive aggression. Garden gnomes? You used to get up to no good, didn't you, Chloe? Doncaster was a wild place. Oh, don't even start. It was boredom, mostly. Nothing to  do  except cause a bit of mischief. Cambridge is a bit… refined for that sort of thing, isn't it? Although, I did see a rather tempting cherub in a garden on the way here… Don’t even  think  about it. This is a lovely house, and I’d rather not explain to ANON why his garden ornaments are missing. Speaking of lovely things, this lasagne is amazing, ANON. Did you make it from scratch? It is good, yeah. Proper comfort food. Beats my usual beans on toast any day. Though, to be fair, most things do. It’s lovely, really. Thanks ANON. I’m just… distracted by the dating drama. He keeps talking about this ‘future’ and I’m thinking, ‘Hold on a minute, we haven’t even agreed on what takeaway to get yet!’ He’s moving fast, then? Maybe that’s what’s throwing you. You don't need to map out your entire life together after three months. It’s okay to enjoy the present. He’s not  fast , exactly. He just… talks about it like it’s a given.

… honestly, the churros were  life-changing . I’m already craving them. Like, I genuinely considered trying to make them when I got back, but then I remembered how much effort that would be. Oh god, don't. You and baking are…an interesting combination. Did you at least manage to avoid burning the flat down last time you attempted scones? Barcelona sounds amazing though. You were only gone for a weekend, but you look completely refreshed. Better than I’ve seen you in weeks. Weeks! That's harsh. Work’s been…a lot. And yes, the scones are a closed chapter. Officially. Barcelona was just…perfect. Sunshine, tapas, wandering around getting lost. It was exactly what I needed. Did  you  have a good weekend? Just you, pottering about? Pretty chilled, actually. I had a family thing on Saturday – Auntie Brenda's 70th. It was…Brenda. Loud, floral, demanded everyone talk about their bowel movements. Standard. I spent Sunday mostly recovering and finally started watching that new true crime documentary everyone's banging on about. Oh, the one about the con artist? Is it good? I’ve been meaning to start it. Though truthfully, after a weekend of sunshine and sangria, I was worried it might be a bit…grim. It's gripping, properly twisted. But yeah, maybe not ideal post-Barcelona vibes. Speaking of which, how was the Gaudi stuff? Did you get to Sagrada Familia? Amazing! Absolutely breathtaking. It's even more incredible in person than in the pictures. I spent ages just staring up at it. Honestly, I’m already thinking about going back. Maybe next year? We should both go! To Barcelona, not just the Sagrada Familia, obviously. Ooh, I’d be up for that! Though, I was also toying with the idea of Paris. It’s been ages since I went, and I really fancy a proper French pastry binge. Paris… that does sound good. Although, I feel like it's always so expensive. Barcelona felt much more…manageable. Although, honestly, my entire budget went on churros and cocktails. Priorities! Rightly so. Anyway, future holidays aside, what are your plans for  this  weekend? Fancy a roast? My mum’s dropped a hint she's making one, and she always makes enough to feed the entire village. A roast sounds  heavenly . Especially after a week of microwave meals. And yes, please! I'll bring the wine, obviously. How’s Ben, by the way?

…and honestly, the paperwork alone was enough to drive anyone to drink. Though, Mrs. Higgins  did  bring in homemade sherry every Friday. Small mercies, I suppose. It was just… endless marking. Endless parent-teacher evenings with parents who clearly blamed  me  for little Tarquin’s inability to grasp fractions. Tarquin. Right. Sounds about right. London schools are… a different beast. Less sherry, more active parental litigation, generally. I used to volunteer at a primary school doing coding workshops. Gave me a whole new respect for teachers. The patience required… it’s superhuman. Patience is definitely a key skill. And a thick skin. I teach history, you see. Year 9s are particularly… opinionated. Especially when you start getting into the Tudors. Everyone's an expert on Henry VIII. Did you always know you wanted to be an entrepreneur, then? Straight out of university? Not exactly. I did a law degree, actually. My parents were, shall we say, keen on a ‘sensible’ career path. But I lasted about six months interning at a city firm. Soul-destroying. So, I chucked it all in and started building websites for small businesses. It spiralled from there. Now I run a digital marketing agency. It’s chaotic, stressful, but…mine. Gosh, that's a leap. Law to websites! Quite the change. I can appreciate wanting something ‘yours’ though. Teaching, you're always working for someone else – the school, the local authority, the government with all its changing policies. It's exhausting trying to navigate it all. And the feeling that you're constantly being assessed… it’s relentless. I bet. The bureaucracy must be horrific. We have our own red tape, obviously, but it's usually self-imposed – trying to stay ahead of Google algorithm updates, for example. Which is arguably less infuriating than dealing with Ofsted inspections, I imagine. What made you go into teaching, then? Always a history buff? Always. My grandfather was a bit of a local historian in Dorchester. He used to take me around the Roman ruins, tell me stories about the English Civil War... It just rubbed off, I suppose. And I genuinely like working with young people, even the Tarquins. When you  do  get through to them, when they suddenly ‘get’ something…that’s a good feeling. Honestly, it's those moments that keep you going. Though, sometimes I fantasize about opening a small bookshop. Quiet life, surrounded by books… A bookshop!

… honestly, I just don’t get ‘im, do you? Liam’s just…  messy . Not like a bit untidy, proper chaotic. I found a sock in the fruit bowl yesterday, a  sock ! Aye, sounds like Liam. He’s always been a bit… free-spirited, hasn't he? Remember when he tried to ‘repurpose’ Mum’s good china as plant pots? Oh, don’t even  start  on the china! I’m still getting nightmares. But it’s the kitchen, isn’t it? It’s always the kitchen. I cleaned it properly this morning, proper scrubbed the counters, and by lunchtime, it looked like a bomb’d gone off. Crumbs  everywhere , dishes piled up… it's exhausting. Well, you know he’s been properly stressed with the essay deadlines. He’s been living on coffee and biscuits, probably just doesn’t notice the state of things. That’s what I  tell  myself, love. I do. But it’s been like this since September! Before the deadlines were even a thing. It’s not just the mess, either. He leaves his stuff absolutely  everywhere . I practically navigate an obstacle course to get to the sofa. Right, the ‘Liam Zone’ expanding again, is it? Expanding and conquering! I swear, he’s gradually claiming the whole flat as his personal space. I feel like a lodger in my own home. And Sarah's even worse, isn't she? Leaving her art supplies all over the living room. Paintbrushes, canvases… it’s like living in a studio. Sarah’s a bit of an artist, innit? Gotta have her space. Though, I’ll grant you, it can be a bit much. I’ve nearly tripped over a sculpture more times than I care to admit. Maybe we all need a rota? Like a proper cleaning schedule, and designated ‘stuff zones’? A rota? Hmm. I’ve tried suggesting things before, but it just… fizzles out. Liam promises to do his washing up, then it’s still there three days later. Sarah says she’ll tidy her paints, then it’s a colourful explosion again. It's like talking to the wind. They’re both pretty good at promising, aren’t they? Look, maybe we need to be a bit more direct. Not ‘suggest’ things, actually  ask  them to do stuff, and explain why it bothers you. Less ‘it would be nice if…’ and more ‘Hey, could you please clear your stuff up?

…and honestly, Doreen, the price of a loaf these days! Used to be, you could get a decent sliced white for, what, twenty pence? Twenty pence! Now it's pushing fifty, easy. Fifty! It’s daylight robbery, it is. Oh, don't get me started, Arthur. I nearly choked in Sainsbury's. Five pounds ninety-nine for a leg of lamb! Five ninety-nine! I remember your mother getting a beautiful leg of lamb for… well, I couldn’t possibly say, it was so long ago, but it certainly wasn’t six pounds. Mother was a wizard in the kitchen, she was. Made a feast out of nowt, she did. Not like now, everything packaged up, pretending it’s fancier than it is. And smaller portions, mind you. Everything's smaller. You barely get enough biscuits in a packet for a proper cuppa. Exactly! And the quality...it's not what it was. I bought some tomatoes, looked lovely and red, but they tasted of absolutely nothing. Watery as anything. I told young Peter – that's Mrs. Higgins' grandson, I’m still doing a bit for her, you know – I said, "Peter, these tomatoes have seen better days, love." He just shrugged. Young people don’t seem to notice things like that anymore. No, they don’t. All glued to those blinking phones, they are. Didn’t even look at the apples. I tried to get some Coxes, proper Norfolk Coxes, but they only had those shiny, imported things. All taste the same, don't they? Like wax. Ugh, dreadful. I did find some nice mushrooms though, for your omelette tomorrow. I remembered how you like them sautéed with a bit of thyme. Ah, you always remember. You’re a good ‘un, Doreen. A real good ‘un. Makes all the difference, a proper omelette. Sets me up for the day. Though I still think I could’ve got cheaper eggs at the market. Should have persevered, but my back was playing up. Don't push yourself, Arthur. Your health is more important than a few pennies off eggs. Besides, the market was absolutely heaving. Full of tourists. All wanting ‘local produce’ at bargain prices. The irony! Tourists. Gawd bless ‘em, but they do clog things up. Still, good for the economy, I suppose. Though I doubt much of that money ends up with folk like us. Did you get the washing powder?

…and honestly, lad, the state of some of those papers this year. You wouldn’t  believe  the number of students who thought pi was 3.1416, and then rounded it to… 3.1! Three point one! After all this time, still. It’s disheartening, it really is.      Right. Sounds… stressful. Is that why you were muttering about ‘irrational numbers’ at breakfast?      Aye, well, stressful  and  frustrating. They're irrational for a reason, aren't they? They go on forever! It's a key concept!      Oh, numbers. Always were a bother to me. Give me a good gossip any day. Though young Thomas, your dad, he was always good with figures. Used to balance the books for old Mrs. Higgins down the road, even after he retired from the docks.      Aye, he was. Clever lad. Though didn’t have the patience for explaining it to anyone. Said it was like trying to teach a pig to sing - wasted effort.      Grandad! That’s a bit harsh.      It's just a saying, lad! No offense meant to anyone. Speaking of wasted effort, are we still on for the bingo tonight, Margaret? My lucky dabber’s calling to me.      We are, Arthur. Though I’m warning you, Doris next door has been practicing. She’s got a new pair of glasses and claims to see the numbers before they even come up.      Doris and her glasses! She thinks she’s psychic. She told me last week I’d meet a tall, dark stranger. All I met was the postman, and he’s got a bit of a limp, poor lad.      Maybe the postman  is  your tall, dark stranger, Grandma! You just need to look closer.      Don’t be daft. He’s delivering bills, not romance. Now, have you made arrangements for getting us back to Hull later, Eileen? My legs are starting to ache.      Of course, love. I’ve asked young David – the lad with the taxi, remember? He’s picking us up at six. It’s a bit of a drive, but better than relying on the buses, especially this time of day.      Good, good. Buses are full of youngsters these days, glued to their… whatchamacallits? Phones, that's it. No respect for their elders.      They’re just… communicating, Grandad. It’s how we all talk now.      He's right, Arthur. It's different, but it's not necessarily disrespectful. Although, sometimes I wish they’d look up and appreciate the world around them.

…Honestly, it’s just  marketing . All this ‘superfood’ bollocks. My Nan sent me a link to some spirulina stuff, said it'd cure my ‘low energy’.
