Honestly, Nan, I'm a student, low energy is the  default  setting.      Spirulina? Sounds grim. My mum’s gone down the collagen route. Says it’s the secret to looking young. She’s started putting it in her coffee. It just looks…wrong. Like a cloudy, slightly unsettling coffee.      Collagen's alright, innit? I mean, it's just protein. Though, the price of it is ridiculous. You’re basically paying a fortune for…bone dust.      You lot are all obsessed with trying to fix yourselves. I just try and go to the gym a couple of times a week. Keeps the existential dread at bay, mostly. Did anyone catch that new fitness tracker review on TechRadar? The one about the Aura Ring? Seems a bit pricey, but the sleep tracking is apparently insane.      Aura Ring? Sounds a bit…much, doesn't it? I'm happy enough with just knowing I’m tired. Plus, thinking about every single metric of your life sounds exhausting. Speaking of exhausting, how’s dissertation going, Liam? You were looking proper stressed last week.      It’s…a slog. Trying to find sources on early medieval land ownership is surprisingly difficult. It’s all arguments and interpretations. No hard facts. And Professor Davies is just  relentless  with the feedback. He’s proper detail-oriented, which is good, I suppose, but…draining.      Davies is a legend though, yeah? Proper scholar. Ruthless, but a legend. I had him for a seminar last year. He spotted a dodgy footnote from a mile off. Absolutely roasted someone.      Roasted? Harsh! My tutor’s alright. Bit of a soft touch, to be honest. Which is probably why I'm still three weeks behind on my readings. Still, better than your Nan pushing algae on you, Liam.      Honestly, it's the thought that counts. She means well. She just gets all her information from Facebook now. Last week it was magnetic bracelets for arthritis.      My Grandad got sucked into that magnetic bracelet thing. Spent a fortune. Didn't do a thing. He then tried one of those posture correctors – ended up looking like a robot. It was hilarious, but also slightly sad.      Sounds about right. My Uncle Barry tried one of those online language learning courses. Swore he was going to be fluent in Spanish by Christmas.

… honestly, I just don’t get why they’re  all  in here now. It's like opening the windows was an invitation. Proper nuisance, they are. It’s the time of year, love. They come in for the warmth. And you know, they don’t half bother young Leo here, do they? He's a right softie when it comes to anything with legs. Mum! I am  not  a softie! I just… don’t like things crawling on me. Especially not those flying ones. They’re really fast. Sounds like the urban wildlife is making its presence felt. Bit different from the pigeons in Trafalgar Square, I’ll grant you. Pigeons are bad enough, Geoff! At least you can  see  them coming. These little flies… they just swoop. Right, shopping list. We need fly spray. Definitely. And some of that sudocrem for Leo’s bite, yeah? It’s still proper swollen. Aye, it is. I put some antihistamine cream on it earlier, but he’s still scratching. Sudocrem’s a good shout, calming for the skin. Anything else on this list, or are we just building a fortress against the insect kingdom? Milk, bread, eggs… Oh, and biscuits. Leo's been studying hard for his mocks. He deserves a treat. And those nice tomatoes for the pasta sauce, you know, the plum ones? Thanks, Liv. I  am  working hard, you know! History is a nightmare. All those dates… It's all about context, Leo. Think of it as a story, not just a list of dates. Makes it a bit more palatable. Speaking of stories, did you see the match yesterday? United absolutely battered City. Don’t even start, Geoff. I refuse to acknowledge that result. It was a fluke. A complete and utter fluke. And the referee… don’t talk to me about the referee. Oh, leave it, love. You'll give yourself a headache. It’s just football. Though I will say, that Rashford lad is something special. Yeah, he was amazing! I was cheering so loud my nan told me to be quiet. Good lad! It’s good to have passion, Leo. That’s what football's all about. Right, back to the list. Do we need anything for tea tomorrow? I was thinking a roast. Ooh, a roast sounds good. Chicken? And we’ll need potatoes, carrots, parsnips… and gravy granules, definitely gravy granules. Can’t have a roast without proper gravy.

…and honestly, Miss Davies just  stared  at me. Like I’d grown a second head! All I said was that the mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell, but apparently, I said it with “insufficient enthusiasm.” Insufficient enthusiasm! What does that even  mean  in biology? Oh my god, that’s so Miss Davies. She’s obsessed with ‘enthusiasm’ for everything. Remember when she marked Liam down for not being “sufficiently animated” when describing photosynthesis? He was literally drawing a diagram. Exactly! It's ridiculous. And then she gave a shout-out to Chloe for her "passion for cellular respiration." Chloe was just repeating what she’d read from a revision guide! She didn’t even  look  passionate. She totally favours the people who just parrot back what she wants to hear. Ugh, P.E. was awful today too. Mr. Harrison made us do shuttle runs  again . My legs are still screaming. Shuttle runs are the worst. Honestly, I think he just enjoys watching us suffer. Did you see Amelia nearly collapse? I did! She went bright red. I tried not to laugh, but it was hard. Speaking of Amelia, have you seen her Instagram lately? She’s totally obsessed with that new beauty guru, Lily Bloom. Lily Bloom? Oh, the one with the ridiculously long eyelashes? Yeah, Amelia's been posting stories of her trying all Lily’s makeup tutorials. It’s a bit much, isn't it? A bit. But it's kind of clever, actually. Amelia's getting loads of likes. She’s proper strategic, that one. I’m still stuck on 200 followers, it’s depressing. Don't worry about followers! I've barely posted anything this week. I’ve been too busy trying to understand quadratic equations. Mr. Evans is convinced we all suddenly understand them after one lesson. Mr. Evans thinks we’re all maths geniuses. He’s living in a fantasy world. Did you hear what happened with Finn in history? No! What? He’s usually so quiet. He apparently asked Mr. Peterson if Henry VIII had Instagram. No way! Seriously? I swear! Mr. Peterson’s face was priceless. Apparently, he just paused, then said, “That is…an interesting question, Finn.” Then he moved on. Oh Finn. He’s a legend. Have you seen that new YouTuber, ‘ScienceSimplified’? She makes explaining tricky stuff actually… well, simplified! ScienceSimplified? No, I haven't. Is she any good? I usually just watch Emma Chamberlain, but I need to catch up on some revision soon.

… honestly, I think it’s just a proper bug. Not like a ‘poor me, feeling sorry for myself’ cold, but a proper, chesty, can’t-breathe-through-your-nose cold. I feel absolutely wiped. Aw, pet. You do sound rough. You’ve been moaning all day. Did you take any Lemsip? I brought some back from Mum’s last time. She swears by the honey and lemon one. Aye, I had some. It took the edge off for about ten minutes, then BAM, back to feeling like I've swallowed a bag of gravel. It’s just…dragging. Remember that time I had that food poisoning in Italy? This feels almost similar, just in my head instead of my stomach. Oh god, Italy. That was  bad . You were green for three days. Honestly, I thought you were going to need to be hospitalised. This doesn’t sound that severe though, does it? Just a bit grim. Have you checked your temperature? Yeah, it's hovering around 37.8. Not massively worrying, but enough to make me feel rubbish. Makes you think doesn’t it? With everything going on, every sniffle feels like the start of something catastrophic. It does, doesn’t it? The constant low-grade anxiety. They’re pushing the updated vaccinations now, you know. I saw an email from the university about it. Might be worth thinking about, even just to rule things out. I keep meaning to look into that. It’s just…hospitals, even the thought of them, give me the creeps. All that disinfectant and people being poorly. It’s a bit much. I get that. It’s not a pleasant place to be. Though they're brilliant, aren't they? When you  need  them. Remember your nan last year? They were amazing with her. They were, yeah. They really were. But even watching that show on TV last night – that medical drama – it just got me thinking. They showed a scene where they were analysing body language, trying to figure out if a patient was concealing something. It was fascinating! Oh, really? What were they looking for? All sorts! Micro-expressions, pupil dilation, how people positioned their feet… apparently, there's a whole field dedicated to it. Makes you wonder how much of what people  say  is actually true versus what their bodies are telling you. They had these cameras everywhere, recording everything. A bit Orwellian if you ask me.

Right. “Quixotic.” Twenty-two points. Honestly, Dad, you let me have the ‘X’. I suspect a little favouritism. Nonsense, Eleanor. Purely strategic. It blocked a potential ‘jazz’ for your mother there, didn't it, Margaret? Always has a nose for a good jazz score, she does. It did, actually. Though I was eyeing up a decent use of that ‘J’ myself. This board is remarkably congested. It’s like the car park at the Trafford Centre on a Saturday. Utter gridlock. You’re not wrong there. Spent a good hour just circling yesterday, trying to find a space for those Christmas presents. Honestly, it's quicker to walk. Tell me about it. I tried to pop in for a loaf of sourdough, ended up abandoning the car and just getting a pre-packaged one from the garage. Shameful, really. Though, speaking of bread, did anyone manage to get a decent bit of sausage from Barker’s this morning? The queue was practically out the door. I did, thankfully. Got there just before nine. Old Mr. Henderson was already serving, looking rather grumpy as usual. He remembers when you didn’t need to queue for ten minutes just to get a Cumberland. Ah, Barker's. A Manchester institution. Reminds me of old school days. Though, the queues weren't so bad when  I  was buying luncheon vouchers. Everything was different then. It’s just… everyone seems to want everything  now . No patience anymore. Sarah was showing me some photos on Facebook this morning - someone complaining about a five-minute wait for a coffee! Five minutes! Facebook. Don’t get me started. It’s just an endless stream of people documenting their perfectly curated lives. I saw Auntie Brenda put up photos of her new kitchen. Granite worktops. Obviously. Brenda always did favour the finer things. Though she did send me a lovely card for my birthday. She remembers, at least. Unlike some… . Hey! I sent a text! Technology, Margaret. It's the future. Though, I did see an interesting article in  Record Collector  magazine this week, about a limited edition reissue of a John Peel session. That's proper culture. Oh,  Record Collector ? You and your vinyl. You’d think in this day and age you’d be streaming, but no. You must have the  physical  object. There's something satisfying about holding a record, Eleanor. The artwork, the weight of it...

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of people at those Drupa exhibitions was breathtaking. Absolutely breathtaking. Not like anything you’d see at a little county fair, mind you. It was… international. Everyone wanting to see what was new. Drupa. Goodness me. That brings back memories. Though I was usually on the, shall we say, less glamorous side of things. The technical demonstrations, mostly. Not the flashy presentations. Still, a vital part, wouldn’t you agree? Oh, absolutely vital! All the glitz in the world doesn’t matter if the blasted thing doesn’t  work , does it? You were the ones making sure it did, I expect. I was all about the… the presentation. Making it look appealing. We had a proper stand, you know, all done in chrome and glass. Very futuristic for the time. Late seventies, wasn’t it, when we really started making waves? Seventy-eight, I think. The Heidelberg deal. That was the big one. Before that, it was just… tinkering, really. Years of tinkering and persuading people that offset printing could be automated. They all thought I was mad, you know. Wanting to replace skilled lithographers with machines! Oh, I remember you mentioning that. A bit of a battle, wasn’t it? But you were right, of course. Always looking ahead, you were. Honestly, your systems… they revolutionised the industry. I sold a good few to publishers, myself. Very high-end stuff. Profit margins were lovely. Well, it wasn’t just me. Brilliant engineers. But yes, I had the initial idea. And the Germans, bless them, they really  got  it. They took a chance. I spent a good six months a year in Germany for a while, demonstrating the prototypes, ironing out the kinks. Mostly in Düsseldorf and Frankfurt. Düsseldorf! I did a few smaller art fairs there. Not the same scale as Drupa, naturally. But the Germans… they appreciate quality. They don’t suffer fools gladly. Which I admired. You had to be prepared, you know? Have your facts straight, your arguments solid. None of this… waffling. Precisely! No waffling. They wanted to see the numbers, the speed, the reliability. German engineers are methodical. Very methodical. We had one particularly challenging exhibition in Frankfurt. The central processing unit kept overheating. Honestly, I thought my career was over. Oh dear! How dreadful. It was. We were about to pull the plug, admit defeat. Then, a young technician – bless his heart – realised the ventilation system hadn't been properly connected.

… honestly, Mr. Davies, it’s just  so  pointless learning all these declensions in Latin. Like, what good is knowing how a noun changes form gonna do me in life? It’s not like I'm gonna be writing speeches to the Roman Senate! Now, now, Ella. Don't knock it ‘til you’ve tried it. It's not about the Roman Senate, it's about understanding  how  language works. And Latin’s the root of so much English, you wouldn’t believe. Think about ‘aquifer’ – directly from Latin, meaning ‘water bearer’. Where d’you think they got that from, eh? Yeah, but we learn the word ‘aquifer’ in Geography, not Latin! And it's all stuff you can just… look up. Google it. No need to memorise cases. Google didn't exist when  I  was at school, love. And it’s good for your brain, all that memorising. Keeps it sharp. Speaking of sharp brains, have you fully decided what you’re wanting to apply for at uni? You were saying something about Philosophy? Bit different to A-Level English Language, innit? It is. But it’s… interesting. It’s about, like,  why  we think things, and questioning everything. Miss Peterson said it’s good for analytical skills. Which, she says, is useful for everything - even English! Sounds a bit head-scratching to me. All that thinking. Anyway, we’re due a service station stop soon. Need a cuppa, I do. And maybe a sausage butty. Not that quinoa stuff you’re always on about. Honestly, quinoa... what  is  it? Birdseed for posh people? It's a grain, Dad! It's full of protein. You should try it. And it's not posh, it’s just… healthier. Honestly, you'd think after all my science lessons you'd be more open to new things. I’m open to a good steak, that's what I'm open to. Right, coming up to the M5 soon. Cornwall, here we come! Did you remember to pack your bike? I saw a poster for a little race down in Newquay. Yeah, packed! I was looking at that race. Might enter, actually. It's only a ten-mile loop. Actually, talking about Cornwall… do they even  have  proper counties down there? Like, I know Devon and Cornwall, but are there little bits in between? They do, they do. Proper complicated history, that bit. Kernow, they call it – the Cornish name.

… honestly, Dad, you wouldn’t  believe  the catering requests we get at these conferences. One bloke last week, insisted on only organic, gluten-free, vegan everything - and it had to be colour-coded by mealtime! Colour-coded, I tell ya! It's a right palaver. Colour-coded food? Blimey, that’s taking the mick, innit? Sounds like a load of fuss for no reason. I ‘ad a builder once who only wanted builders’ tea, strong as you like, three sugars. That were specific enough for me. Oh, builders and their tea. A constant, that is. Reminds me of old Arthur down the pub, used to say a good brew could solve any problem. Speaking of brews, is that a Yorkshire pudding I smell? Aye, it is! I’m attempting a roast. Trying to bring a little bit of Yorkshire ‘ome to Cambridge. Though the oven ‘ere’s a bit temperamental. It doesn’t get as proper hot, like mam’s does back in Doncaster. Roast's good. Proper comfort food, that. Smells better than anything I usually cook – usually just chucking some pasta on after work. What’s the occasion anyway? Not your birthday, is it? No, no birthday. Just… feeling a bit homesick, I suppose. And Dad's been on about wanting a proper roast since he arrived. Plus, thought it’d be nice to have a proper catch-up. How’s work, Liam? Still hammering away? Yeah, mostly. Got a big job on down by the river, new flats goin’ up. It’s alright. Pays the bills. Though me nan’s been poorly, she’s in hospital with a chest infection. That’s a bit worryin’. Oh dear, that’s not good. Send her our best, lad. And tell her we’re thinkin’ of ‘er. Nans are precious things. I remember my own, bless ‘er, always had a biscuit ready. Definitely. Give her a big hug from us both. And tell her I'm sending a postcard - I always used to send postcards to my nan. It cheered her right up. What about you, Dad? You been keeping busy since…well, since you retired? Busy enough. Mostly just potterin’ in the garden, watching the telly, and getting under everyone’s feet, apparently. Your mother keeps telling me I need a hobby. A  hobby ! I’ve lived seventy years, I’ve got plenty of hobbies – namely, relaxing! Though I did try that online chess… nearly threw the computer out the window.

… honestly, the shift last night was  mental . Stag do. All wanting complicated cocktails they'd seen on Instagram. Like I’m a bloody magician, not a bartender. You wouldn’t believe the requests. Oh dear. Sounds… eventful. Still, better than marking essays, I suppose. Though sometimes I wish my students were as enthusiastically demanding as stag dos. At least  they’re  having fun. Fun for me is when someone just asks for a pint of lager, you know? Less fuss. How’s the teaching going then? Still battling teenagers with dwindling attention spans? It’s a challenge, definitely. This term I’m doing a module on dialectology, actually. Really fascinating. We’ve been looking at how language changes even within relatively small geographic areas. It's made me hyper-aware of accents, which is probably why I noticed yours instantly as properly Brummie. Guilty as charged. Born and bred just down the road, practically. You can’t escape it. My mum still tears me apart if I try to ‘posh it up’ at all. What about you? Bit of a different sound altogether, aren't you? Hertfordshire way? Hitchin, to be precise. It’s... a bit of a melting pot, actually. Lots of London commuters, so the accent's fairly neutral. I think I pick up things. Though my family are proper ‘Hertfordshire’ – quite distinctive, apparently. It’s funny how ingrained it is. Studying language makes you realise how much of your identity is tied to the way you speak. Tell me about it. I got stick at uni for my accent, a bit. Went to Warwick, loads of southerners. Felt like I was translating sometimes. Did a history degree, though, which was a good distraction. Anything to avoid proper work, eh? Ended up pulling pints for a living. Warwick’s lovely, though. But I can imagine a culture shock. History’s brilliant, though. I did my Masters in Applied Linguistics, then a PGCE. It's satisfying, helping people unlock a language. Though it doesn’t pay  amazing . Nah, no way. Teaching’s always undervalued, I reckon. This job’s alright, brings in enough for rent and a bit of football. Speaking of, you following the Villa at all this season? We're actually doing alright, which is a shock to everyone. I try to keep up! My brother’s a huge football fan. I wouldn’t say I’m an expert, but I enjoy a good match.

…and honestly, Doreen, you wouldn’t  believe  the traffic getting ‘ere. Round the A47, just solid. Every Tom, Dick, and ‘Arry tryin’ to get to the coast, I reckon. Though why anyone'd  want  to go to Great Yarmouth in November is beyond me. Still, got your lovely coffee, thank you, Barbara. Lovely and strong, just how I like it. A bit like me, eh? Strong willed. Oh, Arthur, you and your Yarmouth stories! It’s always something with that road. And you are strong-willed, dear, there's no denying that. More stubborn, if I'm honest. Here, have a biscuit. Shortbread. I made 'em myself. Right, while you two are reminiscing about Norfolk gridlock, perhaps we can get back to the donation box? I’ve almost got the base secured, but I’m a bit unsure about the finish. Do we varnish it, or go for a paint? Something bright, I think, to attract attention. Varnish, definitely varnish. Paint’ll peel, won't it? And it needs to last. We’re tryin’ to raise money for bell ringing, not repaint it every six months. Though, Barbara, did you ever get round to lookin’ into those banners? For the village fete? Oh, Arthur, the banners! Yes, I did. Found a company online, quite reasonable, but they require the artwork digitally. I was hoping Derek could sort it, he's so good with computers. I can handle the digital artwork. No problem at all. Just give me the dimensions and a rough idea of the design. We’re aiming for something eye-catching - perhaps a picture of the bells, or the church tower? More importantly, have you decided  where  we’re putting this box? I was thinking outside the post office. Good footfall. Post office is good. Though Old Man Hemmings might complain. He complains if the sun’s shinin’ too bright, that one. Reminds me of me sister, Elsie, always a moan. You know, speaking of complainin’, I was readin’ about that… what’s it called? Munchausen’s Syndrome? Horrible thing. People makin' themselves ill for attention. Honestly, Arthur, one minute you're talking bells and the next it's medical conditions! Where did  that  come from? It's a dreadful illness, of course, but… It’s a bit of a leap, Arthur, don’t you think? We’re trying to focus on fundraising. Perhaps we should also consider a smaller donation tin for the coffee shop?

… honestly, the algorithm is just  feeding  me stuff I’ve already seen. Like, three cat videos in a row? I swear TikTok thinks I live and breathe feline content. It’s infuriating. Seriously? Mine's been alright. Mostly just football highlights and, uh, vaguely concerning DIY stuff. Probably because I spent three hours trying to fix that shelf last weekend. You and that shelf, Liam. It’s become a saga. Though, speaking of concerning content, anyone else actually  enjoy  those really rubbish horror films? The ones where the acting is dreadful, the plot makes no sense, and the special effects look like they were done on a Commodore 64? Oh my god, YES! I live for those. It’s so bad it’s good. Like, I watched one last night, a vampire thing, and the vampire just…sparkled. Regularly. It wasn't  Twilight  sparkly, it was just…dusty glitter. Dusty glitter vampires? That sounds magnificent. Honestly, sometimes I need a break from genuinely scary stuff. Remember when we tried to watch ‘Hereditary’ all together? I was a mess for a week. Don't remind me. I practically hid behind a cushion the entire time. You, Sarah, were totally unflinching. Creepy. Honestly, I'd built up the suspense in my head so much it was kind of a let-down. Though that scene with the…well, you know. Still unsettling. Anyway, how is everyone’s week been? Anya, how are things at work? Still battling spreadsheets? Battling is an understatement. The new system is…optimised for chaos, I think. It takes five clicks to do something that used to take one. I’m seriously considering a career change. Maybe I’ll become a professional sparkly vampire critic. Liam, are you still seeing Chloe? How’s that going? You were pretty keen on her. It's…complicated. She’s lovely, she really is. But she keeps talking about wanting to go backpacking around Southeast Asia for six months next year, and I’ve just been offered a bit more responsibility at work. Feels like we’re on different paths, you know? That  is  tricky. Long-distance backpacking while you’re trying to climb the career ladder. Not exactly compatible. You need to figure out what  you  want, honestly. Don’t get pressured into anything. Totally. Boundaries are important. Speaking of wanting things… I’m already planning my next holiday. Thinking maybe Italy. Florence, Rome, all that.

…No, honestly, Gerald, you wouldn’t  believe  the traffic getting out of Ipswich. Absolute standstill. They’ve got those roadworks again, you see, near the Orwell Bridge. It’s a right bottleneck. Orwell Bridge… aye, always a problem that. Used to be alright, back in the day, but with all these…well, all these  people  now, using the roads. Never used to be like this. Though, mind you, when  I  was driving, used to get stuck behind tractors most of the time, goin’ up to Dereham market. That was a trial. Oh, tractors! You and your Dereham market stories, Gerald. Always the same. Still, Ipswich traffic sounds dreadful, Arthur. Were you driving the Volvo? I was, yes. Old Bess. She handled it alright, bless her. But she’s getting on, just like me, truth be told. Fifty-seven thousand miles she’s done now. I reckon another year or two, and I’ll have to start thinkin’ about…well, you know. Replacing ‘er? Good luck with that. New cars are all computers now, not proper engineering. Give me a Ford Cortina any day! Something you could  fix  yourself. None of this pluggin’ a diagnostic tool in. Exactly! Though, the Volvo’s quite comfortable, I must say. Good seats. That’s important for a long drive. Took me nearly two and a half hours, door to door. What’s the hold-up getting  you  home, then, Margaret? Is David driving? David is, yes. Though he’s got that little Fiat now. Honestly, Arthur, it’s like sitting in a shoebox! Keeps going on about fuel efficiency, but I feel terribly vulnerable in it. And he insists on using the sat nav even for roads he knows perfectly well. Sat navs! Another curse. They send you down lanes not fit for a bicycle. Last time I trusted one, it got me stuck behind a farm. Had to reverse for a good quarter of a mile! And they never account for roadworks, do they? Never! Back in my day, we had maps. Proper Ordnance Survey maps. You  learned  the roads. Knew every twist and turn. Now everyone relies on a little plastic box telling ‘em where to go. Losing a skill, that is. Honestly. It's true. Though David says they're always updating the maps. Says it's efficient. I still prefer a good old map, myself. Reminds me of holidays with your mother, Arthur, spreading a map across the bonnet of the car.

…and honestly, the thought of packing  another  box fills me with dread. Birmingham was bad enough, but this move to Cheshire… it’s a whole new level of ‘stuff’ isn’t it? Thirty years in one house, you accumulate things. Things you don’t even  remember  owning.      Tell me about it. Even helping  you  pack felt like an archaeological dig. Honestly, Mum, you had Christmas decorations from the nineteen-eighties still in their original boxes.      They were perfectly good decorations! Just… vintage. And don’t ‘Mum’ me, Aoife, you’re nearly forty yourself now.      Vintage is a polite word for ancient, Mary. Though I have to say, seeing all those old photos during the clear-out was lovely. Brought back a few memories, even for me.      It did, didn’t it? Though honestly, looking at photos of our holidays… airports! Oh, the  stress  of airports. I'm not getting any younger for queuing, you know. Remember that one in Malaga, Liam? The one where they lost your luggage?      Don't remind me. Three days in Spain wearing practically the same clothes. And the customer service was atrocious. Honestly, I think the chap at the lost luggage desk actively enjoyed my misery.      It's always the same. Promise of a smooth journey, and then everything goes sideways. I had a delayed flight to Barcelona last year, ended up sleeping on the floor of Gatwick. Not my finest hour. They offered a voucher for a sandwich, can you believe it?      A sandwich! For ruining your holiday! The cheek! That’s why I'm leaning towards trains more and more. More comfortable, you can actually  see  the countryside, and no baggage allowance headaches. Although, getting to Manchester Piccadilly then onward… that's a bit of a faff.      You'll get used to it. Cheshire’s well-connected, even if it involves a change here and there. We'll sort it out. Speaking of sorting, have you thought about getting rid of the old Volvo, Mary? It's a lovely car, but it's... well, it's seen better days.      Now, Liam, don’t you start on the Volvo. She’s a perfectly reliable car! A bit thirsty, admittedly, but reliable. I've had that car fifteen years. It's got sentimental value.      Dad has a point, Mum. You barely use it anymore, mostly because you’re worried about the M6. A smaller car would be easier to manoeuvre, and better on the fuel, especially with all the driving you'll be doing visiting us.

…and then Mr. Henderson just  looked  at me, all stern, and said, "Honestly, Bethany, you’re spending far too much time on that TikTok. It'll rot your brain, you know." Honestly, Mum, it's not  that  bad! Everyone’s on it. Mr. Henderson. Right, the geography teacher with opinions on everything. He sounds delightful. But he’s not entirely wrong, sweetheart. Everything in moderation. Although… I have rather good news, actually. About something a bit more pressing than TikTok. Oh? What? Is it about college? Have you heard back from anywhere yet? I’m stressing, honestly. I really want to get into Brighton. Not yet, love. College applications are a whole other saga for another day. This is… well, remember your bike? The one that vanished last month? Luna! Oh,  no way . You found it?! Seriously? Where was it? I thought it was gone forever! I was so gutted. I loved that bike. I did! Well, sort of. PC Davies called this morning. They’d recovered a bike matching Luna’s description during a routine stop-check down near the West Marina. Apparently, a lad was trying to sell it to someone. No way! Trying to  sell  it? The cheek! Was it…was it obvious it was mine? Did it have all my stickers still on? It did. And the little bell you insisted on, the one that sounds like a tiny sheep. That was a dead giveaway, apparently. They questioned the boy, but he claimed he "bought it off someone" and didn’t know it was stolen. Classic, isn’t it? Ugh. Seriously. I bet it’s one of those kids who hang around the skatepark. They’re always eyeing up everyone’s bikes. Was it damaged? Is it okay? Thankfully, no. A little dusty, and the tyre pressure was low, but otherwise, it seems to be in good condition. I’ve arranged to pick it up this afternoon. I thought we could maybe cycle along the front afterwards? Get some fish and chips? YES! Oh, Mum, that’s amazing! I can’t believe it. I thought I was going to have to save up for ages to get another one. Luna and me have been on so many adventures. Remember that time we cycled all the way to Camber Sands? How could I forget? You were absolutely exhausted on the way back. Complaining about every hill! And insisting on stopping for ice cream every five minutes.

Right, I officially surrender. Rhys is a  monster  at Ticket to Ride. Honestly, building routes across the whole of bloody England before anyone else... it’s just not fair. Now, now, Sarah. Don't be a sore loser. It’s tactical, that’s all. You were distracted, weren't you? Talking about the logistics of getting a decent Full English down here. Distracted by the  important  things, you mean. A good fry-up is non-negotiable on a country break. Especially when the closest thing to a proper café is… well, another twenty minutes drive. You boys and your preoccupation with breakfast! I remember when I was stationed in Singapore, a Full English was a legendary quest. You’d pay a fortune for one that vaguely resembled the real thing. Thankfully, Hereford is somewhat better equipped. Oh, Singapore! My Nan used to talk about her time there with your wife, Alun. Apparently, the food was… an experience. Not always in a good way, she said. Though she did bring back some lovely batik. See? Food  is  important! It's a cultural touchstone. And frankly, it’s more interesting than meticulously calculating train routes. It's amazing how seriously people take this game. It’s just coloured plastic, isn't it? Although… I am curious. Rhys, how  do  you always manage to block everyone so effectively? It’s a gift, Sarah. A Welsh gift. We’re strategic thinkers, naturally. Think about it – we build railways  for a living  – figuratively speaking, of course, as teachers. We understand network dynamics. You understand how to be annoying, more like. Seriously, cutting me off from Plymouth? Ruthless! Actually, there's a fascinating bit of railway history about the lines down to Plymouth. During the Victorian era, getting the gradients right was a monumental challenge. They had to use incredibly complex calculations, employing things like Bézier curves, believe it or not. Long before computers! Bézier curves? In railway engineering? Now  that  is fascinating! See, Alun? This is the kind of conversation I want. Forget the trains on the board, let’s talk about the physics of real trains. Growing up in Cape Town, the railway system was…well, let’s just say it was less about gradients and more about hoping things stayed on the tracks. Very different beast. Oh, my brother worked on the railways for years. Said the biggest problem wasn’t the engineering, it was the signal boxes.

Right. That's… underwhelming. Honestly, I thought ‘quixotic’ would be a valid word. It  feels  valid. It isn’t, love. Checked it already. You were hoping for a triple word score, weren't you? Typical. You always go for the high-risk, high-reward plays. Me, I’m all about solid, dependable points. Like this ‘area’. Perfectly respectable. Respectable is boring, Ben! It’s Scrabble, not tax returns. And yes, I was. You know I am. It’s the principle of the thing. It’s… aspirational wordplay. Aspirational? Right. Listen, your aspiration is consistently beaten by my… pragmatism. Anyway, this is nice, isn't it? Being back at your parents’. It feels… slower. It  is  slower. Mum’s already asked four times if you want more biscuits. It's lovely, but… relentless. London life feels a million miles away. Especially the pub culture. You don’t get people offering you a slice of Victoria sponge with your pint in a London pub, do you? No, you get a slightly sticky floor and someone aggressively trying to sell you scratch cards. It's a different vibe. I’ve been thinking about that actually, about how different drinking cultures are, even within the UK. Down south, it’s all about speed, isn’t it? Get in, have a couple, get out. Absolutely. And volume. London pubs are  loud . Up here, it’s more… drawn out. Chatty. People actually  talk  to each other for longer than five minutes. It's a generational thing too, I think. My grandad would spend an entire afternoon nursing one pint of bitter. He’d have conversations with the barman he’d been having for fifty years. My grandfather was the same. Though his tipple was a whisky, neat. It’s funny, isn’t it? How much our… daily routines are shaped by these unwritten rules. Even something as simple as how long you’re expected to linger in a pub. It's definitely a cultural marker. Massive. And it extends to games, too, doesn’t it? We’re sitting here, calmly playing Scrabble, in a quiet room. Imagine trying to do this in a crowded pub in Shoreditch. Disaster. I wouldn't try. Though I did once attempt a game of chess in a particularly rowdy Wetherspoons. It didn’t end well. Someone knocked over my king during a particularly enthusiastic rendition of ‘Sweet Caroline’. Oh, Ben! That sounds… perfectly chaotic.

… honestly, the sheer volume of cardboard from unpacking is ridiculous. I thought I’d be sensible and break everything down flat, but it’s still taking over the living room. And the council’s bin collection is next Tuesday, which feels like an eternity away. Tell me about it. We had a similar mountain after getting the new sofa delivered. Ended up having to take a trip to the recycling centre which, let's be real, is a mission. At least you’ve  got  a sofa now. Still waiting on delivery for ours. Supposedly next Friday. You young ones and your flatpack furniture. Back in my day, things were built to last! We had one sofa, a proper one, and it saw us through twenty years and three kids. Though, admittedly, by the end it looked like it had  been  through a war zone. Twenty years! That’s… ambitious. Everything feels so disposable now. Although, I did find a lovely vintage dresser on Facebook Marketplace. Needs a bit of sanding and painting, but it's solid wood. I'm hoping to get started on it next weekend. Ooh, good find! You’re always so crafty, aren’t you, Chloe? I can barely assemble an IKEA bookcase without wanting to throw it out the window. Proper DIY is beyond me. It's therapeutic, honestly. A good distraction from spreadsheets and admin all day. Though, speaking of distractions, anyone seen the news about the NHS waiting lists? It’s appalling. My Nan’s been waiting months for a hip replacement. Don’t even get me started. I had a routine check-up last month and they couldn’t even get me in with my usual GP. Had to see some locum who barely looked at my notes. Years I've been going to Dr. Davies and now this? It's just not good enough. It’s scary, isn’t it? I remember Mum having to jump through hoops to get Dad an appointment when he wasn’t well. And it’s only getting worse. It makes you wonder what you’re actually paying taxes for. Exactly! And it’s not just the GPs. It’s everything. Even getting a dentist appointment is a nightmare! I’ve been putting off booking one for ages. You should really go, love. Don't wait until something's seriously wrong. I was telling Gareth – that's my husband – just yesterday about old Mrs. Hughes from down the street.

… honestly, Mum, it’s just  bonkers  out here. Look at this queue. What’s even happening up ahead? Just a solid wall of red lights. Standard Friday afternoon, darling. Heading towards the North Circular is always a gamble. You shouldn’t have offered to drive me to collect Auntie Maureen’s things, really. Should’ve just got a cab. No way, wouldn’t hear of it. You were stressing about getting everything sorted and I had the day free after lectures. Besides, it’s good to catch up, innit? Even if it’s stuck in traffic. So, how  is  Auntie Maureen, really? You sounded a bit… vague on the phone. She’s… declining, love. It’s not sudden, it's just… a gradual fading. She's mostly confused these days. That’s why she wants me to have her books, you know. She keeps saying ‘they need a good home.’ It's mostly first editions, actually. A few proper gems. Wow. First editions! That's… amazing. She always did have good taste. Bit of a hoarder though, wasn't she? Remember that time we tried to clear out her attic and found fifteen identical porcelain cats? Don’t remind me. Nearly gave your father a heart attack. Speaking of which, have you told him about… well, about the potential manuscript I’m looking at? The one from the French writer? Oh yeah, vaguely. You mentioned it. Something about a post-war romance? Is it good? You were sounding pretty excited. It  is  good, actually. Really good. But it’s a problem. The author wants to go entirely digital. No print run. Just ebook. And the  TLS  are adamant they won’t review anything that isn’t available in hard copy. It’s this ridiculous battle, isn’t it? Print versus digital. I feel like a dinosaur sometimes. That  is  a pickle. Though, honestly, I get both sides. I read most of my course material online now, it’s just… easier. But there’s something about holding a real book, you know? That smell, the weight of it… Exactly! And the prestige of a physical review! It's about permanence, darling. Digital’s so… fleeting. Although, on the flip side, it means fewer trees get chopped down. It's complicated. This author, Jean-Luc… he’s got a real story, though. Lived through the Liberation of Paris, you know? No way! That’s mental.

… honestly, the worst bit wasn’t even the sunburn, it was the pigeons. Hundreds of ‘em, just waddling about in Venice like they owned the place. Proper brazen, nicking chips right out of people’s hands. Pigeons, eh? That's Italy for ya. Worse than Wigan market, that. You get one tryin' for your pasty there, you give it a look and it scarper. Oh, don’t even  start  on Wigan market. Remember that time Gran nearly had a heart attack when that seagull went for her sausage roll? Ooh, now  that’s  a story. I've seen some dive-bombing seagulls in Scarborough, mind, but nothing beats a determined northern seagull going after grub. Though Venice sounds…intense. Proper Hitchcock vibes. I keep picturing Amy surrounded by a feathered mafia, demandin' protection money in the form of crisps. Very funny. It wasn’t  funny  at the time. I had to practically barricade my gelato. And the gondolier was just…watching, smirking! Like it was entertainment for him. He probably bet on it. He’s thinkin’ ‘easy money, these tourists.’ Did you at least get a decent picture for the ‘gram? Gotta get  something  for all that pigeon warfare. Loads! Mostly blurry photos of flapping wings and beady little eyes. Honestly, the actual city was lovely. But I'm tellin’ ya, those pigeons were a menace. What about you, Leo? Any holiday escapades worth sharing? You were off gallivanting in Spain, weren’t you? Spain was… eventful. It involved a very questionable paella, a lost passport, and me trying to explain to a police officer that “siesta” wasn’t a legitimate excuse for forgetting where I parked the rental car. Oh, Leo! You’re a disaster. A beautiful, chaotic disaster. Was the paella at least good  before  it made you question your life choices? It tasted…fishy. Extremely fishy. And it was served by a man who looked suspiciously like he’d just wrestled a octopus. See?  That’s  a story. Pigeons are amateur league compared to a possibly-octopus-wrestling chef and a lost passport. Lost passport? You're joking! Did you get it back? Eventually. Turns out, I left it at a bar after attempting a very embarrassing rendition of  Livin’ on a Prayer . The bartender remembered me, thankfully. He was very amused. Charged me a ‘finders fee’ of two beers. Serves you right. Honestly, you’re a magnet for chaos.

...Honestly, the condensation inside the tent was biblical. Absolutely biblical. Woke up feeling like I'd been swimming, not sleeping. But, you know, even  that  – the sheer discomfort – it’s…part of it.      Oh, you and your ‘embracing the hardship’, Alistair. Sounds awful, though. You’re a braver man than I, spending a January night exposed like that. I’m quite happy with central heating and a good book, thank you very much. Though I  do  understand the appeal of being truly…away.      Aye, Dad’s right about that discomfort being part of it. It strips things back, doesn't it? No distractions. Just you and…well, everything. It’s why I started taking students on shorter winter walks – not full-on camping, mind, but overnight stays in bothies. It's a good lesson in resilience.      Bothies are a bit tame for my liking, young man! Though a sensible starting point, I suppose. It’s the self-reliance, Elspeth. That’s what I get from it. No phones, no emails, no demands. Just figuring out how to stay warm and dry. It’s incredibly freeing. Last time, near Dartmoor, I had a stag practically breathing down my neck, curious as anything.      A stag! Alistair, you’re courting disaster! Honestly, you should be taking someone with you. Especially these days. I know you're fit as a fiddle for your age, but you can’t be gallivanting around the moors on your own. What if you’d fallen and broken something?      Nonsense, Elspeth. I’m perfectly capable. I’ve been doing this for years. And I  tell  people where I’m going, obviously. But it’s the solitude, you see. It clears the head. All this research… it gets a bit overwhelming sometimes. Staring at data all day. This…this is an antidote.      I think Mum’s got a point about safety, though. Even a seasoned camper can run into trouble. We had a student last year twist her ankle badly on a seemingly harmless path. It took us ages to get her down. And the signal out there is patchy at best.      It’s a calculated risk, Calum. Everything is. Look, I'm not suggesting everyone should be out there battling the elements. But for me, it’s profoundly restorative. The way the light changes on the snow, the sound of the wind… it’s a different level of immersion in nature than just a weekend walk.

…Aye, but that's what I’m sayin’, isn’t it? Like, everyone raves about  Dune , right? Visually spectacular, all that. But when it comes down to it, the characters were just… flat. Proper cardboard cut-outs. Paul Atreides just mopes around bein’ special, and I didn't  feel  anything for ‘im, ya know? Not like with, say, Kvothe from  The Name of the Wind . Right, the classic Rothfuss debate. Though I think you're being a bit harsh on  Dune . It’s less about individual character arcs and more about the scope of the world-building, the political machinations. It's a grand opera, almost. And honestly, Timothée Chalamet does his best with what he's given. It's Herbert's writing that's…distant. Grand opera that bored me stiff for two and a half hours, then. Look, I appreciate world-building, I do. But what’s the point if I don’t  care  who's gettin’ stabbed in the back in this fancy desert world? Kvothe, though…you feel his struggle. His arrogance, his loss. Rothfuss makes you invest. And that’s why it’s so infuriatin’ he hasn't finished the series! Tell me about it. The waiting is agony. I’m on chapter five of a reread, just trying to keep the embers alive. But moving away from tortured fantasy protagonists…what have you been reading  besides  lamenting unfinished series? I know you were ploughing through that collection of short stories by Angela Carter. Oh, she’s brilliant, isn’t she? Utterly brilliant. Completely bonkers, but brilliant. Like, “The Bloody Chamber” - re-tellin’ Bluebeard as proper gothic horror with a feminist edge. It’s just…so sharp. And the language! It's all so lush and disturbing at the same time. Makes you think about fairytales in a completely different way. Sounds intense. I’ve meant to read some Carter for ages. I've been… mostly technical papers lately, unfortunately. Although, I did manage to get through a biography of Isambard Kingdom Brunel. Fascinating man. Proper Victorian engineering genius. Brunel, aye? Always a good shout. Practical, ya know? Not like all this existential ponderin’ in books. Speaking of practical…I’m starvin’. Did you remember to get those pasties from Greggs? I was thinking a steak and onion one would really hit the spot. Of course I did. I  knew  that was coming. Three steak and onion, one sausage roll, and a jam doughnut.

…and honestly, the whole thing with Mrs. Higgins trying to explain Excel to the Brownies was  hilarious . They just glazed over. Little faces, completely blank. She kept saying things like “pivot tables are your friends!” and I just wanted to intervene and say, “No, Mrs. Higgins, pivot tables are absolutely  not  their friends at eight years old!” Pivot tables? What are pivot tables? Sounds boring. Is it like Lego? Can you build stuff with it? No, darling, it's not like Lego at all. It’s… complicated. It's what I use at work to, well, organise numbers. And Mrs. Higgins thought it was a good life skill. Bless her. The Brownie Promise evening was much more successful, thankfully. Did you both remember all the parts? I did! I remembered to do my best and be truthful! And to help other people! I forgot one bit. Was it about being… kind to animals? That’s right! Kind to animals. You'll get it next time, love. Speaking of remembering things, you two were building an  enormous  Lego castle earlier. What was the story behind that one? It was for Princess Luna! She’s got a dragon, but he’s a friendly dragon. He helps her fight the bad guys. And it needs a moat! A really big moat with…with crocodiles! And a drawbridge! A drawbridge and crocodiles. Excellent additions. It sounds like a very clever princess and a very sophisticated defence system. You know, when  I  was little, I didn’t have all this Lego. We had… well, we had my Dad’s old typewriter. A what-er? A typewriter! It’s a machine where you press keys and letters appear on paper. No screens, no electricity, just…clack, clack, clack. It was incredibly noisy. I used to love pretending to be a journalist. I'd type out ‘news’ about my dolls. Did it have PlayStation games on it? No, darling,  way  before PlayStation games! This was… a long, long time ago. Before computers were really common. Although, Dad did eventually get a computer. A really big, clunky one. Honestly, it probably had less power than your PlayStation now. My PlayStation is really good! I can play ‘Adopt Me!’ and I got a unicorn! It cost loads of robux. Sounds exciting! It's amazing how different things are. I remember learning to type on that old computer, practicing for hours.

… honestly, Arthur, you look like you’ve slept in your clothes. Not a criticism, mind, just an observation. You’ve got a bit of, well, everything on that jumper. Jam, I reckon? Probably is, Doreen. Didn’t bother changing. Comfortable, see? And frankly, this is my ‘Bradford casual’ attire. Windsor’s a bit… sharper, generally. Besides, it’s your marmalade that’s the culprit. Glorious stuff, but sticky as owt. Sharpness isn’t everything! You’re on holiday, Arthur. Relax! Though I do wish you’d use a napkin. Now, have you tried the blueberries? I got them from that new farm shop near Haworth. Proper fruit farm, you know, not just supermarket stuff. They were picking them yesterday. Blueberries are lovely, thank you. Reminds me of a job I did near Kent, years ago. Massive fruit farms there. Strawberries as big as your fist. Though, you know, efficiency’s gone out of it. Everything’s standardized, pre-packaged… less flavour. Like those deserted medieval villages we were talking about last time. All planned, neat, then… gone. Aye, that’s a thought. Makes you wonder, doesn’t it? All that effort, all that life, just… vanished. I was reading about one near Ilkley, Wharram Percy. Completely empty now, aside from sheep. It’s that roadworks that get me though, same as it’s been for years! They started near the bypass last autumn, still digging! You'd think they were tunneling to Australia. Roadworks are the bane of my existence. Always disrupting things. Engineer’s perspective, I suppose. Though most of the time they seem to be employing people who’ve never actually  seen  a road before. Speaking of disruptions, have you had much junk mail lately? I’m drowning in it. Offers for funeral plans, insurance… It’s like they’re anticipating my demise. Oh, don’t even start me on the junk mail! It’s terrible. And the phone! Constant calls about PPI… it’s exhausting. I barely answer it anymore. Honestly, it's enough to make you want to move to a desert island. More coffee? I made a fresh pot. And I've got some mint growing on the windowsill – fancy a leaf in your brew? That sounds lovely, Doreen. Mint coffee, now that's something. You've got a good touch with herbs, you do. My late wife, bless her, tried growing them. Said she couldn't tell a basil from a bindweed.

… honestly, I just think she’s overdoing it with the vitamins, David. Honestly, a woman her age needs a bit of common sense, not a whole pharmacy tucked into her handbag! And then she was showing me this new face cream – apparently, it’s got snail slime in it.  Snail slime , can you believe it? Oh, Mum. You and your skepticism. She's just trying to feel good about herself, love. And honestly, snail slime? It's probably better than some of the chemicals they put in the other stuff. Remember that rash you got last year from that fancy serum? That was different! That was a reaction, this is… deliberate sliminess. Honestly. Still, she was going on about how fabulous she feels, anticipating New Year’s. She's already planned a whole weekend in Brighton. Can you imagine, Brighton in January? Sounds bracing. Though, Mum, Brighton's got some really good vegan restaurants now. Might be worth a trip ourselves, actually. I saw a post on Facebook about one called Terre à Terre… apparently, it's unbelievable. Facebook, always Facebook, Tilly. Honestly, you’d think you live in there. And Brighton’s alright, if you don’t mind the seagulls trying to steal your chips. I'm worried about getting there myself, though. Remembering the directions is a nightmare. Last time we went, I ended up driving round in circles near Crawley. I’ll navigate, darling. I’ve finally mastered using Google Maps on my phone. Though, I still prefer a proper map, if I’m honest. Feels more… secure. It's like relying on a compass instead of GPS. Secure? David, you nearly drove us into a field in Devon using a proper map last summer! Honestly, you and your “sense of direction”. It's a myth! That was… a misinterpretation of the contours, Mum. A slight misinterpretation. Anyway, speaking of feeling good, did you take your blood pressure tablets this morning, love? Oh, don’t start lecturing me! Yes, I did. First thing. Honestly, you sound like a doctor. And Tilly, no judging. I had a little glass of prosecco with lunch. It’s nearly New Year! No judgment! Just concerned. It interacts with your medication, doesn't it? And speaking of prosecco, I got you both something for Christmas… Actually, it's more for Mum. It’s that lavender hand cream you like – the one from the little shop in Ashford.

… honestly, the ending of  The Tourist  just felt… rushed. Like they had all these brilliant threads with the mystery and then just tied them up with a bit of string in the last episode. Did  you  watch it? Yeah, I did! I get what you mean. It was good, don’t get me wrong, Jamie Dornan was phenomenal, but it needed another couple of episodes to really land. It felt like they were conscious of budgets or something. Though, compared to some of the rubbish on at the moment, it’s still miles ahead. What have  you  been watching? Besides obsessing over questionable TV endings? Fair enough. Just been trying to switch off, really. Work's been… hectic. They’re pushing this new campaign for the garden furniture company – you wouldn’t believe the briefs. "Evoke rustic charm, but also modern minimalism, appealing to the aspirational homeowner yet remain accessible to the budget conscious." Like, pick a lane, people! Oh, god, copywriting briefs. They’re the worst, aren't they? So much contradiction. Sounds exhausting. How are you finding the actual writing, though? Still enjoying it? Mostly. It pays the bills, which is the main thing right now. Rent in London is just… obscene. I'm seriously considering moving back to Kent, you know? Mum keeps hinting she's got a spare room, and honestly, the thought of having a garden again… and not having to remortgage myself every month… It's tempting. Back to Ashford? That’s a big shift. Though, I can see the appeal. I'm lucky, I’m still living at home while I finish my Masters. The privilege is  real . Although, even with that, money's tight. This part-time survey programming is… not exactly lucrative. It's just to keep me afloat and away from asking the Bank of Mum and Dad for everything. You’re doing a Masters though, that’s brilliant! What is it in again? Computational Linguistics. It’s fascinating, but terrifying. The stuff they’re asking us to learn about AI… it's a bit much sometimes. It feels like everything's changing so fast. Makes me wonder if there  will  be jobs in my field by the time I graduate. Don't even get me started on AI taking over jobs! My boss was talking about using an AI writer for some of the simpler stuff. Said it would “free up creative bandwidth” – which basically translates to ‘we might not need you for much longer’.

… honestly, I just feel completely knackered after that walk. It wasn’t even  that  hilly, but this weather just drains you, doesn’t it? Feels like wading through treacle. You’re telling me. I tried a quick jog this morning, just around the block, and I was puffing like an old steam engine. Edinburgh air, even though it’s…well, relatively clean, still feels heavy this time of year. So, how’s the transcription going? Still wading through legal jargon? Sadly, yes. Mostly depositions. Endless ‘hereby’s’ and ‘notwithstanding’s’. It’s soul-destroying, frankly. Pays the bills though. How’s the admin world treating you, David? Still battling bureaucracy? You have  no  idea. They’re reorganising again. Which means everyone’s tip-toeing around, terrified of stepping on anyone’s toes. It's exhausting. Though, on a brighter note, Carol was showing me houses online again. Oh, houses? Don't tell me you're both falling down the rabbit hole of Rightmove again. It’s a dangerous pastime, that. Especially now. Mum! Perfect timing. Biscuits are exactly what I need. And yes, David was just showing me some. They’re utterly ridiculous, the prices. Even for something tiny and needing a complete overhaul. Exactly! Carol and I were looking near Twickenham, thinking it might be a bit more reasonable than further into London. But even there, a semi-detached that needs new windows is going for…well, let’s just say more than I earn in a year. Twickenham! Oh, darling, you’re dreaming. I remember when you could get a proper house in Twickenham for peanuts. My sister bought on Wellesley Road in ‘88 for, I swear, less than eighty thousand. Can you believe it? Now, you’re lucky to get a garden shed for that. It's insane. It feels like nobody can afford to actually  live  anywhere anymore, just…exist in rented boxes. It’s making me seriously reconsider my plans. I was thinking of maybe upsizing eventually, but… Exactly my thought. Carol keeps saying we should look further out, maybe even Essex. But then the commute becomes a nightmare. Essex? Oh, bless you. Don't even go there. Though, truthfully, anything’s better than endlessly scrolling through Rightmove. Speaking of endlessly, I was trying a new recipe last night - a Moroccan tagine. It took  ages . Oh, you and your cooking! Is it as complicated as it sounds?

… honestly, it’s just endless tagging, innit? Like, ‘is this a passive construction?’ ‘is this an example of deontic modality?’ It sounds fancy, but it's just hours staring at text. And Professor Davies is  very  particular about the tagging scheme. Proper pedantic, he is. Sounds… stimulating. Though, I suppose all research has its dull bits. My modelling software crashed  again  this morning. Lost three hours of calculations predicting bridge stress. It wasn’t exactly a picnic. At least you’re dealing with language, something inherently… interesting? Interesting when I’m actually  using  language, yeah. Not when I’m dissecting it into its constituent parts like some linguistic Frankenstein. How’s the bridge going, actually? Is it a big one? It's a replacement for a little one in Norfolk, actually. Rural stuff. But it's a good project, lots of ground investigation needed due to the soil composition. More paperwork than actual engineering sometimes, to be fair. Did you see the Budget yesterday? Absolute shambles, wasn't it? A bit. I skimmed it. Honestly, politics just stresses me out. All that talk of ‘growth’ and ‘fiscal responsibility’… feels completely disconnected from actual life, you know? Especially for someone like me, just trying to pay rent and not live on beans. Did it affect engineers at all, do you reckon? More funding for infrastructure? A little. There’s talk of accelerating some HS2 phases, which is good for some firms, but a lot of the cuts seem to be hitting local authority projects. Roads, drainage… the bread and butter stuff. My dad's a contractor, so he’s already bracing himself for things to get leaner. He reckons a lot of smaller companies will struggle. Right, that’s rough. It’s always the little guys who get squeezed. He still doing okay, though? He’s resilient. He’ll adapt. He always does. Speaking of things that are a bit… extra and disconnected from reality, have you seen  Wicked  is coming to Cambridge?  Wicked ?! Oh my god, seriously? I’ve wanted to see that for  years . It's been on my list forever. I always thought I'd have to trek down to London. Yeah, they announced the tour dates last week. They’re doing a month at the Corn Exchange. I was thinking of trying to get tickets. Actually, I was thinking… you fancy coming with? Are you kidding? I'd absolutely love to!

…and honestly, the whole thing with that new development down by the docks, it’s just  criminal . They’re knocking down perfectly good Victorian warehouses, you know? Character! History! Gone, replaced with glass and steel boxes that all look the same. It's not progress, it's… sanitisation. Aye, tell me about it. Drove past there yesterday. Used to be Old Man Hemmings' timber yard, that was. Proper rough and ready, but had a soul, you know? This lot just want to line their pockets. They don’t care about the city, just the pound notes. Still, pays my road tax, I suppose, all the construction traffic. A pragmatic perspective, as always, Alistair. Though, road tax doesn’t quite compensate for the aesthetic vandalism. You remember that little art house cinema they wanted to put in one of those warehouses? Fantastic project, but the council, predictably, sided with the developers. The Scala? Yeah, proper shame that. Me and Sheila used to go there, back in the day. Showed all sorts of weird and wonderful films. Speaking of films, you catch that new one with Cillian Murphy? Oppenheimer, is it? I did, actually. A harrowing piece of work. Superbly acted, of course. Murphy is phenomenal. Though, it left me feeling… rather bleak. Reminded me, in a strange way, of some of Edward Hopper's paintings. That same sense of isolation, of impending doom. Hopper, eh? Never really got him, to be honest. Give me a good Turner any day. All that dramatic light and storms…now  that’s  art. You still doing your painting, then? Haven’t seen any new canvases lying about. Sporadically. Life gets in the way, doesn’t it? Lectures, marking essays… plus, this backyard was looking a right state. Hence the painting. I'm trying to create a bit of a Zen garden vibe, actually. A space for reflection. Ambitious, I know. Zen garden in Liverpool 8? That’s… optimistic. I’m more of a practical man myself. Speaking of practical, you still got that ladder? I need to give me gutters a clean-out this weekend. Been putting it off for ages. The aluminium one? Yes, it’s in the shed. Help yourself, Alistair. But be careful, it's a bit wobbly on the uneven paving. And for goodness sake, don't fall off. I don't want to explain that to your Sheila. Don't you worry about me.

… honestly, I still think we should’ve stopped at that roadside  bar mleczny . It looked utterly charming. Proper Polish milk bars, you don’t get that anymore, do you? Just everything’s…polished now. Sanitised for the tourists. Mum, we had a perfectly good breakfast in the van! Porridge and those weird Polish biscuits you found. And we’re on a schedule, remember? Tarnow by tonight, Auntie Kasia’s waiting. Besides, those places are usually… well, a bit basic. Basic? Darling, basic is  authentic . And frankly, after fifteen years of Cambridge ‘authenticity’ - meaning overpriced cafes and pretending to read Proust - I’m craving basic. It’s liberating. It’s… freeing, isn’t it? This whole trip is. Though, liberating also feels a bit harsh when describing my current financial state. How much have we spent on diesel, actually? I’ve been keeping track. Roughly £150 so far, just on fuel. And the tolls were about £30. Plus the campsite last night. It’s not horrendous, but it’s adding up. Thankfully, Auntie Kasia’s letting us stay for a week, so that’s a massive saving. Kasia is a saint. Truly. Remember when I tried to convince her to come to Cambridge for a ‘cultural exchange’? She nearly choked on her pierogi. “Cambridge? What for? I have everything I need  here .” She's a wise woman. Though, goodness knows what she thinks of me, appearing on her doorstep in a campervan after…well, you know. She’s just glad to see you, Mum. She worries. You haven’t exactly been bursting with activity lately. This is good for you, getting out. And honestly, needing a bit of a clear-out was obvious. All those boxes in the spare room... Don’t remind me. Decades of accumulated… stuff. Mostly books, and things my mother gave me. I felt terrible chucking it, but honestly, they were just weighing me down. It's like… travelling light isn't just about possessions, is it? It's about… everything. Exactly! Less baggage, literal and metaphorical. Look, there’s someone hitchhiking up ahead. Do we… ? Absolutely not! Honestly, Sarah, have you learned nothing from all those true crime documentaries we binge-watch? Hitchhikers? In Poland? It’s a recipe for disaster. Mum, don’t be ridiculous. It's probably a perfectly nice student. He looks young. And it's daylight. Doesn’t matter! We don't know his story.

...Honestly, Dad, I still think turning left back there was wrong. Google Maps said to go straight on. We’re practically going  towards  Blackpool, not Preston!      Now, now, lass. Trust yer old Dad. I know these roads like the back o’ me hand. Google Maps doesn’t know about the little shortcuts, does it? This’ll avoid all that traffic on the A585.      He’s right, actually, Anya. This route  is  quicker. I used to drive this way all the time when I visited your auntie in Lancaster. Though, it does bring back memories… less pleasant ones, admittedly, of getting stuck behind a tractor for a full hour.      A tractor? Seriously? That sounds awful. Are we nearly there yet? I need to get to Primark before they sell out of everything good. My friend’s birthday is next week.      Patience, pet. We’ll be in Preston in about twenty minutes. Speaking of birthdays, remember that cake your Gran made you when you were seven? The one shaped like a unicorn?      Oh my god, yes! It was epic! And it tasted… vaguely of cinnamon, I think? Gran always put cinnamon in everything. Even shepherd’s pie, sometimes.      She did, didn't she? A very… enthusiastic cook. It’s funny the things you remember. I was telling my mum on the phone yesterday about moving to London. She’s worried, of course. Thinks it’s too busy, too expensive.      London  is  pricey, love. But you’ll be alright. And it’s got everything. Remember when we took Anya to London for the first time? She was mesmerised by Hamleys! Nearly bankrupted me.      It was AMAZING! I wanted every single thing in that shop. Still do, actually. Anyway, Mum, are you feeling okay? You’ve been a bit quiet since we left St. Anne’s.      I'm fine, darling. Just a little tired. These train strikes are a nightmare, aren’t they? Makes it so difficult to get anywhere. I had a meeting in Manchester planned, but had to cancel. It’s just… feeling a bit off, truth be told.      Off? What d’you mean, off? Don’t go starting to worry me now. You haven’t been… feeling unwell, have you?      Well… I took a test this morning. And… it’s positive.      No way! Really? Oh my gosh, Mum! That’s… huge! Congratulations!      Well, I’ll be! Another grandchild! That’s brilliant news, love!

Honestly, this attic is a monument to… well, to  things . Your grandfather collected everything. Broken radios, chipped teacups, pamphlets about the price of barley in 1978. Honestly, why?      He was a hoarder, love. A gentle one, but a hoarder nonetheless. You’ve got to admit, though, some of this is quite charming. Look, this photo of you at Blackpool. You had that amazing red coat.      Oh, don’t remind me. I looked like a pillar box! And cold. It was always cold at Blackpool. Still, better than dealing with this… What  is  this thing, even? Looks like something out of a science fiction film.      Woah. That’s…old school tech, nan. Like, really old. My dad showed me something similar once. It's a…a Betamax player, I think? They used to record videos on tapes. Before DVDs, before streaming, before anything.      Betamax! Goodness me. All this clever technology and now…dust. It's a bit like life, isn’t it? All whizzing about, and then… stillness.      That's a bit philosophical for a clear-out, isn’t it? Though you’re right, it does make you think. I was chatting to Sarah at school today, she was telling me about her son. Seems he's struggling, really struggling with anxiety. It's awful to see these young people so burdened. He won’t even  look  at his phone anymore, says it's “too much.”      Oh, dear. Poor lad. It’s that constant bombardment, isn’t it? Used to be, if you wanted to avoid bad news, you simply switched off the wireless. Now it follows you everywhere. It’s a wonder anyone’s left with any peace of mind. It reminds me a little of…well, Arthur, my brother. He had a touch of the black dog, you know. Didn't talk about it much back then, people weren't as... open.      The black dog? What’s that, Grandma?      It’s an old phrase, pet. Means depression. A heavy sadness that hangs around. Arthur… he found solace in humour, oddly enough. Absolutely obsessed with Tommy Cooper. Knew every trick, every ‘just like that!’ He said it was the absurdity of it all that kept him going. “If life’s going to be ridiculous," he’d say, “you might as well laugh with it.”      That's lovely. It's good he found something that helped. Sarah said her son’s trying comedy now, actually.

… honestly, the trackpad’s still a bit sticky, innit? Even after I cleaned it. It’s not  terrible , but… it’s a new laptop, yeah? Shouldn’t be sticky. Yeah, that is a bit odd. Did you try a proper clean with isopropyl alcohol? Not just, like, a damp cloth? That’s what my IT lecturer always went on about. Apparently, the oils from your fingers build up. Isopropyl alcohol? Sounds a bit… serious for a trackpad, don’t it? I just wipe mine with whatever’s handy. Usually a bit of old t-shirt. Works for the garden shears, so… Yeah, you’d probably get away with anything, you and your shears. No, I used one of those screen cleaning wipes, the one with the little bit of liquid in. Thought that’d do the trick. Maybe I need to get proper stuff. It’s just… annoying. I was hoping to get a proper YouTube binge on tonight, catch up on some MMA breakdowns. Speaking of YouTube, have you seen that Korean mukbang channel I sent you? The one with the lady who eats, like, a whole lobster in one go? Ridiculous. Oh, yeah! Saw a clip, mental. Proper competitive eating. Makes me feel a bit bad about my dinner, which currently consists of beans on toast. Top-tier fuel for a laptop testing session, obviously. Beans on toast? Alright for some! I’ve been experimenting with that halloumi recipe I saw online. Got it marinatin’ in lemon juice and herbs. Proper healthy, that is. Well, relatively. Halloumi, eh? Fancy. You’re turning into a proper chef, aren’t you? Remember when your food consisted entirely of kebabs after a night out? Hey, kebabs are a culinary masterpiece! Don’t knock ‘em. And I'm tryin', alright? Gotta think about the back, y'know? All that bendin' and liftin' in the garden. Need to keep the joints oiled and fuelled… with halloumi. You are getting old. Speaking of old, anyone remember that massive, boxy TV my nan used to have? The one that took up half the living room? We used to have to fiddle with the aerial to get a decent picture. Oh blimey, yeah! The one that warmed the whole room up? Felt like you were watchin' telly  inside  a radiator. This screen’s a bit of a step up, wouldn't you say? . Massive understatement. Seriously though, this is a decent bit of kit.

… honestly, I think it’s the lighting. It’s doing a lot of the heavy lifting. It  looks  lovely, doesn't it? All these fairy lights and exposed brick. Very ‘Shoreditch’, which is ironic considering we’re in Tarnow. Though, I suppose every small city is trying for that vibe these days. It  is  nice. A massive step up from that cafe near the market square. Remember that one? The one that smelled permanently of cabbage and despair? This is… ambitious. And the pierogi were pretty good. I’m still full, actually. Oh, that cafe! Good heavens. You could practically taste the history…and not the good kind. Ambition is a good word. I wonder how long it’ll last. Tarnow’s lovely, but people are… set in their ways, aren't they? They like what they know. Maybe. Though, there's a real influx of younger people here now, teaching English, like me. They’re looking for places like this. It’s a bit of a bubble though, isn't it? We all hang out together. A bubble. Yes, exactly. It’s… comforting, in a way, but also a bit isolating. It reminds me, and this sounds horribly dramatic, of being in recovery. You surround yourself with people who  get  it, but it doesn't necessarily translate to the 'real' world. Recovery? I didn’t realise… Oh, it was years ago. A bit of a…mess with alcohol. Cambridge can be rather conducive to that. Too much time, not enough responsibility, a healthy dose of self-loathing… the usual recipe. It’s funny, isn’t it? How we construct these identities. "Eleanor, the recovering alcoholic." It’s so reductive. It's not reductive, it's part of your story. And it takes a lot of strength to… address something like that. I admire you for it. I’ve seen what addiction does to families, through a friend at uni. It’s brutal. Thank you, dear. It  was  brutal. And it's always lurking, that part of me. Hence the semi-retirement. Keeps me… occupied, less likely to fall into old patterns. Plus, teaching a few Japanese students online keeps the brain ticking over. Though, honestly, sometimes I miss having a proper purpose. Something… bigger. You  have  a purpose! You’re a brilliant conversationalist, for one. And you keep me grounded when I start getting all caught up in lesson planning and marking.

… honestly, Grandad, I just think it’ll be a really fun day out. Bournemouth’s lovely, but it’s… well, it’s Bournemouth. We need a bit of  grit , you know? Something different. The Dorset Steam Fair looks amazing! All those old engines… Grit? Grit? My dear, I lived through the sixties! I know a thing or two about grit. And Bournemouth's perfectly pleasant. Though the prices… don’t even  start  me on the prices these days. Remember when you could get a decent fish and chips for a shilling? Oh, don't we all, Arthur? Though a shilling wouldn't buy you a single chip now, would it? Look, Lily, it  does  sound good, a bit of a change. But your Grandad's right to ask about access. His knees aren't what they used to be, and we need to make sure it’s suitable. Is there proper disabled access? I did check the website, Mum. They’ve got designated parking, wheelchair hire, and they said most of the main areas are accessible. There’s a map showing accessible routes too. I can print it out for you both. They even have disabled toilet facilities, which is… important. Good, good. That’s a relief. Last thing we need is me stranded miles from a loo. Though, frankly, I reckon they build things these days to be…soft. All this health and safety. In my day, you just got on with it. Arthur, everything isn’t about ‘your day’. You fell over a paving stone last month! And nearly took Mrs. Peterson with you. It’s good they’re thinking about accessibility. Anyway, what about tickets? How much are we looking at? It’s a bit pricey, actually. Around £25 each if we book online, more on the gate. I was thinking we could all chip in? I’ve got some savings from my part-time job. Twenty-five quid! Cor blimey. That’s… that’s nearly what my rent used to be! Everything's gone up. Did you see that house down on Poole Road sold last week? Apparently, a developer snapped it up. They're just tearing down everything decent and building flats. Don’t get started on property prices, Arthur. You’ll give yourself apoplexy. It's ridiculous, isn't it? I'm looking at retirement, and there's just no way I can afford anything decent around here.

…and honestly, this Yorkshire pudding is  almost  as good as Mabel’s used to make. Almost. Though Mabel always did have a knack, didn’t she? Never quite understood how she got it so…airy.      It's a good effort, love. Mrs. Higgins at the bakery uses lard, you know. Apparently, that’s the secret. Though I stick to oil myself, healthier.      Can I be on my phone a bit longer? There's this really cool… compilation of fails on TikTok.      Fails, eh? Sounds riveting. Though perhaps after a bit of conversation, lad? Your grandmother’s only just arrived, and she's regaling us with tales of Mabel’s Yorkshire puddings. A national treasure, that woman.      Oh, don't you encourage him, David! This newfangled technology. Honestly, I don't know what the world's coming to. I tried Twitter, you know. Your sister, Susan, thought it would be a good way to “connect.” Utter chaos. Just people shouting at each other. And the abbreviations! I needed a dictionary just to decipher what they were saying.      It’s not for everyone, Mum. You’re more of a letter-writing woman, aren’t you? More…considered.      Precisely! A beautifully crafted letter. Now  that’s  communication. This house, though… it feels lovely. A bit drafty, mind you. I felt a chill right through to my bones when I came in.      We’re getting the windows insulated next month, Mum. It’s an old house, you know. Full of character, but character needs a bit of modern help sometimes.      Can we go to the cinema tonight? The new Marvel thing is out.      We’ll see, Liam. We need to unpack some of your grandmother's things first, and I promised to help Mrs. Peterson with the church fete stall. She's trying to get local artisan businesses involved - a cheesemaker, a potter… It's lovely, really, supporting the community.      Supporting the community is vital. Kendal’s changed so much, you know. Used to be filled with little shops, proper butchers and bakers. Now it's all chain stores. Dreadful. And the young people… they all drift away to the cities. No sense of belonging anymore.      It's happening everywhere, Mum. Though Thirsk is holding its own, thankfully. There’s the market, and a few independent shops… it’s got a lot of heart. Speaking of which, I was talking to old Mr. Abernathy at the bookshop.

…and honestly, the dentist said her bite is  slightly  off. Just slightly. He wasn’t massively concerned, but suggested we keep an eye on it. It all feels so dramatic, doesn’t it? A tiny little bit off and suddenly we're talking about braces! Mummy, can I have a biscuit? A chocolate one? In a minute, sweetheart. We’re talking about your sister. Honestly, it's always “Mummy, biscuit” when something important is being discussed. I want a biscuit too! And can we talk about Easter chocolate after? 'Cause I want to know if I can have a big one.
