Not a little one. A  big  one! Right. Biscuits after. And we’ll talk about Easter chocolate later. Now, Lily, about your sister… she might need to have a little check-up with a specialist. It’s nothing scary, honestly. It just means someone who  really  knows about teeth will have a look. Will it hurt? Not at all, darling. It’ll be just like a normal dentist appointment, but with someone who's extra good at looking at teeth. Speaking of check-ups, did you two remember what Mrs. Davison said about the hearing tests at school next week? Oh, yeah! She said we have to wear headphones and listen for beeps. It’s boring. It's important, though. Just to make sure everything’s working perfectly. Now, Anya was telling me about Ashaad today. Apparently, he’s having a proper party for his tenth birthday. Ten! That’s old! It is getting up there. It’s funny, isn’t it? Ashaad and Leo – birthdays just a day apart. Just like you two! It must be chaos for their mums. Imagine trying to organise two parties so close together. We get two cakes! That’s the best part. Last year, you made that chocolate one… and the one with the sprinkles! I did, didn’t I? And this year…well, we haven't decided yet. What would you like? A Monet cake! Like the water lilies! A Monet cake? That’s…ambitious. Very artistic of you, Lily. Though I'm not sure how I'd manage those water lilies. Maybe we could  look  at Monet paintings while we eat the cake? We talked about him in art, remember? Can it be a chocolate Monet cake then? And can we have roast potatoes with it? Roast potatoes with cake? Now, that’s a combination!

… honestly, Mum was going on  again  about the garden needing a proper prune. Like I have the time! Between deadlines and trying to actually, you know,  live  a little, pruning roses isn't exactly top of the list. Oh, classic Mum. She’ll always find something. Is it the ramblers again? They were looking a bit enthusiastic last time I was round. The ramblers, the hedges, the entire front border apparently needs ‘attention’. She keeps sending me photos. It’s passive-aggressive gardening. Sounds about right. Speaking of attention, how’s the copywriting going? You were stressing about that new client last week – the one doing the ethically sourced dog biscuits? Ugh, don't even  start  me. They're lovely people, genuinely, but the brief… it was like trying to write a haiku about industrial plumbing. 'Rustic, yet modern. Sustainable, yet premium. Appealing to millennials, but not  too  try-hard.’ Honestly! I think I nailed it eventually, but it aged me ten years. Sounds brutal. At least you  have  work. Things are… interesting at the hospital. We're completely swamped. Post-COVID backlog is still massive, and everyone's generally just exhausted. Saw a lovely woman today though, making amazing progress after a stroke. Little wins, you know? Definitely. Those are the things that make it worthwhile, aren't they? It sounds seriously draining though. You should be taking more time for yourself. Remember that pottery class we talked about? I know, I know. It feels selfish when I’m thinking about hobbies when everyone else is needing so much. But yeah, pottery… that does sound nice. We should actually book it. What about finances? How are you managing? Everything’s gone completely mental with bills. Don’t even. I genuinely think my energy bill is actively mocking me. I’m trying to budget, properly budget, but it feels like I’m just shifting money from one slightly terrifying pile to another. I'm considering getting a second freelance gig, but the thought frankly fills me with dread. Maybe not a  gig , but perhaps some smaller projects? I've been looking at side hustles myself, honestly. Thinking about doing some private tutoring. It’s good money, and relatively low stress. Honestly, anything that doesn’t involve crafting copy about dog biscuits sounds appealing right now. Remember when we used to make those truly awful friendship bracelets in year seven? That was a significantly less stressful creative outlet.

…Honestly, the hills around Almondsbury were  brutal . But Dad insisted. Said it built character. Every Saturday, rain or shine, we’d be out on those bikes. I was always trailing behind, desperately trying to keep up with my brother. He was a natural. I was… less so. Though, looking back, it was good for me. Probably why my knees are shot now, but good for me.      Character building, eh? Sounds like my childhood in Ramsgate. Not hills, mind you – mostly dodging seagulls and trying to build sandcastles before the tide came in. Though I remember Old Man Hemmings, the dentist, letting me watch him work once. Absolutely fascinated me. Bit of blood, a lot of drilling…      Hemmings? Good chap, Hemmings. Knew my father. Used to say he could tell a man’s age by his teeth. Likely true. Speaking of dentistry, those early years on the NHS… different world. We had ‘perks,’ you know. Not like now. Remember the medical officers’ sailing trips?      Sailing trips? You’re having me on, Arthur.      Absolutely true! The Royal College of Surgeons would organize them. Lectures  all at sea  with your oral surgeon! Sounds awful now, doesn’t it? But it was the ‘60s. Everything was… freer. Used to get really good deals on holidays too, because of the NHS connection. Though nothing like the bargains you get now. Have you seen those Prague deals, Margaret?      Prague? Oh, yes! I saw one online. Ridiculously cheap. Apparently, they’ve revitalised the Old Town Square. Sarah went last year, said it was stunning. She managed to get into the National Theatre, even though it was supposedly sold out. She said she just asked nicely and mentioned she was a member of a cultural society– worked a treat.      That’s the trick, isn’t it? A bit of charm. Speaking of events, how’s the planning going for the jive?      It's coming together. We've booked the old barn just outside town. It’s been beautifully converted, all exposed beams and stone floors. They’re putting in a proper sprung dance floor, which is essential. And they're building a small stage for the band. It’s going to transform that place.      That barn is lovely. Shame about the rest of the town, though. It’s been so…declining for years.      Ruined, I’d say. Absolutely ruined by those dreadful concrete developments in the ‘70s. They flattened perfectly good Victorian buildings!

…so, the thing is, TikTok’s reach with that age group is undeniable. Even my niece, who’s barely ten, is all over it. But building a  sustainable  educational resource on a platform that changes its algorithm every other week? It feels…precarious, doesn't it? Like building a house on sand. I agree. It's brilliant for grabbing attention, massively viral potential, but longevity? Questionable. Though, thinking about it, we could use it as a feeder – short, snappy explainers that  direct  people to something more robust. Something we control. That's where the case studies come in, right? Longer form, properly researched, materials. Exactly! The TikToks are the honey, the case studies are the hive. We’d need to focus on visual literacy, though. Because kids these days…they’re consuming moving images constantly. They're fluent in meme language, but can they actually  deconstruct  a film technique, or understand framing? That’s the gap. Absolutely. And that’s where my experience with media studies comes in handy. I’ve got a whole library of resources already, mostly built around A-Level film studies. But adapting that for, say, 14-16 year olds who aren’t necessarily planning on university…that’s the challenge. They need it to be accessible, practical. Accessibility is key. And we need to move beyond just ‘film’. Think advertising, political campaigns, even those ridiculous influencer videos. Everything's trying to persuade them visually. We could build a series around ‘spotting the spin’, dissecting the techniques used to influence perceptions. Oh, I love that! ‘Spotting the Spin’ - that’s a great title. Maybe broken down into modules – narrative structure in ads, colour psychology, sound design… We could even create augmented reality exercises, overlaying annotations onto video clips. That’d be cutting edge. AR, that’s…ambitious. Although, not impossible. It’d require some coding expertise, which neither of us possesses, obviously. We’d need to outsource that element. The cost…that’s always the kicker, isn’t it? It is. Maybe starting smaller. High-quality video essays, accompanied by downloadable worksheets and quizzes. Think Khan Academy, but focused specifically on visual media. And making sure it aligns with curriculum requirements – UK national curriculum, Australian curriculum… it’s a headache, but necessary. I’ve got contacts at a couple of schools in Dorset, I could bounce some ideas off them. Brilliant! Excellent. Dorset’s a good starting point. Gets us real-world feedback early on.

…and honestly, the sheer  scale  of it just gets to me every time. It's not just ‘blue,’ you know? It’s every shade imaginable, and then some you didn’t even  know  existed. Did you see Old Man Hemmings down the beach today? He was out with his metal detector, convinced there's a Roman shipwreck just offshore. Hemmings and his shipwrecks. That man’s dedicated. Though, knowing his luck, he’ll probably find another rusty tin can. It’s endearing, though, isn’t it? That unwavering belief. It reminds me a bit of Aunt Carol and her insistence that she saw the Loch Ness Monster on her honeymoon. Oh,  God , Aunt Carol. The photos! That blurry, green…thing. She still carries them around, convinced it’s irrefutable proof. It’s funny, isn’t it, how the sea – and large bodies of water generally – just seem to inspire that kind of…myth-making? It’s a blank canvas for our hopes and fears. Absolutely. I think it's the unknowable depths, isn’t it? We know  something  is down there, vast amounts of something, but we can’t truly comprehend it. It’s the ultimate mystery. Remember when we went diving in Cornwall, and you practically had a panic attack? Don't remind me! It wasn't a panic attack, it was…an acute awareness of my own mortality! Being suspended in that darkness, just everything  blue  fading to black…and the silence! It was oppressive. You were so calm, gliding around like a seal. Well, I’d done a bit more training than you, darling. Plus, I find the quiet incredibly soothing. It’s the closest I get to meditation. Though, thinking about Cornwall... did I ever tell you about Ben’s disastrous sailing trip? Ben? No, what happened? Last I heard he was boasting about becoming a proper sailor. He always was a bit overconfident. Oh, he was. He chartered a little sailboat for a weekend with James and Sarah. Apparently, they got caught in a surprisingly nasty swell. James was seasick within five minutes, Sarah spent the entire time berating Ben for his navigational skills, and Ben…well, Ben tried to be the stoic captain, but ended up capsizing about a mile offshore. You’re kidding! Capsized? Ben? The man who can’t even parallel park without causing a minor incident? No, honestly. The Coast Guard had to fish them out.

… honestly, I just don’t  get  it. All this sheer stuff. It's February! You’d catch your death of cold. Look at her, practically wearing nothing! Oh, come on, Elsie, it’s  fashion . It's not about practicality. It's about making a statement. It's art, innit? Besides, it's a runway, they’re not expecting people to actually  wear  that to Tesco. I think it's interesting how they're playing with texture though. See that little bit of velvet edging on that completely see-through dress? It’s a nice little counterbalance. And the colour palette is really muted, very 'new season'. Muted? It’s grey and beige, basically! Me nan’s got curtains like that. No offence, but I feel like fashion’s lost its joy. Used to be vibrant, you know? Like, proper dresses. I saw a picture of me mam in the ‘80s, massive shoulder pads, bright colours…  that’s  fashion. This is just…expensive nothing. Oh, the ‘80s. Don’t get me started. Shoulder pads were a menace. But I think things cycle, don't they? Minimalism is having a moment. After years of, like, maximalism and influencers buying everything, people are craving a bit of…simplicity. And there’s a reaction against fast fashion too, I think. This is all about craftsmanship and quality, even if it’s, well, an impractical sheer dress. It hints at a slower, more considered approach to clothing. Craftsman- what? It’s probably machine-made in a factory somewhere, love. Don’t let ‘em fool ya. Speaking of clothes, are we still on for that vintage shop raid next weekend? I need a proper coat, one ya can actually wear, not something that looks like it’s been attacked by moths. Definitely! I’ve been promising myself I'd find a proper trench coat for ages. I’ve got a list of places in Brick Lane. We could meet at Liverpool Street, then head in? Ooh, Brick Lane sounds good. I’ve not been in ages. I need a new bag, something a bit more… sophisticated. My current one’s covered in glitter and dinosaur stickers, thanks to Leo. Glitter and dinosaurs! You're a legend, Chloe. Right, Brick Lane it is. Saturday okay for everyone? I'm working a late shift Friday, doing the set-up for that corporate do. Honestly, the amount of bunting they want…it’s criminal.

…and honestly, Mrs. Davies was  not  impressed with my lighting choices. She said it looked like I was trying to recreate a horror film, not a still life of apples! Honestly, though, I was going for dramatic. Dramatic apples, eh? Sounds about right for you, Lily. Always a flair for the…theatrical. Remember when you tried to stage a play in the garden with the garden gnomes? Mum,  please  don’t bring up the Gnome Rebellion. That was a dark time. Bertram ended up missing a hat for weeks. But seriously, photography is frustrating. It’s not just pointing and clicking like everyone thinks. No, it’s not. It’s about seeing, isn't it? And knowing how to  show  people what you see. It's a lovely skill to have. Are you enjoying the A-Levels, generally? Is photography still the plan for uni? Mostly. History is… intense. So much memorising. And photography  is  still the plan, definitely. Unless I completely bomb the portfolio review. That’s what I’m terrified of, actually. Failing to get into the course. Oh, darling. You won’t. You’re so talented. And even if... well, even if things don't go exactly to plan, it’s not the end of the world. There’s always another route. Remember when I was convinced I'd be a marine biologist and then realised I get seasick just  looking  at a boat? You did! You spent a whole summer researching dolphins. Dad found your notebook filled with drawings of very wobbly dolphins. He did, didn’t he? It’s good to explore, Lily. It's good to adjust. Speaking of adjusting, work's been…interesting. Old Mr. Henderson had another forgetting episode. Thought I was his daughter, Susan. Kept asking me about his prize-winning roses. Oh, bless him. Is he alright? It must be scary for him. He's…managing. It's sad to watch, though. It reminds you how fragile things are, doesn't it? I was talking to Brenda about it, and she was saying her aunt's got early stages, and she's absolutely terrified. It’s funny, isn't it? We spend so much time worrying about silly things, and then something like that happens and you realise what truly matters. It is. It's just... hard to  not  worry about silly things. Like, whether my photos will be good enough. Or if Ethan will actually text me back.

…and honestly, the fella who did the patio, he just bodged it. Proper bodged it. You wouldn’t believe the gaps between the slabs, Doreen. Gaps! A robin could build a nest down ‘em, easy. Reminds me of old Mr. Henderson’s work, always cut corners, that one. Oh, Arthur, you’re always finding fault with someone’s workmanship. Though, I do agree, you need someone reliable. Speaking of nests, did you see those baby birds in Maggie’s rose bush? Tiny little things, all beak and fluff. They are lovely, aren't they? Saw them this morning on my walk. Beautiful. Though, the cockerel next door is driving me round the bend. Starts crowing at four in the morning! Can’t get a decent night's sleep for it. Four in the mornin’? Crikey! That's no good. I ain't slept proper in a week, mind. Got that application form for the blue badge, see. All those questions. It's a rigmarole, I tell ya. "Describe your difficulties with walking…" Well, where do I  start ? It's everything! Can’t walk far, can’t stand long, can’t even bend to tie me laces properly these days. Oh, Arthur, that sounds dreadful. I can help you with that form, if you like. I’m quite good with things like that. Did it ask about needing help with… well, all of it really? Aye, it did. And then it asked about how it affects me socially. Sociably! Like I’m goin’ to the pictures every week! I used to love a bit of footie, you know. Norwich, always. But gettin’ to Carrow Road… forget about it. It's a whole operation just to get to the shops now. It's frustrating, isn’t it? Losing those little freedoms. I’ve got a couple of… challenging children in my class this year. One lad, bless him, just hasn’t got a filter. Says whatever’s on his mind, no matter how inappropriate. It’s exhausting trying to manage it all, plus the paperwork. Oh dear, sounds like you need a holiday! Still, I always thought teaching was a noble profession. You're moulding young minds, aren't you? Unlike some… . Now what did I do? Just statin’ a fact about patios! Anyway, thinking of gettin’ one of them 3D printers. Young Tim down the road’s got one, prints all sorts.

…and honestly, the thought of her navigating the NHS on her own gives me the shivers. It's just…different over there, isn’t it? More streamlined, perhaps. Though, admittedly, having to pay out of pocket for everything wasn't exactly a picnic either. Different is putting it mildly, Moira. It's a monumental undertaking, isn’t it? Bringing someone from Australia, settling them in. Especially after all this time. Fifteen years, you said? Fifteen years next month. It feels…surreal. I’ve been Skyping, of course, and we visit when we can, but it’s not  living  with her. Not being able to just…pop round. And now she’s actually doing it. Selling up everything, leaving her life. It's brave, isn’t it? But also…a bit unsettling for me. Brave, absolutely. And, understandably, unsettling for you. You’re used to things being a certain way, and this is a big shake-up. Have you thought about where she’ll live? Still looking at that little flat near the seafront? That's the plan. It's small, but perfectly formed. And the location is brilliant. She loved it when we viewed it together. I’ve put a deposit down, thankfully. Trying to handle everything from here is a headache. Renting, utilities… it’s all so complicated. God, I miss just having a simple life. Retirement isn't quite the quiet existence I’d imagined! Trust me, I understand that. Suddenly you're dealing with broadband packages and council tax. It's not exactly relaxing. Are you worried about her finding work? That’s a big thing, isn't it? Teaching qualifications don’t always transfer seamlessly. That is the bugbear, isn’t it? She’s qualified, of course, excellent even. But the system here… It’s all about experience  within  the UK system. She’s emailing schools, sending out CVs, but the responses are… lukewarm, to say the least. I keep telling her not to despair, that it’ll happen, but I'm secretly worried she’ll end up having to take something below her skill level. It breaks my heart a little, seeing her ambition potentially sidelined. She’s a resilient girl, your Fiona. Always has been. She’ll land on her feet. Perhaps some supply work to start with? Get her foot in the door? She's already registered with a few agencies. That’s what I suggested.

…and honestly, the whole thing with the SNP pushing for another referendum just feels…exhausting, doesn't it? Like, haven’t we been through enough of this already? It’s not like anything fundamentally  changed  since 2014. Exhausting is a good word for it, David. A very good word. Brighton’s seen its share of political drama over the years, but this Scottish business…it just rumbles on. I used to teach a lot of Scottish students, you know. Brilliant kids, passionate. You could always tell where they stood on the issue, of course. I can imagine. It's such a deeply held feeling for a lot of people. Though the arguments seem to be the same recycled points, endlessly debated. Speaking of things endlessly debated, how did that interview go for the Head of Department position? Any news? Oh, that. Right. Well, it went…okay. Perfectly  okay . They said they were very impressed with my experience, naturally. Thirty-odd years in the classroom, you pick things up. But they also seemed…keen on someone with a more ‘dynamic’ vision. Which, as far as I can tell, translates to ‘younger and willing to implement a load of pointless new initiatives.’ Oh, the “dynamic vision” brigade. They’re everywhere. It's code for ‘we want someone cheaper who'll do what we tell them’. Don't beat yourself up about it, Arthur. You’re a fantastic teacher. Everyone says so. Remember old Mrs. Higgins? She still sends me Christmas cards talking about how you saved young Timmy Peterson from academic ruin. Ah, Timmy Peterson. That was a case. Right little terror, he was. But yes, Mrs. Higgins is a kind soul. It's just…it would have been nice. A bit of a capstone, you know? Getting to shape things at that level. I get it. But honestly, shaping things rarely lives up to the hype. More meetings, more paperwork, more headaches. You're doing vital work where you are. And… how’s your daughter, by the way? Last I heard she was applying for that gallery internship? She got it! Alice got the internship in London. She's over the moon, absolutely buzzing. It’s unpaid, naturally, which is a bit of a sticking point, but she’s found a room share with a couple of other art students. Says it’s ‘bohemian’ and ‘characterful’. I suspect it’s damp and infested with something.

… honestly, the sheer  volume  of plastic toys they have over there is astonishing. And wrapped in plastic! It’s just… excessive. We were at a birthday party, little Timmy’s sixth, and the presents just kept coming. Mountains of it. Sounds about right. Remember that trip to Florida with work? The shops were just… overwhelming. Everything supersized, including the consumerism. Still, Timmy sounds like he had a good birthday. Yeah, it’s definitely a different culture. More ‘go big or go home’ than here, isn’t it? Though, I guess we have our excesses too. Just… different ones. Right, so if I attach this here… hopefully it’ll actually launch the marble. This mousetrap game is proving more difficult than I thought. Well, it  is  engineering, darling. Though slightly unconventional engineering. You’ve got good ideas, Leo, just needs a bit of tweaking. Your Grandad used to build things like this, you know. Complex contraptions with string and pulleys. He’d have loved this. Oh, your Grandad would have  adored  this! He always said a good puzzle was better than any television programme. He’d have been dissecting the mousetrap within five minutes, trying to ‘improve’ it. Speaking of puzzles… remember that time you tried to explain cricket to that American couple in Virginia, Margaret? It took nearly an hour and they still looked utterly baffled. Don’t remind me! They were lovely people, truly. But the concept of a game lasting five days with seemingly nothing happening? Completely beyond them. They kept asking if there was a scoreboard showing  immediate  progress. "It’s a test of endurance, dear," I said. They just blinked. It's funny how different things are considered entertainment. I was talking to a friend who spent a year teaching in Texas, and he said the parents were just…helicoptering over everything. Every test, every minor setback. It’s like they were trying to insulate their kids from any form of disappointment. That’s what I've heard. It’s a very driven culture, apparently. Pressure to succeed from a very young age. Makes you wonder about their childhoods, doesn't it? Ours felt much more…free-range. Free-range like those chickens Mum keeps trying to convince us to eat? Don’t be impertinent, Leo. Though your mother  is  rather keen on self-sufficiency. But yes, freer than a lot of modern childhoods, I think. We were allowed to roam, get muddy, build dens… fall over and scrape our knees.

… honestly, the silk market was  mad . Utterly mad. But I think I navigated it. Mostly. You wouldn’t believe the sheer volume of… everything. Mad how? Tourist-trap mad, or genuinely overwhelming mad? And more importantly, did you get what you went for? You were on a mission for decent cashmere, weren’t you? Both, actually. Tourist-trap  and  overwhelming. The stallholders are… persistent, let’s say. And yes, the cashmere mission was partially successful. But I got distracted. Severely distracted. Distracted by…? Let me guess. Shiny things? You have a weakness for shiny things. Okay, guilty. But not  just  shiny. I found this incredible tailor, tucked away down a side street. He showed me some fabrics and… well, I may have commissioned a coat. A coat? Just a coat? You sound suspiciously vague. Knowing you, it's not just ‘a coat’. Is it lined with unicorn tears and woven from moonlight? Don’t be ridiculous. Though, it  is  lined with silk, a beautiful deep burgundy. And it’s not just any coat, it’s a cheongsam-inspired coat. A sort of fusion, you see? I was thinking something I could wear back home, with jeans, or over a dress. Something a bit different. A cheongsam-inspired coat… that sounds… ambitious. And very you. Did you show me a sketch, or are you springing this on me now? I’m picturing something incredibly dramatic, all mandarin collars and… No sketch! I didn’t think to. It was all a bit impulsive, I admit. He just had this amazing bolt of tweed, a really proper, Yorkshire-mill-looking tweed, but in this deep teal, and then he showed me some silks… It just… clicked. I explained I wanted the silhouette of a cheongsam – the fitted waist, the slant – but in something a bit more autumnal, a bit more wearable in Norwich weather. Norwich weather. Right. So, practical  and  fabulous. Excellent. How much did this impulse buy set you back? Don't tell me it was extortionate. My lecturer salary can only stretch so far supporting your fashion whims. It wasn’t  extortionate . It was… reasonable. Considering it's bespoke and made with incredibly good quality materials. Around £300, I think. £300? Not bad, actually. For bespoke tailoring, that’s a steal. Although, I'm picturing the inevitable alterations when it arrives. You know your proportions better than anyone, and Chinese tailors...

…and honestly, the ref was blind, absolutely blind! Didn’t see that clear knock-on in the 22nd minute. Cost us the game, it did. A blatant forward pass right before that too. Could’ve been a different story altogether. Yeah, but Ireland were getting hammered in the scrums, Dad. They couldn't hold them, could they? It wasn’t  just  the ref. Honestly, you two. It’s a game. Relax. Though I have to admit, the shouting did wake Leo up briefly. He thought you were arguing again! Oh, boys will be boys, and rugby will always bring out the passion. It reminds me of the schoolyard arguments we used to have about the Scottish and English teams. Fierce stuff, that was. Though nowadays, I mostly just enjoy seeing young people active. Do  you  still play rugby at school, love? Nah, not rugby. I tried it in Year 7, but I’m better at football. We’ve got a match next week, actually. Important one, quarter-finals. Football, is it? Right so. Still, good to be involved in something. Keeps you fit. Remember your Grandad, Mary? He was a fierce footballer back in his day. Could’ve gone pro, he could have. He always said he preferred having a steady job though, didn't he? Said the glory didn’t pay the bills. Speaking of which, are we all set for Oisin’s birthday on Saturday? I’ve got the cake ordered, a dinosaur one, naturally. Dinosaur! Excellent. Little man’s obsessed, isn’t he? I’ve got his present wrapped and ready to go. A proper adventurous book, about a wee dinosaur who goes exploring. Grand. I'm picking up the bouncy castle on Saturday morning. Mary, did you manage to get enough of those little party hats? I think so. I got a pack of twenty. Should be enough between the kids and a few of the adults indulging their inner child. Right, cards. Have we all signed Oisin's card yet? I left it on the kitchen counter. I signed it earlier, Mum. Wrote a really cool drawing of him as a T-Rex. A T-Rex, is it? Wonderful. I just wrote the usual, “Happy Birthday, hope you have a great day.” Bit boring, I know. Nonsense, dear. Simple and heartfelt is always best. It’s the thought that counts, isn't it? Now, it's getting late.

… honestly, the sheer volume of baby stuff is baffling. Like, how do people  need  this much paraphernalia? Auntie Carol’s already sent three different types of bottle steriliser! Three! As if one isn’t enough to make you question your life choices. Oh, the steriliser brigade are strong. My sister got sent five muslins.  Five . Apparently, babies are perpetually needing wiping, which I guess is fair. But five? It’s just…excessive. How’s Leo coping with the impending doom, then? He seems pretty chill for a soon-to-be big brother. He's mostly just asking if the baby will take his dinosaurs. Which, honestly, is a fair question. I keep saying they’ll both have dinosaurs, but I think he’s secretly imagining a tiny human solely dedicated to dismantling his meticulously arranged prehistoric kingdom. It’s kind of sweet. It's just...everything's feeling a bit crammed at the moment. We’re seriously starting to feel the pinch in the flat. Still thinking about moving then? You were mentioning that place near Grantchester, wasn’t it? A bit further out, but sounds lovely. Yeah, we had another look on Saturday. It’s…nice. A proper garden, which is the big draw. And a spare room, which is less about the baby and more about Leo needing his own space to, you know, strategise dinosaur defense. The downside is the commute for me, obviously. But it's only a bus ride, and a chance to finally listen to all those linguistics podcasts I've downloaded. That does sound good. It's a proper step though, isn’t it? Moving with a little one on the way...brave! Speaking of steps, I finally had a clear-out of my wardrobe. You're always moaning about needing more space, and I was thinking… anything you fancy pinching? I’ve got loads of stuff I haven't worn in ages, and your style's way better than mine. Oh, you  angel . That would be amazing, honestly! I’m trying to be sensible and not buy loads of new clothes because, well, baby. But a little wardrobe refresh could be exactly what I need. Anything vaguely work-appropriate would be a lifesaver – sensible skirts, blouses…you know the drill. Compared to your slightly more…artistic choices, mine are quite beige, really. Beige is good! Beige is professional! And easily accessorized. I've got tons of stuff that falls into that category.

…No, seriously, I’m telling ya, Old Man Hemmings down the road, he reckons his accent’s proper RP.  Proper  Received Pronunciation. Like he went to Eton or somethin’. It's just… Bedfordshire posh, innit? Sounds like he’s gargling gravel. Hemmings? He’s always been a bit of a character. I think he  wants  to sound like that BBC newsreader. It’s a bit of a performance, really. You pick up things teaching, you know? The whole idea of ‘correct’ pronunciation… it’s a social construct. Social construct? Sounds a bit fancy for a Tuesday night in yer nan’s lounge, don’t it, Liam? I just know when someone sounds a bit… off. Like when tourists try and do a London accent. Painful. Exactly! And it's not just the tourists. I was chatting to this bloke yesterday, tryin’ to sell an old guitar – a Squier Strat, mint condition - and he tried to haggle me down sayin' it wasn’t “a proper instrument.” Like my gear ain’t good enough because  he  thinks he knows about guitars. Oh, the guitar world is full of gatekeepers. What were you asking for it? I might know someone… actually, scratch that, probably not. Everyone wants a Fender these days. £200. Figured that was fair. I mostly use it for messin’ about, but it sounds decent. Been gettin' back into it, actually. Good stress relief, y'know? Better than watchin’ all that UFC stuff you’re into, Stefan. Hey! UFC’s strategic! It’s a chess match with punches. And it’s useful. You gotta know how to defend yourself these days. Especially workin’ like I do, wanderin' around people’s gardens. Seen some dodgy characters. Speaking of dodgy, anyone watch that new true crime doc on Netflix? The one about the… well, I won't spoil it. It’s unsettling. Reminds you how quickly things can go wrong. Nah, I'm still workin’ through  Peaky Blinders  again. And tryin’ to finish that board game I got off eBay. ‘Terraforming Mars’. Gets proper complicated. Mum keeps offerin’ me biscuits, distractin’ me mid-strategy. Biscuits are essential to any good board game. Though, speaking of essential, I'm off the fags again. Fourth time this year. Feels better already, though I miss ‘em down the pub. Good on you, Stefan. Tough habit to kick. I’ve been trying to eat a bit better myself.

… honestly, the price of petrol is just  criminal  now, isn’t it? I filled up yesterday and nearly had a heart attack. It was like, seventy-five quid for a half-tank. Tell me about it! I'm dreading my next fill-up. I’m seriously considering cycling more, even with the… Peterborough weather. At least it’s free fuel, right? Though, admittedly, getting soaked isn’t exactly appealing. Cycling? You? No offence, darling, but you haven’t voluntarily done any strenuous activity since we finished that hiking trail in the Peak District. And  that  was mostly complaining. Hey! I enjoyed parts of that! The pub at the end, specifically. Look, I’m just saying I’m thinking about it. It’s just… driving is becoming so expensive. Especially with the commute. You don't have that problem, lucky you, working from home most days. True, I'm definitely saving a fortune on petrol. Although, saving  is  proving difficult in general. I was looking at car insurance quotes today for when my renewal comes through, and they’re all insane. Seriously. I’m half tempted to just… not drive at all. Not drive? But you said you needed the car for getting back to Mum and Dad’s? And for those pottery classes you're taking? I know, I know. It’s just… the costs are piling up. It wouldn't be so bad if the car didn’t drink petrol like it was going out of fashion. Remember when we were looking at getting a more economical car a few years back? Before you got promoted and suddenly had a company car? Right, when I was still driving that… well, let's just say it was a character-building vehicle. The Fiesta. Honestly, for what it cost to keep that thing running, we could've put a deposit down on something newer. I didn’t realise how much I relied on having a reliable car until I had one. Exactly! And now  my  reliable car is becoming a money pit. I’m trying to figure out if it’s worth getting it serviced, or if it’s just throwing good money after bad. It's an old Volvo, you know they can be deceptively expensive to fix. Definitely get a quote. A good mechanic can tell you straight. Maybe it’s just something small. Have you tried Dave down at the garage on Oak Street?

…and honestly, lad, I don’t know  why  they keep changing the bin collections. It’s a right palaver, isn’t it? Last week it was Tuesday, this week it's Friday. You’d think after all these years they’d get it sorted. Yeah, Grandma was going on about it too. Says Mr. Henderson next door missed it and his recycling's overflowing. He’s not best pleased. Mr. Henderson  never  is pleased. Grumpy old soul. Remembers when we just had one bin for everything! Simpler times, eh, Arthur? Aye, simpler times, Maggie. Everything's too complicated now. All this sorting… what's the point anyway? They just mix it all up at the depot, I reckon. Don’t start that, Arthur. You know that’s not true. It’s about the environment. Although, I’ll grant you, the system  is  a bit chaotic. Right, I was thinking, seeing as you two are here, could one of you possibly give the lawn a trim tomorrow? It's looking a bit wild. Tomorrow? I was gonna meet up with Ben and Liam to practice for the mocks. History’s killing me. Oh, the mocks. Right. Well, perhaps Arthur could give it a go? You always had a good eye for a straight line, didn’t you? My eyes aren’t what they used to be, lass. Can barely see the lawn, let alone trim it straight! And my back…don't even ask. Besides, I’m currently engaged in a very important strategic game of dominoes with Maggie. Highest score wins bragging rights for the week. Don’t you lie, Arthur! You’re letting me win. You always do! Now, now. Don’t bicker like children. Right. I suppose I can tackle it myself, then. It'll just add to the pile. Honestly, being a GCSE maths examiner is less stressful than dealing with household chores sometimes. Honestly, I saw some answers last year… you wouldn’t  believe  some of the things they try to get away with. Like what? Go on, tell us. Oh, where do I begin? One lad, bless him, tried to “prove” that pi equals three using his shoe size. A  shoe size ! And another attempted to solve a quadratic equation by drawing a picture of a cat. A cat! Oh, that's brilliant! Kids these days, eh? No common sense. They're too busy with their phones and their… their TikToks and things.

…and honestly, the whole “buried treasure” thing has really taken off with you two, hasn’t it? You’ve been drawing maps all morning. Leo, is that one for Captain Blackheart’s lost doubloons? Yep! It’s got a tricky bit though, ‘cause the X is  under  the garden gnome! But Dad says I can’t actually dig up Mr. Grumbles. My map has a secret code! It’s… …numbers! Each number means a letter. I’m still working on it, it’s hard. That sounds brilliant, Poppy! You’re little codebreakers, the two of you. Reminds me a bit of Shakespeare actually, all those hidden meanings and puzzles within the language. Which, speaking of, Shakespeare Week is coming up at school. We’re doing  A Midsummer Night’s Dream . Shakespeare? Is that about pirates? Not quite, love. It’s about fairies and magic and… well, a bit of a confusing love story. We might even try and go to Stratford-upon-Avon, see the Globe Theatre. Would you two like that? Stratford? Is it near the circus? Well, no, not exactly. But we’ve got something  way  more exciting lined up for next weekend! Remember I told you about the circus workshop? The REAL circus? With the big top? The very same! It’s at the actual circus grounds, not just a tent in a park. You’ll learn juggling, balancing, maybe even a little bit of trapeze! Though I suspect that might be a bit ambitious for the first session. Can I learn to make someone disappear? Like a magician? Maybe! They have a magic section as well. Although, I wouldn’t put too much faith in actual magic, my sweet. Mostly it’s clever tricks. It's all about illusion. I want to learn to escape from a box! That’s a very good ambition, Leo! Now, all this adventure talk is making me hungry. How about some lunch? Sandwiches okay? With crusts cut off? Please? Crusts will be surgically removed. What about after lunch? I was thinking we could finish looking through those Easter pictures Grandma sent. Remember the bunny ears? I made a really messy chocolate face in those photos! I remember! A very chocolatey face. And then, after that, I thought we could maybe start planning that stop-motion animation project you two were asking about. The one with the Lego pirates? Exactly! We could use the treasure maps as a backdrop.

…Honestly, the whole thing was utterly ridiculous. They just didn’t  understand . I’d explained, quite clearly I thought, about the… well, the navigational charts being somewhat optimistic. And the frankly appalling state of the engine.      Optimistic charts, you say, Margaret? Sounds like a recipe for disaster, even  before  the Saudi coast guard got involved. Jeddah to Cyprus in what, a fishing boat?      It wasn't a  fishing  boat, David, it was a… a coastal cruiser. A small one. And the idea was perfectly sound! A bit of an adventure, you see. I’d finished my contract teaching at the international school, had the boat seemingly in good order, and thought, why not? It was either that or fly back, and frankly, the idea of another airport…      Saudi Arabia then, Margaret? That’s a bit of a leap from Almondsbury, isn’t it? What was teaching like over there? I always imagined it being… restrictive.      Restrictive is… an understatement, Arthur. It was certainly  different . The children were bright, eager to learn English, of course. But the societal constraints… well, you had to be mindful. And the heat! Goodness, the heat. No, it was the sailing that was the relief, honestly. Until  they  turned up. They thought I was involved in some sort of smuggling operation. Can you imagine?      Smuggling? From Jeddah? What were you planning on bringing in, Margaret – dates and desert roses?      I wish it had been that simple, Bernard. Apparently, attempting to leave Saudi waters with a boat and a questionable engine is inherently suspicious. They kept asking about ‘contraband.’ I kept explaining about my desire for a quieter life in Cyprus. They weren't convinced.      And alcohol, I suppose, wasn’t part of the discussion? Trying to explain a wine cellar to a Saudi authority… now  that  would be a story. I remember being in Morocco once, trying to get a beer. You had to know the right people, the right cafe… it was a whole operation.      It’s a curious thing, isn’t it? The differing attitudes to alcohol. I spent some time in Spain years ago, and it was just… ubiquitous. Part of the culture. Then you go somewhere like Saudi, and it’s simply non-existent, legally speaking. Creates a certain… tension.      Tension? It creates a thirst! Though, I did once have a rather remarkable experience trying to explain to a customs official in Thailand that a particular dental instrument looked  very  much like a… well, a rather discreet bottle opener.

…Honestly, the state of the bathroom this morning was beyond a joke. Flannels  on the floor , toothpaste splattered everywhere… it's like a bomb went off. And he just sauntered out, whistling!      Oh, tell me about it. Young lads, aren’t they? My Darren was the same. Thought the bathroom was a personal art studio when he hit fifteen. Used to find glitter in the most  unexpected  places. Are you speaking about Jamie, then?      I am. Jamie. It's just… the lack of consideration. I asked him politely to just  rinse  his mouth out after brushing, that's all. Basic hygiene. And it was met with a grunt. A grunt, Brenda!      It's not  that  bad, Mum.      Jamie! Don't ‘Mum’ me when you're deliberately ignoring me. You heard what I said about the bathroom.      Yeah, yeah. Sorry. I was just… sorting out something for school. Mr. Henderson wants us to start thinking about work experience.      Work experience! Goodness, where does the time go? Darren ended up at a builders’ merchants. Absolutely hated it. Said he spent the whole week stacking boxes and trying not to look bored. Though, it did teach him the value of a good cup of tea, apparently.      That's the worry, isn’t it? What does Jamie even  want  to do? He’s talked about being an explorer, a footballer, a… YouTube star. All within the same week.      It’s a big world, Mum! And YouTube is a legit career now!      I know, I know. It's just… I want him to have opportunities. He's bright, he really is. I was thinking maybe something creative, given he's always sketching. Or even helping out at a marketing firm for a week? I could maybe arrange something.      That’s a good idea, actually, Sarah. You're always busy with your proofing jobs, he'd learn a lot. It’s good to get a taste of the real world. Unlike some of those 'influencers' he's probably watching! Speaking of which, is he… seeing anyone at the moment? Darren’s niece had her heart broken last year and it was awful to watch.      Oh,  that . Yes. There’s a girl, Chloe. Apparently, she’s in his History class. He’s being ridiculously secretive about it. All moping around and cryptic text messages. I tried to ask, and he just slammed his door. Honestly, it's all a bit melodramatic.

… honestly, I still can’t believe how much truffle oil they put on  everything  here. It’s lovely, don’t get me wrong, but a bit… much. Like, truffle oil on chips? Come on. Ah, you’ve gotta embrace it, love. They're proper proud of their truffles ‘round here. My friend, Marija, she showed me where her brother goes foraging. Proper dedication, it is. Up at dawn, dogs and everything. Dogs find truffles? That's cool! Do they get to eat them? Apparently, they’re trained  not  to, young man. Though I imagine the temptation must be enormous. It’s all about scent, you see. The dogs can sniff them out underground. Remarkable, really. Similar principles to some of the new diagnostic work with stem cells, actually. Identifying minute changes in cellular odour… Oh here we go. Stem cells at 8 am on a Croatian road trip. You’re incorrigible, aren't you, David? Well, it's interesting! And it demonstrates the power of observation. Just like this truffle hunting. Deduction. Pattern recognition. Skills they don’t seem to be fostering enough in the education system these days. All this focus on rote learning… Now, now, David. Leave the education system alone. Ethan’s doing alright, aren’t you, pet? And it’s not all rote learning. They're doing project-based things now. My niece, she had to build a working model of the digestive system! It was messy. Loads of yoghurt and biscuits. Oh, I can imagine! Right messy. Speaking of messy, remember Uncle Barry trying to cook paella in America? Absolute disaster. He nearly set the apartment on fire. Don’t remind me! The smoke alarm wouldn’t stop. And the smell… it lingered for weeks. He insisted he’d watched a “proper chef” on the telly and knew exactly what he was doing. Chefs. I’ve consulted for a few restaurant chains, you know. The demands are incredible. The pressure. It’s less about cooking and more about logistics and people management. Yeah, but some proper chefs are artists, aren’t they? Like that bloke, Marco Pierre White. Proper fiery temper, but brilliant. Though I've heard he's calmed down now. He smoked like a chimney, didn’t he? Terrible habit. I used to see nurses trying to sneak a cigarette behind the hospital. You wouldn’t get away with that now, would you?

… honestly, it’s just  exhausting  trying to explain to people what I actually  do . “Language Research Co-ordinator” sounds so… grand, doesn’t it? Like I’m orchestrating linguistic revolutions. When really, half my week is spent wrestling with transcription software and chasing down participants who promised they’d record themselves saying ‘bath’ and ‘grass’ ages ago. Sounds delightfully academic, actually. Beats writing ad copy about sustainably sourced dog biscuits, I can tell you that. Though, you’d be surprised how much linguistic nuance goes into persuading people their pooches  need  ethically produced treats. Dog biscuits? Seriously? That’s digital marketing now? I thought you were doing, like, fancier stuff, Liam. Tech companies or something? Nah, branched out. More money in pet products, apparently. Plus, it lets me use my linguistic training – subtly, of course. It's all about framing. "Nourish your best friend" versus "Give your dog a biscuit." Huge difference in conversion rates. That  is  fascinating, actually. The power of framing. Reminds me of some of the research we’re doing on regional dialect shifts. How subtle changes in phrasing can completely alter perception. We’ve got this one researcher, brilliant chap, studying how the use of ‘like’ has evolved amongst younger speakers in the East of England. It’s… a rabbit hole. ‘Like’ is  everywhere . I probably say it ten times a conversation. My mum absolutely hates it. Says it makes me sound indecisive. Oh, mums. Mine’s the same, though hers is a crusade against ‘literally’ being used to mean ‘figuratively’. It drives her mad. And being from Aylesbury, I’m very aware of how my accent shifts depending on who I’m talking to. Around here, in Cambridge, I subconsciously soften the vowels, I think. Try to sound… less ‘Bucks’. Do you? I hadn’t noticed. I just assume everyone in the South sounds posh. No offence. None taken! It’s the stereotype, isn't it? I mean, I went to a pretty decent state school, and my dad’s a mechanic. I’m definitely not naturally “posh.” It’s just… adaptation, I suppose. We’re all chameleons, linguistically speaking. I've noticed that with myself. Back home in Cambridge, I don't even  think  about how I'm saying things. But when I'm talking to my aunt in Cornwall, I find myself dragging out the vowels a bit, almost subconsciously trying to make it easier for her to understand me.

… honestly, I still think driving all the way from Calais was a bit mad, even split between the two of us. My back is  killing  me. Though, honestly, anything is better than flying these days, isn't it? The sheer chaos at airports… You say that  now , after I did the majority of the driving from, well, pretty much Paris onwards? You were quite happy navigating and critiquing my playlist for the first six hours! And yes, airports are a nightmare. Though I think we avoided the worst of it getting  to  Calais, thankfully. I’m just glad we remembered the vignette for Poland. That would have been a disaster. Oh, don’t be like that. The playlist  was  a bit…enthusiastic. A lot of aggressive Northern anthems, if I recall. And I did my fair share of the admin, booking the campsites and painstakingly researching the best route to avoid the school holidays traffic. Though, looking back, perhaps “best” is a strong word. This road is…rustic. Rustic is kind. It’s definitely… characterful. Still, nearly there. Just another twenty minutes or so according to the satnav, and then we’re at Kasia’s. Hopefully, she’s made enough pierogi. She always goes overboard. Oh, I certainly hope so! I’ve been dreaming about her pierogi since we decided to come. It's the only thing that’s kept me going through some of these…interesting…driving experiences. Are you sure we have the right address? This feels… very residential. Positive. Kasia sent me a Google Maps link, and I triple-checked it. It's number 17, right? We should be looking for a slightly newer build, blue shutters, a rather flamboyant garden gnome… A garden gnome? Seriously? Kasia has a garden gnome? That doesn't sound like her at all. She always struck me as a minimalist. Although, I suppose living in Poland changes a person. Everything feels…different. In a good way, mostly. It just feels… slower. Less frantic than Cambridge. People embrace their kitsch here, I think. It’s part of the charm. And yes, a rather discerning gnome. Apparently, he’s called ‘Bogdan’. She sent a picture. Honestly, it's the only way I was confident we weren't meandering towards someone else's property. This whole trip was your idea, remember? ‘Let’s have a European adventure!’ you declared. Well, it  is  a European adventure!

… honestly, it’s just  awful . That new Man United kit. Absolutely dreadful. It's like they asked a child to design it. All those red stripes, criss-crossing… what were they thinking? Dramatic, aren’t we? I didn’t think it was  that  bad. A bit busy, maybe. Though, yeah, it’s not exactly a classic. Remember the Newcastle one a few years back? The one that looked like a barcode?  That  was properly ropey. Oh god, don’t even  mention  that. That was insulting to the colour black, never mind the football club! But this… it’s just… modern for the sake of modern. They’re chasing trends, not heritage. And it's all fuelled by the sponsors, isn't it? Adidas wanting to look ‘youthful’ and ‘dynamic’. Definitely a sponsor-driven thing. It’s the whole ‘lifestyle’ branding now. They want the kit to sell as fashion, not just as something you wear to the match. Which is… I don't know, a bit depressing, really. Especially when you think about what kits used to be like. Simple, iconic. Exactly! My grandad still has his 70s Sunderland kit. It's just a red and white stripe, proper thick ones. It’s beautiful in its simplicity. You wouldn't catch anyone wearing a modern kit ironically these days because it’s  already  trying too hard. Speaking of sponsors… did you see the uproar about the potential McDonald’s sponsorship of the England women’s team? Oh aye, that was a right mess wasn’t it? Honestly, the irony! Promoting healthy lifestyles through a fast-food chain. It screamed hypocrisy. Though, let’s be realistic, they’ll take anyone’s money, won't they? The FA need funding. It's a difficult balance, isn’t it? They need the money to invest in grassroots, and sponsorships are a massive part of that. But there's a line, surely. McDonald’s… it just feels… particularly egregious. It sends such a mixed message to young girls getting into the sport. It does. And the backlash was pretty immediate, thankfully. I saw some cracking tweets. People pointing out how many of the Lionesses are actually really vocal about healthy eating. Like, imagine having to promote a Happy Meal as part of your sponsorship deal! Awkward. Seriously awkward. It highlights the really problematic nature of sports sponsorship full stop, doesn’t it? We’re celebrating athleticism and peak physical condition, and then plastering it all over adverts for sugary drinks and junk food.

… honestly, it’s just the principle of it, innit? She got a  fortune  from Gran, a proper fortune, and she’s blowing it on… well, frankly, just rubbish. Designer handbags and weekend breaks. I mean, Gran wanted it to be used wisely. Tell me about it. It’s always the way, though, isn’t it? Easy come, easy go. Especially when it ain't  their  effort puttin’ the money in the bank to begin with. Still, not our business, really. Though it does… rankle, doesn't it? When you’re struggling to keep the lights on. Exactly! And don't even  start  me on the lights. The gas bill came this morning and… well, I nearly choked on my toast. Mum's fretting already about winter. I was thinking maybe a day trip with the kids, just something to get us out, but realistically, even train tickets these days… A day trip? Where were you thinkin'? Brighton? I remember when you could practically get a return for a fiver. Now it's… what, thirty quid each? Criminal. And don't trust the trains anyway. Last time I went to London, crammed in like sardines, and then delayed for two hours because of “leaves on the line.” Leaves! In  September ! Classic. I was thinking maybe Rye. It’s a bit closer, but still, the costs add up. I’ve been trying to keep an eye on eBay for deals on winter coats for Leo and Maisie. They grow out of things so fast, it’s ridiculous. I just won one for Leo, thankfully. Five quid! Five quid? Result! You’re a whizz on that eBay, you are. I tried it once, years ago, to sell some old footie cards. Got completely rinsed. Bid up by some bloke in… I dunno, sounded foreign. Thought I was getting a good price, then he just didn’t pay. Nightmare. Oh, that’s awful! You have to be careful. I always check their feedback. Actually, that reminds me… last week, I was waiting for the bus and this man asked me for directions. He had a really strong accent, and I instantly thought… and I feel terrible saying this… I instantly thought he was trying to con me. Honestly, it was awful realising how quickly I jumped to that conclusion. It happens. You see things on the news, don't you? Blokes targeting old ladies and all that.

… honestly, the traffic was  brutal . Sat nav kept trying to take me down roads that were basically farm tracks. Honestly, you’d think for the price of these things they could filter out unsuitable routes. Did you manage to get to Morrison's alright, Brenda? Aye, just. Went a bit roundabout, avoiding the city centre. Took me nearly forty minutes, which is ridiculous for five miles. They’ve got those temporary lights on Oundle Road again, haven't they? Absolute nightmare. Temporary lights…they’re never temporary, are they? Always drag on for months. Reminds me of when they were building that bypass, back in…oh, goodness, must’ve been the seventies. Took them a year and a day. Old Mr. Henderson used to camp out there, protesting. Said it ruined his view of the cows. Oh, Peterborough. Always something. Anyway, I just needed a few bits. Thought I’d treat myself to a decent bottle of wine. Work’s been…intense. Had a potential client threaten to go with a competitor  yesterday . Classic bluff, I reckon, but still. Enough to raise the blood pressure. Oh dear. Sales, eh? Always stressful. Still, you’re good at it, love. Always have been. Better than my Darren ever was at anything, bless him. Thanks, Brenda. It's…a juggling act. It's amazing how much time is spent just  managing  people. It's less about the actual accounts these days and more about fire-fighting. Speaking of juggling, did you make that apple crumble for tea, Mum? It smelled heavenly when I came in. I did indeed. Got a lovely batch of Braeburns from the market. Though, I say, this little wart on my hand is getting right on my nerves. Been trying all sorts of creams. Doctor says it’s nothing to worry about, just age, but it's unsightly. I read you can put garlic on 'em, Mrs. Davies. Crushed garlic. Supposed to draw it out. Bit smelly, mind. Garlic? Oh, I don’t know. The smell! Though, desperate times… I remember your grandmother swearing by vinegar. Put vinegar on everything, she did. Even her roses! Honestly, you two. Garlic, vinegar…sounds like something out of a witch's recipe book. I'm sticking to the doctors' opinions, thank you very much. Though, food is always a good distraction. Anyone fancy a biscuit with their coffee? I got some lovely shortbread. Ooh, go on then.

… honestly, it was  so  awkward. Mrs. Davies, she tried to be all cool, saying “Right, guys, let’s just… vibe with Shakespeare,” and everyone just stared. Vibe with Shakespeare? What does that even  mean ? Oh my god, no way! She actually said ‘vibe’? That’s… peak Davies, isn’t it? She’s trying so hard to be relatable. It just comes across as… well, you know. Exactly! It feels like she watched one TikTok and thought she understood teenagers. And then she asked if anyone had, like, "Shakespearean inspo" for their character analysis. Inspo! Honestly, I nearly choked on my pen. Seriously! She’s a trainee teacher, innit? You’d think they’d tell them to tone it down a bit. Mr. Harrison, he’s alright. A bit boring, maybe, but at least he  teaches  us stuff. Did you finish that titration for Science? I’m stressing. Titration? Ugh, don’t even  mention  titration. I completely messed it up. I added too much indicator, and the colour change was… muddy. Miss Lewis was so unimpressed. She kept giving me this look. It’s not even about the mark, it's the look! Oh, I know the look. The ‘you-should-be-trying-harder’ look. I think I got away with it, but I had to ask Chloe three times to explain the calculations. She’s a lifesaver, that one. Speaking of lifesavers, have you seen Leo in Art? He's created this massive sculpture out of recycled plastic bottles. No! Seriously? Leo? The one who can barely draw a stick figure? I know, right? It's genuinely incredible though. It's supposed to represent the ocean, all these different shades of blue and green. He says it’s a protest against pollution. Very dramatic. That’s… unexpectedly brilliant. Maybe I underestimated him. I’ve been too busy worrying about the English test next week. It's on poetry, and I just can’t  get  Wilfred Owen. All that imagery of war… it's depressing. I know what you mean. It's heavy stuff. But if you focus on the symbolism, it’s easier. Miss Davies – ironically – actually explained it quite well. She said it’s about the loss of innocence, and how war strips people bare. Oh,  now  she’s explaining things properly. Maybe she only does it when she’s not trying to ‘vibe’. I just wish she’d pick a persona and stick with it.

…No, but seriously, Mrs. Davies was going on about it in RE today. How nuns  choose  to live like that. Like, voluntarily giving up everything. It’s… weird, innit? Weird is one word for it, Leo. It’s a commitment, a very specific one, to their faith. It’s not for everyone, obviously. It’s not something  you  would choose, is it? No way! Imagine never having a Playstation, or… or going to a football match! Or, like, getting a girlfriend. It's a bit extreme, isn’t it? Goo goo… nun! Shiny! Shiny habits, Finn thinks. Bless him. Leo, it's a different worldview. They believe they’re serving a higher purpose. It’s like… remember that film,  The Matrix ? Oh, yeah! The one where everyone thinks everything’s real but it’s all a computer simulation? Exactly. They believe this life isn't the  whole  picture, that there's something beyond. For them, dedicating themselves to God is… stepping outside the ‘Matrix’, in a way. Finding the true reality. But that’s, like, extreme escapism, isn’t it? Just… ignoring the real world? And what about Scientology? Old Mr. Henderson in the village keeps going on about it. He said it'll make you 'clear'. Sounds dodgy. Scientology  is  dodgy, love. That’s… a whole other can of worms. It’s very different to something like Catholicism. It’s about money and control, not about genuine spiritual seeking. Don't even go there. It’s best to just nod politely and walk away. But how can you  tell  the difference? Mrs. Davies said all religions are about faith, and believing in something you can’t prove. That’s true, to a point. But look at the actions. Look at the people involved. Does it feel open and welcoming? Or does it feel… secretive and demanding? Does it try to help others, or just take from them? Think about Mr. Henderson. He’s constantly trying to recruit people and asking for donations. That's a red flag. Right. So like, helping Ms. Peterson with her shopping when she can't get out is good, but trying to get everyone to give you their life savings isn’t? Precisely. You're a bright lad. And look, faith is personal. Your friend, Ben, his family are really religious, aren’t they? Yeah, they go to church every Sunday. Ben never talks about it much.

…Honestly, like, I just can’t get my head around the quickstep. It’s  all  about looking effortless, isn’t it? And I’m over here looking like a startled penguin. Mr. Henderson just keeps saying “Flow, lass, flow!” as if it’s that easy.      Flow, lass, flow. Sounds… encouraging? You’re doing dancing lessons? Since when?      Since last month! Carol from work convinced me. She's dead good. Says it’s brilliant for confidence. I’m mostly embarrassed, to be fair. It’s a world away from spreadsheets and tagging linguistic data, that’s for sure. Speaking of which, I’m still slightly behind on the Old English corpus. Professor Davies wants the clause structure analysed by Friday.      Oh, the joys of academia. Sounds… stressful. I’m drowning in stress myself, dealing with this infrastructure project. They want me to justify every single calculation, like I haven’t just spent three years at uni and another one doing a Masters for this. Anyway, fancy a holiday to escape it all? I was thinking maybe Cornwall? Proper cream teas and dodgy pasties.      Cornwall sounds reet good, actually. We were talking about it with Mam and Dad. They were reminiscing about when they went back in the 80s. They said it hadn’t changed a bit. Though Dad did go on about the metric system again. "Everything was bigger back then," he said, "proper pints, proper distances!" He's a right one for imperial measurements, is my Dad.      Classic Dad. He's not alone. I had an argument with a builder last week about the length of a cable run. He swore it was eight feet, I showed him on the tape measure it was closer to 2.4 metres. He almost had a heart attack.      See! It’s madness. Right, are we turning off here for the A19? Google Maps is being a bit vague.      Yeah, just up here. Though, honestly, Google Maps is usually terrible around Sunderland. Remember when it tried to navigate us through that industrial estate last time?      Don't even  start  me on that. I thought we were going to end up in a scrap yard. Speaking of endings…did you see that new series on LoveFilm, 'The Serpent'? Honestly, terrifying. And the actor playing Charles Sobhraj is amazing. Actually reminds me a bit of that bloke, what’s his name…the one who was in ‘Bridgerton’?      Regé-Jean Page?

… honestly, I still can’t believe how cheap the lavender honey was at that market this morning. Like, ridiculously cheap. Proper good stuff too, not that watered-down tourist tat. Aye, that market in Grožnjan was lovely. A bit hilly for pushchairs though, wasn’t it? Glad young Jamie didn’t complain too much. You alright back there, love? I’m fine, Mam. Just listening to music. And it wasn’t  that  hilly. I did okay. It’s quite a drive to Motovun, isn’t it? Thought we’d have covered more ground by now. Lovely scenery though. Much more… authentic than some of the coastal resorts. Authentic is a good word. It's miles better than Pula, even. All those stag dos. Ugh. Though, I did see a proper good mural in Pula, mind. All these little Istrian towns are bursting with art. Remember that tiny gallery in Bale? The one with the driftwood sculptures? Oh, I loved that one! Such interesting pieces. It’s nice to see people using natural materials. Speaking of natural, have you both tried the olive oil here? It’s nothing like what we get at home. Proper fruity. Can we get some to take home? For chips? Regular chips just aren’t the same without good olive oil. Absolutely. I’ve been meaning to ask, have you considered hiring a car for a few days, even just to explore further afield? This one's fine, perfectly functional, but it’s not exactly inspiring is it? A little…beige. Beige is putting it nicely, Dad. It's a practical vehicle, that’s all. And to be fair, driving here is…an experience. Those roads! Seriously narrow. I’m glad  you’re  doing the driving. It’s not so bad, once you get used to it. It's just you've got to be assertive. Though I’m dreading trying to reverse this thing anywhere. Honestly, I’ve handled easier births. Mam! Speaking of handling… I saw a caravan the other day. Massive thing. Gets you thinking. Perhaps a camping holiday next year? We could do Center Parcs, or even venture further afield. France, maybe? Camping? Absolutely not. I’ve seen  Sons of Anarchy . Campsites are just…asking for trouble. Too many people crammed together, too much potential for drama. I’d rather stay in a nice little Airbnb, thank you very much. Oh, don’t be silly, love.

…No, seriously, I’m just sayin’, it’s a bit weird, innit? Liam’s suddenly obsessed with… well, games that involve, like,  that . And he’s been askin’ proper strange questions. Oh, you mean…  adult  games? Liam? That's… unexpected. He always struck me as incredibly vanilla. Vanilla? Liam? Are we talkin’ about the same Liam who tried to convince us he could build a functional trebuchet in his garden? He’s anything  but  vanilla, love. He’s just… socially awkward about certain things. I think it's just a phase. Uni can do that to people, expose them to new ideas… and, well, new things. Though I agree with Chloe – asking questions like he did was a bit much. What  exactly  did he ask, anyway? Right, well, he was on about… recording stuff? For, like, “research purposes”. Said he wanted to ‘understand the mechanics’. Mechanics! Like he's building an engine, not… you know. And then he was askin’ if anyone had… experience. Recording? Oh, goodness. That’s… a whole other level. That’s illegal, isn't it? Without consent? Calm down, Amelia. He’s a bit of a weirdo, but I doubt he’d actually  do  anything. He’s probably just read something online and got a bit carried away. Trust me, knowin’ Liam, it's more likely to involve a spreadsheet and a highly detailed analysis than actual… anything. He's a planner, not a doer, usually. See, that’s what I’m thinkin'. It’s the planning that freaks me out! He was specifically askin’ about… anal. Like, what’s the best way to… prepare. Honestly, I nearly choked on my tea. And he kept using words like ‘pressure points’ and ‘dilation’. It was horrific! Okay, yeah, that’s… intensely awkward. That’s definitely crossing a line no matter how ‘research-minded’ he is. Poor whoever he was asking! It's not just awkward, it's predatory. Even  talking  about things like that without someone explicitly consenting is… wrong. Especially considering his supposed 'research' angle. That's a pretty flimsy excuse. Look, I’m not defendin’ his tact, alright? He’s got none. But Liam's not malicious. He just… doesn’t  get  social cues. Remember when he asked Mrs. Higgins if her cardigan was hand-knitted during her husband’s funeral? Oh, God, don't remind me! That was terrible. But this is different. This feels… deliberate.

…Aye, well that's what I’m sayin’, ya can’t beat a proper chip butty, can ya? Not this fancy stuff they try to sell ya now with rosemary salt and all that nonsense. Just chips, bread, and lashings of brown sauce. Simple. You’re a creature of habit, aren’t you, Dave? I mean, a chip butty's good, don’t get me wrong, but there’s a whole world of food out there. I had this amazing ramen the other day, down in Spinningfields. Seriously good stuff. Proper broth, spring onions, the works. Ramen? Sounds a bit…foreign, doesn’t it? Not really my cup of tea, that. Give me something I  know . Something me mam used to make. She did a cracking shepherd's pie. Though, she always put a bit too much Worcester sauce in it for my liking. You two are miles apart. Dave’s all about the comfort food, solid Northern grub. And Sarah’s always chasing the latest culinary trend. I’m somewhere in the middle, I reckon. I like a bit of both. It’s not a trend, Mark! It’s just…expanding my horizons. And honestly, you should try proper ramen. It's not just noodles in soup, it's an art form. It’s got umami, you know? That savoury…depth. Depth? It’s soup, lass. Soup’s soup. I’ll stick to a brew and a biscuit, thanks very much. Speaking of biscuits, did any of you get chance to try those new shortbread fingers in the canteen? They were a bit dry, weren’t they? Not like Grandma’s, obviously. Nothing is. I saw ‘em, but I went for a flapjack. Needed somethin’ a bit more…substantial for a mid-morning sugar rush. Teaching those first years about Boolean logic really drains you, you know? Tell me about it! Trying to explain the difference between AND and OR to someone who looks like they’ve never seen a computer before is…challenging. I swear, I aged ten years during that session. I could murder a decent pastry right now. Pastry? Now there's talkin’. A good Eccles cake. Now  that's  a Northern classic. Filled with currants, dusted with sugar. Perfect with a cup of tea. Eccles cakes are good, I’ll admit. Though I think I prefer a Bakewell tart. Almond paste, jam, icing…it’s a little bit posh, but still lovely.

…Honestly, I still don’t get the appeal of TikTok. All those fifteen-second dances. It just feels… frantic. Like everyone’s trying to compress their entire personality into a blink of an eye.      You sound like my dad, Geoff. He calls it ‘the fidget platform’. Though, you’ve gotta admit, some of it  is  quite clever. I saw one the other day about cataloguing Dewey Decimal System books using only hand gestures. It was surprisingly engaging.      Oh, I’ve seen that one! Brilliant, wasn’t it? It’s a good way to reach a different audience. We're forever banging on about the joys of library organisation, aren't we? Maybe a TikTok tutorial is just what we need. Though, I’m not sure I have the moves.      Me neither. I struggle to operate the self-checkout machine without looking like I'm wrestling with a robot. And don’t even mention Instagram. It's all filtered perfection. Give me a good, old-fashioned book any day. Real paper, real stories. None of this digitally enhanced nonsense.      I get where you’re coming from, Geoff. It is a bit… curated. But it’s also how people are connecting now. I’ve started using Instagram for the library’s book recommendations. Short video reviews. Little ‘shelfie’ contests. It’s actually increased engagement. Surprisingly.      It's about meeting people where they are, wouldn’t you say? We can’t expect everyone to come  to  the library; sometimes, we need to go  to  them. Though I do worry about the echo chambers. Everyone just reinforcing their own views. It’s a bit like those old chain letters, but on steroids. Remember those? "Send this to ten friends or you’ll have bad luck!"      Oh, aye, I remember those. My Nana used to be obsessed with them. She'd be photocopying them at work and getting the office into a right state. Said it was preventative medicine against misfortune. Funny woman, she was.      That  is  funny. It’s the same principle though, isn’t it? Spreading information, building communities… only now it’s algorithms and hashtags instead of photocopiers and superstition.      Very true. And the speed of it all! It’s breathtaking. Someone can have a global debate about the merits of e-books versus physical copies before I've even finished my morning cuppa.      Global debate… sounds exhausting. I prefer a quiet cuppa and the Daily Mail, personally.

...Honestly, Richard, I’m still not entirely convinced about Tunbridge Wells. It feels… a bit  comfortable  doesn’t it? We’re talking about end-of-life care, about reaching those who truly  need  it, not just serving a demographic that can afford a nice garden and a Waitrose on the high street.      Now, Penelope, that's a rather sweeping generalization. Tunbridge Wells has pockets of deprivation, believe me. And access is key. We’ve looked at the catchment area – it’s surprisingly broad. Sevenoaks, Crowborough… even reaching into parts of West Kent that are currently underserved. The transport links are excellent, which is crucial for visitors.      Transport links are all well and good, but what about the existing provision? I’ve been quietly asking around, and the fragmented nature of local health services in West Kent is deeply concerning. The coordination between the hospitals, GPs, and current community nurses feels… lacking. Will we be fighting to simply  fill the gaps  another service is supposed to be covering?      That’s precisely what the business case addresses. We’re not attempting to duplicate, we’re integrating. We’ve had preliminary talks with the Kent and Medway NHS Trust already. They’re… receptive. They  know  there’s a need for more specialist palliative care. And we need to demonstrate our ability to work  with  them, not against them. That’s why the consultation process is vital. Have you had a chance to look at the proposed stakeholder engagement strategy?      I have, and it feels… a little light on genuine patient voices, Richard. A few focus groups, a questionnaire on the website… It needs more depth. What about direct liaison with the local hospices? St. Julien’s, for example, does brilliant work. Don’t we need to understand their existing capacity, their expertise? We don’t want to step on toes, or worse, end up replicating services they already offer effectively.      A very fair point. I’ll add a specific action point to strengthen the hospice engagement. Perhaps a joint workshop session? We need their buy-in. Ultimately, this isn’t about competition, it's about providing the best possible care for patients. Speaking of which, the preliminary architectural sketches are in – I’d be interested in your opinion. We’re thinking of something less institutional, more… home from home. Lots of natural light, gardens, quiet spaces.      That sounds lovely, Richard. But ‘home from home’ can be expensive.

Oh, look at this one! Sarah and me, Blackpool, 1998. We look  awful , don’t we? Crimped hair, matching shell suits… what were we thinking? Blackpool, eh? I remember you talking about that trip. A right laugh, apparently. Though, honestly, the shell suit era… a dark time for fashion generally. You both look properly windswept. Oh my god, that  is  bad! But wonderfully, hilariously bad. You’re both pulling the same pose too! Is that intentional? Completely unintentional. We didn’t realise until years later when Mum pointed it out. She still brings it up, the cheeky cow. Speaking of Mum, did she ever tell you about Great-Grandad, the one who worked at Ascot? The stable lad? Bits and pieces. Something about muck-sweeping and a bit of betting, if I recall correctly. Didn't he nearly get sacked for backing the wrong horse? Nearly! He apparently put the house money on a nag that came in last. Gran always said she was grateful she didn't kill him then and there. Makes you think about Royal Ascot now, doesn’t it? All the glamour, and someone in our family was literally shovelling… well, you know. It's such a contrast! I’ve been doing some research for a campaign at work - luxury brands, ads for Ascot, the whole shebang. Apparently, there’s a real push for more diversity in the audience this year. It's interesting. Good. About time too, I reckon. It’s always felt a bit… exclusive. Right, what are we having? Smells lovely, love. Chicken casserole. Simple, but does the job. You had a long day at work, didn't you? How did the interview go for the new admin assistant? Painful. Honestly, she was lovely, bright as a button, but she kept… fidgeting with her phone. Constantly checking it. Said she was waiting for a delivery, then a message from her mum. It's just unprofessional, isn't it? That’s so awkward. Like, just put it away! It’s twenty minutes of your time, surely you can disconnect? It's the generation, I think. Attached to their devices. I saw a nurse the other day, texting during a handover. Honestly, you wouldn't believe it. Safety critical information! I had a word, obviously. You always do. You’re the voice of reason, you are. Did you get a new phone case, by the way?

…No, seriously, ‘The Descent’ absolutely ruined caving for me. Ruined it! I cannae even  think  about going down a hole in the ground now without picturing those pale, screeching… things. It’s daft, innit? It’s just a film. Daft, maybe, but I get it. Some films just burrow under your skin. Though, I thought ‘The Descent’ was pretty well-made, technically speaking. Good practical effects. Not just jump scares, you know? Aye, it were well made, I’ll grant ye that. But that's what makes it  worse ! It feels… realistic. Like it  could  happen. ‘Hereditary’ was like that too, proper unsettling. I had to sleep with the light on for a week after that one. Oh, ‘Hereditary’! That one was…oppressive, wasn't it? The whole atmosphere was just…wrong. But I think I prefer films that go for genuine psychological horror, rather than just buckets of gore. Like, ‘The Babadook’. That was genuinely scary, because it was about grief and motherhood, not just a monster under the bed. ‘The Babadook’ were good, yeah. Creepy as owt. But I do like a good jump scare now and then.
