The light, the colours… Vienna, of course, holds a special place, being where I was born, but Italy… that's where I truly felt alive. Did you get to see the Louvre, at least? Yeah, did the Louvre. Did the Eiffel Tower. Did all the touristy stuff. It was nice, proper buzzing, but honestly, I felt a bit… lost in translation, even with the few phrases I’d picked up. My French is atrocious. Well, that's understandable. Languages are tricky. I spent years trying to perfect my Italian, and even then, I'd still occasionally say something completely ridiculous. German, on the other hand, came much easier. Perhaps because of the roots, you see? My mother was Austrian. It has a certain… logical structure. Though, even  she  struggled with English pronunciations! Used to call a ‘herb’ a ‘hurb’ for years. A 'hurb'! That's brilliant! I’m trying to pick up a bit of German now, actually. Thought it might be useful. Though, I'm swamped with Classics stuff at the moment. Homer’s  Odyssey  is… a lot. Classics! That’s marvelous, dear. It’s so important to understand the foundations. It’s why I always encourage people to look beyond the surface. Just like with art, there's always a story beneath the colours, you see? Your father, bless his soul, always said you had a good head for that sort of thing. He'd be so proud of you going to university. Thanks, Gran. I miss him.

Honestly, Dad, you nearly gave me a heart attack back there! Changing lanes without indicating on the A31… it’s just asking for trouble. People drive like lunatics, especially on bank holiday traffic.      Oh, don’t be dramatic, love. I saw a gap, took it. Been driving longer than you’ve been alive, you know. Besides, everyone’s in a rush getting to Dorset. It's a free for all.      He does enjoy a bit of a gamble, doesn’t he, dear? Though I do agree with Chloe, it’s a bit nerve-wracking. Remember that time he tried to overtake a lorry on a roundabout near Harlow?      That was different! That lorry was going slow as molasses. And Harlow… don’t even get me started on Harlow. Used to be a nice little place, now it’s all concrete and takeaways. Never understood why your mum insisted we moved there.      Right, we’re spiralling. Dorset, sunshine, fresh air… let’s focus on that. Speaking of focusing, this Sat Nav is playing up again. Keeps trying to send us down farm tracks. It’s worse than Windows 8, honestly. Utterly useless interface.      Oh, those Sat Navs! I had one try and take me through a field last week on my way to Mrs. Peterson’s. Had to call her and explain I was going to be late because of a rogue GPS. It's a nightmare sometimes, this modern life.      Modern life. Hmph. Back in my day, you had a map. A proper Ordnance Survey map! And you  read  it. None of this relying on blinking lights and a robotic voice. Though, I’ll admit, trying to fold those maps back up was a skill in itself.      True. It’s a lost art. Anyway, how’s work, Mum? Had a decent few days off? You deserve it after all the hours you put in.      It was lovely, thank you. Actually managed to spend a whole afternoon at that little antique shop in Bishop’s Stortford. Found a beautiful little mantle clock. Proper 'Mantiques', as they call them. Old Thomas, the owner, gave me a good price.      Mantiques, eh? Waste of money, if you ask me. Just dust collectors. Though, I suppose if it keeps you happy… Still, wishing I hadn’t had to pay that solicitor last month. Dreadful business with Aunt Mabel’s will. He charged a fortune just to write a few letters!

…and honestly, Doreen, I still reckon they’re charging too much for them tomatoes. Two pound fifty a kilo! Back in my day, you could get a whole carrier bag full for that. A  whole  carrier bag. Oh, Arthur, you say that every week. Everything feels expensive, dear. It's just… the way things are now. Remember when a pint of milk was, what, twenty pence? Nineteen nine-farthing, if memory serves! And a packet of Woodbines… tenpence. Tenpence! Now it’s… well, I don’t even  buy  Woodbines anymore. Too much for my lungs, and my pocket. Not that I ever 'ad a proper pocket, mind. Never worked, did I? Always relied on your Fred, bless 'is soul. Don't start on that again, Arthur. You helped around the house, you ran errands when you were able. And your Fred loved you dearly. It wasn’t all on him, not by a long shot. And you  did  try, once or twice, to get a job down at the factory, didn’t you? Briefly. Briefly. Didn’t take to it. All that noise and… hustle and bustle. Preferred my own company, to be honest. And a good book. Though even them’s gone up in price, hasn’t they? Seen some in the shops, paperbacks costing a tenner! A tenner! Well, authors have to eat, Arthur. And printing isn't cheap. You’ve still got your old collection, haven’t you? All those Biggles books… and the Agatha Christies. Stacked up in the spare room, they are. Collecting dust, most of ‘em. Haven’t read Biggles in… oh, must be twenty years. Though I do still enjoy a good Poirot. Gets the little grey cells working, you know? You always say that. “Gets the little grey cells working.” You’re as sharp as a tack, Arthur, don't you sell yourself short. More sharp than me, even. I used to struggle with those mysteries. Too many names to keep track of. You were always better with the children, mind. You had a knack for it. All those little 'uns you looked after. Remember young Timothy Higgins? Always covered in mud. Oh, Timothy! Such a sweet boy, even when he was up to mischief. And little Sophie Carter, always drawing. They all grew up so quickly. It’s funny, isn’t it? Seem like yesterday I was changing nappies and reading stories.

… honestly, I just don’t  get  the hype around this new band, ‘Celestial Static’. Everyone at work’s lost their minds, saying they’re the next big thing, but it just sounds like… noise, doesn’t it? Like someone deliberately trying to make a washing machine sound artistic. Noise, huh? That’s harsh, love. I mean, I’ve only heard a couple of tracks, but I can see what people are on about. It’s a bit experimental, yeah, loads of layered synths and stuff, but it’s got a… vibe. Reminds me a little of early Portishead, but more chaotic. Chaotic is a polite way of putting it! Portishead is sophisticated chaos. This is just… well, chaos. Remember when we went to that gig in Leeds, that awful post-punk band? It was  exactly  like that. Gave me a headache for a week. And honestly, half the people raving about Celestial Static just want to seem 'in the know', don't they? Maybe. There's always that. Though, I think sometimes people genuinely connect with stuff that isn't traditionally "good." It’s a bit like your grandma’s gardening, innit? She swears by talking to her tomatoes, and they  do  look remarkably healthy. Don’t you dare bring up Nana’s tomatoes and compare them to sonic atrocities! Though, you’re right, they  are  doing brilliantly this year. She’s finally tackled that patch at the back, the one that always gets shaded. Speaking of which, have you managed to get the runner beans in yet? I was thinking of popping over tomorrow and giving you a hand. Actually, yes! Got them in on Saturday. Though, the weather’s been a right pain, hasn’t it? One minute blazing sunshine, the next torrential rain. Keeps throwing off my watering schedule. I'm starting to think I need one of those automated systems. Automated gardening? That defeats the whole point! It’s supposed to be therapeutic, getting your hands dirty. Remember how stressed you were before you started? All that PhD pressure. The garden's been a lifesaver, hasn’t it? It has, honestly. And it's good to feel like I'm actually  producing  something, you know? Unlike writing about the socio-political implications of 18th-century pamphlets. Nobody really cares about those, do they? Don't be daft. People care.  I  care. It’s fascinating stuff, and don’t sell yourself short.

… honestly, it’s just frustrating, innit? Like, I  get  the statistical modelling, I really do. But explaining to Mrs. Henderson why her social media engagement numbers are down because of algorithm changes… it feels so… pointless. Especially when half the time she doesn’t even  understand  what an algorithm is. Sounds… stimulating. Welcome to the world of applied research, eh? Though at least you  have  a research job. Remember me, adrift in the sea of post-doc applications? Still nothing concrete. Aye, well, that’s what I meant. You’re brilliant, proper brilliant, and you’re still battling it. It's just… everyone keeps saying ‘the job market’s tough’ like it’s some act of God. It's a system failing people, Liam. Especially us lot, saddled with debt from university. Tell me about it. I’m looking at potentially needing to take another teaching assistant role just to keep afloat while I apply. It’s soul-crushing. Honestly, sometimes I wonder if I made the right decision going back for the PhD. Don't say that! You  love  your research. Remember when you explained the socio-economic impact of post-industrial decline in the Black Country? You were firing on all cylinders! Yeah, well, firing on fumes currently. It’s the fees, isn't it? Still ridiculous. My student loan is a monster. It feels like I’m working just to pay interest. You were lucky, weren’t you? Finished just before they went completely stratospheric. A bit. And my parents helped, which I feel guilty about, even now. But even then, it was a hefty chunk. And seeing people our age, proper qualified people, stuck in dead-end jobs because they can’t afford to take a risk… it’s grim. My cousin, Chloe, she’s a history graduate, works in a betting shop. A  betting shop , Liam! That  is  rough. It’s just… the narrative of ‘get a degree, get a good job’ feels like a complete fabrication now. It used to be a reliable path. It's a con, that's what it is. A beautifully marketed con. Speaking of distractions from the bleakness of existence… did you get tickets for  Wicked ? I did! Front row stalls. Absolutely bonkers price, but I couldn't resist. Elphaba is… well, she's  iconic . You're coming with, obviously. Obviously! We  need  a bit of magic in our lives right now.

Right, so, this is good, yeah? But a bit… predictable. The badger helps the squirrel find his nuts, standard. I was thinking something a bit different for  my  book. Maybe… a hedgehog who’s a detective?      A hedgehog detective? That’s… quirky, Leo. It could work. Though, remembering how long it took you to finish that Lego spaceship, I’m not holding my breath for a whole  book .      Mum! I’m serious! I’ve got loads of ideas buzzing around. I just need to, like, get them out. And it'll be a shorter book than a spaceship, promise. Maybe he solves mysteries  about  family trees? Like, who was Great-Great-Grandpa Angus and why did he move from Scotland?      Angus? Oh, that one. A stubborn man, your Great-Great-Grandpa. Left Glasgow for… well, he said opportunity. Though his sister, my own grandmother, swore it was a woman. A Romani woman, she said, with eyes like the sea.      Oh, here we go. Another family legend. They’re lovely, Gran, honestly. But Leo's trying to write a children’s book, not a historical novel.      No, Mum, that's brilliant! It  is  a mystery! Angus disappeared from everything and everyone in Glasgow, then showed up in Bristol! That's a perfect story! And maybe the hedgehog detective has to interview all the family members – like, illustrated portraits of us all!      He  was  a secretive man. Never spoke much about his life before he came south. Your grandfather, bless him, spent years trying to piece it together. Found some census records, old postcards… nothing concrete. Said Angus was a bit like a ghost.      See, Leo? Footnote material, maybe. It's good to know the family stuff, but kids aren't going to be fascinated by a missing great-great-grandpa unless there's, y'know, action. Speaking of which, how does this hedgehog detective  solve  mysteries?      With his nose! He sniffs out clues! And he has a magnifying glass, obviously. And he has a sidekick – a sassy robin. She points out the obvious things he misses.      A sassy robin, you say? Excellent. Children love a bit of cheek. Reminds me of your Uncle David, actually. Always had a glint in his eye. Though, he was more of a practical joker than a sassy robin.      David. Honestly. He and your father… they were so different. It was always clear things weren’t going to last.

… honestly, I just can’t be bothered with it all the time. Like, Chloe was going on about needing to wax her legs for this party next week, and I just thought, ‘Eeh, no thanks’. Too much faff. You  are  a Yorkshire woman through and through, aren't you? Just embracing the natural state of things. I mean, I get it. Waxing is… unpleasant, to say the least. Though, I do shave my legs most of the time. It just feels…cleaner, I suppose. Cleaner? Aye, but at what cost, lass? The ingrown hairs! The constant need to keep on top of it! I’d rather just spend the time reading, or even watching telly. Honestly, it feels like there’s this pressure, especially with social media, to be completely hairless. It's daft. It  is  daft, isn’t it? And you're right about the pressure. Instagram's just a sea of perfectly smooth legs and underarms. It's not realistic! I definitely don't look like that all the time. I mean, I’m lucky, I don't grow much hair anywhere really, so it’s not a massive ordeal for me. But I can see why you’d just say ‘sod it’. Lucky you! I’m like a little bear, honestly. Not overly hairy, but enough that it’s… noticeable. And me nan used to go on about it, bless her. “A proper lass always keeps herself neat, you know!” Honestly, the things she used to say. It's like, nan, I'm trying to pass my A-Levels, not win a beauty pageant. Oh, grandmothers are the worst for that kind of thing! My grandma's always asking if I'm wearing enough layers, even in summer. It’s a different kind of pressure, but still… judging! Have you thought about, like, hair removal cream? It's less painful than waxing and doesn't require constant shaving. I’ve tried it. Made my skin all itchy and red. No good. I’ve started working part-time at that bakery near campus, you know, ‘The Crusty Loaf’? It’s good money, helps with rent, but it's  tired  work. Up at four every morning. Ooh, The Crusty Loaf! I’ve heard their croissants are amazing. Up at four?! That sounds horrific. How are you coping? Coffee. Lots and lots of coffee. And the smell of fresh bread helps, I suppose.

… honestly, it’s just daft, innit? Like, why  is  the alphabet the order it is? I was explaining it to little Leo the other day, and I just… drew a blank. It's not like it's logically arranged. A, B, C… what even  is  the reasoning? That's a proper head-scratcher, that is. It's not like it’s based on frequency of use, or anything sensible. It’s all down to Phoenicians, apparently. And then the Greeks nicked it, changed a few things, and the Romans standardised it. A right historical hot potato, really. Phoenicians! See, even  saying  that feels…archaic. It’s just…we learn it as kids, don’t we? No one questions it. It’s like assuming everyone knows what a ‘parsnip’ is. Back home in Sunderland, half the kids probably couldn’t tell you what one is, let alone the origins of the bloody alphabet. Fair point. Parsnips are a bit niche, even for Birmingham. Speaking of things people assume everyone knows… you alright, you’re knocking that gin back a bit quick, aren’t you? Rough day at the lab? Nah, lab’s fine. Just… thinking. And Leo's mam keeps going on about me needing to ‘relax’ more. Hence, gin. It’s medicinal, basically. Though, I did overhear a chat in the office today. Someone was talking about trying magic truffles. Magic truffles? Seriously? That's… bold. Not my cup of tea, personally. Remember Mark at uni? Tried something similar and ended up convinced he  was  a badger for three hours. Oh God, I'd forgotten about Mark the Badger! That was legendary. But it got me thinking, though, y’know? About escapism. What people do to switch off. Feels a bit… grim, though, needing to alter your brain chemistry to cope. Yeah, there's a line, isn’t there? A pint after work is one thing, changing your perception of reality is another. Though, I suppose boxing does that for some people. My mate Liam’s proper hooked. Says it’s the discipline, the control. Boxing? Liam? That’s a surprising combination. He always struck me as being more into… poetry. Still, everyone’s got their thing. It’s just… I was watching a football match last weekend, and the racist abuse directed at that player was disgusting. Makes you realise how little has actually  changed , despite all the talk. Tell me about it.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork for the Heritage Lottery Fund these days is just… exhausting. It’s not like it was even ten years ago. They want  everything  justified, down to the colour of the lime wash. Oh, darling, you’ve hit the nail on the head. It's become a profession in itself, grant writing. I spent three weeks on the application for the Dorton Rectory repairs - three weeks! And even then, you’re never  guaranteed  anything. They love detail, don't they? It's about demonstrating absolute respect for the fabric of the building, and that takes… well, it takes demonstrating you’ve thought of  everything . Precisely! And this Old Mill House project… it’s a beauty, don’t get me wrong. Stunning location, lovely bones, but the owner, bless her, thinks a full-on kitchen extension in Cotswold stone is ‘sympathetic’. Sympathetic to what? A modern lifestyle? It’s going to scream 'add-on'! Oh dear. That's… challenging. Did you gently explain the potential issues with the planning department? They’re increasingly strict about additions to listed buildings, you know. Especially in sensitive areas. I’ve tried. She's... enthusiastic. And has a very firm idea of what she wants. I’ve outlined the conservation principles, the potential for a less intrusive design – maybe a sympathetic timber-framed structure tucked into the existing build - but she keeps talking about a 'farmhouse kitchen'. Honestly, it makes my teeth itch. Right. Well, sometimes you have to be… strategic. Frame it as a longevity issue. ‘A truly sympathetic extension  protects  the value of the original building, ensuring its survival for generations.’ Flattery gets you everywhere, you know. And subtly point out the potential costs of fighting a planning refusal. Litigation is frightfully expensive. You’re a genius, Penelope. I should just pay you a consultancy fee for crisis management. It’s just… I don’t want to lose the project, but I also refuse to put my name to something that actively damages the character of the building. My reputation is all I have, really. Being self-employed… it’s a bit precarious at times. Absolutely. And you're right to protect it. I had a similar situation with the Gardener’s Cottage at Ashridge. The owners wanted to replace all the original sash windows with uPVC. U-PVC! I nearly choked on my biscuit. I had to do a full presentation on the thermal efficiency of restored timber frames, the importance of breathability…and the historical inaccuracies of modern materials.

…and honestly, the difference between ‘nowt’ and ‘now’un’ is  so  ingrained. People down south just wouldn’t get it. They’d look at you like you’d grown a second head if you said ‘how’s now’un goin’?’ It's not just the words, it's the rhythm, the quickness of it all. You’re right, it’s more than just lexical items, isn’t it? It’s prosody. I was actually reading a paper on vowel shifts in the West Midlands the other day, and it’s fascinating how even within a relatively small geographic area, you get such distinct patterns. It’s almost a sonic fingerprint. A sonic fingerprint! I like that. It totally is. And that’s what I was trying to explain to Professor Davies in that meeting. He was saying our data on dialect levelling was inconclusive, but I think he’s missing the  nuance . People aren’t necessarily  dropping  the features, they’re just…modulating them. Younger speakers are using them strategically, for identity. He’s always been a bit of a prescriptivist, Davies. Thinks everything should conform to Received Pronunciation. He probably hasn’t spent much time outside of Oxford. Strategic use, you say? Interesting. Give me an example. Right. Like, me talking to you now, I'm probably using a bit more ‘standard’ English than I would if I was back home with me mam and aunties. But if I  was  back home, and wanted to signal I was being particularly ‘Sunderland’, I’d lay it on thicker. It’s conscious performance, almost. That’s brilliant. So, it’s not a loss of dialect, but a shifting relationship with it. A toolkit? Exactly! A toolkit. I need to write that down. It’s far more complex than a simple decline. It feels like he thinks all regional variation is just…laziness or a lack of education. Ugh, typical. Academia can be so detached from reality. Listen, don't get too worked up about it. It’s a long game, research. You've got solid data, you've got a compelling argument. It'll come across. Fancy a biscuit with your tea? I got some ginger snaps. Oh, go on then. Ginger snaps sound perfect. Thanks. You've been burying your head in academic papers all week, haven’t you? Still no progress on the syntax of Brummie slang? Slow progress. It's a baffling system, honestly.

…and honestly, the amount of food they  waste  at school is criminal. Honestly, criminal. I saw plates coming back almost full yesterday. It’s just… baffling. But Miss Emily said we had to try everything! Even the Brussels sprouts. I know, darling, I know. Miss Emily’s a good teacher, she wants you to have a balanced diet. But sometimes, a tiny little person just doesn’t  want  a mountain of sprouts. Sprouts are yucky. They smell like feet. They do a bit, don’t they? Look, it’s okay not to like everything. But we need to make sure you're eating  something  good at lunchtime. That's why I was asking about the school dinners. Are you both actually eating much of them? I like the chips! And yesterday they had chocolate cake! But Leo didn't eat his fish. It had bones! And it smelled like the sea. I don't  like  the sea. Too many wavy things. Right. Okay. No fish then. Listen, if you’re both really struggling with the dinners, we can talk about packing you a lunch. It might be a bit more effort for me, but I'd rather you ate something you enjoyed and were full for the afternoon. Can we have sandwiches with… with cucumber and cream cheese? Like Granny makes? Absolutely. That sounds lovely. We can have cucumber and cream cheese sandwiches. Though Granny  does  put an awful lot of cream cheese in hers, doesn’t she? We might need to scale it back a little bit for school! And a biscuit! A chocolate one! And a biscuit. Of course. We'll discuss biscuit allocation later. Right, that’s lunch sorted, potential lunches at least. Now, about the tennis tournament next week… I need to send in the five pounds for the entry fee. Has anyone seen my purse? Under the sofa cushions? That’s where everything goes. Good thinking! Aha! Found it. Five pounds… Right. And I also need to confirm if you two are happy to have your faces painted. They’re doing face painting at half-time. Can I be a lion? ROAR! A very fierce lion. Yes, you can be a lion. What about you, Lily? Ooh, can I be a… a clown? A really sparkly clown? A sparkly clown. That’s a good one. Though, you know, sometimes clowns can be a little bit… scary for some children.

…and honestly, the sheer  audacity  of some of the points made at that Cambridge debate! Claiming history should solely focus on ‘national stories of triumph’. Triumph?! What about the uncomfortable truths, the bits that made us… less glorious? Sounds like a bit of a row, then? They always stir things up, those Cambridge fellows. I remember back in my day, the history lectures were firmly rooted in empire. All kings and queens and battles won. No mention of the… sticky bits. It’s dangerous, though, isn’t it? Sanitising history like that. I mean, my team are constantly battling misrepresentation in advertising – spin is part of the job, sure, but deliberate historical revisionism feels… different. It’s not about selling a product, it’s about shaping perception of the past. Exactly! And it feeds directly into the current national curriculum. It’s so focused on dates and names and battles. My Year 9s can tell you when the Battle of Hastings happened, but they can’t articulate  why  it mattered beyond ‘William the Conqueror won’. It's rote learning, not understanding. You know, when  I  was at school – Reading Grammar, you understand – it was all classical education. Latin, Greek, the Romans. Very little about British history, actually. They believed it gave you a… grounding. A proper education. Though I always felt a bit disconnected. Never saw much point in declensions, to be honest. Sounds delightfully archaic, Dad! Though I suppose everything feels disconnected when you're learning about the Punic Wars instead of the impact of the Industrial Revolution on Ayrshire. I had a pretty good history teacher, actually, at Ayr Academy. He made it  relevant . Talked about local impacts, the struggles of the miners… That’s what’s missing! Relevance. And a move away from this obsession with academic degrees being the only path. I was thinking about this with a student today - bright lad, wants to be a game designer. His parents are absolutely fixated on him doing a ‘proper’ university degree, but he’d learn so much more from a really intensive coding bootcamp followed by an internship with a studio. I wholeheartedly agree. It’s the same in advertising. We're constantly getting applicants with Firsts from Russell Group universities who have absolutely no practical experience. We’d rather take someone with a 2:2 who’s built a portfolio of real-world projects. It's about demonstrable skills, not just theoretical knowledge.

…No, no, I’m telling ya, that wireless, it weren’t no good even  during  the war. Static all the time. Old Man Hemmings down the lane, he had a right good set, valve radio it was, but even  he  struggled to get the news clear. You needed a proper aerial, strung right across the garden, and even then… crackle, pop, gone. Couldn't rely on it for nothin’.      Oh, don’t start on radios, Arthur. You and your wireless woes! I remember listening to Vera Lynn, though. That was lovely. Even through the static, her voice… it just carried you, didn’t it? Made you feel like things might be alright, even when everything was dreadful.      It's astonishing to think of a time when information was so… fragmented. We live in an age of instant communication. Though, ironically, perhaps  less  reliable truth. My grandfather, he fought in the Somme. He rarely spoke of it. Said it was too awful to put into words. He just… built things. Furniture, mostly. Always building. I still have his sideboard, actually.      That sideboard is a beast, Robert. Solid oak, if I remember rightly. Nearly broke my back helping you move it last year. He was a skilled man, your grandfather. Proper craftsmanship. Something you don’t see much of these days. It's all flatpack and disposable now.      Aye, proper craftsmanship. My grandad, he was a farm labourer. Never built nothin’ fancy, but he could fix  anything  with a bit of twine and determination. Grew up right ‘ere in Norfolk, Costessey it was. Lovely land back then. All fields. Now it’s all houses, isn’t it? Just houses and roads.      Harrow was different, even then. More built up, even back when I was a girl. Though we had fields around the edges. I remember playing in them with my sister. We used to build dens. The police used to shoo us off the farmer's land, of course. Didn’t like children trampin’ about.      The police… they’ve changed, haven’t they? Used to be Bobby on the beat, knew everyone by name. Now it’s all cars and paperwork. And less visible, if you ask me. Though I suppose the problems they’re dealing with now are vastly different. Not rationing and blackouts, that's for sure.      They're dealing with a fractured society, I suspect. A deep unease. And a constant barrage of information, much of it deliberately misleading.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of stuff Mum’s accumulated is just…astounding. I thought  I  had a lot of books, but hers is a whole library’s worth! Are you sure we’ve got everything in the van? I'm still worried we've left something vital. Relax, lad. I’ve done three trips already, front to back. It’s all in there. Everything that matters, anyway. Your mum just…holds onto things. It’s a habit. Like that ceramic cat she had since she was a girl. Absolutely hideous, but she wouldn't part with it for the world. Oh, the cat. Right. I’m just…it feels a bit final, doesn’t it? The last drive from Mum’s. Bittersweet, really. Aye, it is. Though, truth be told, this house was getting too much for her on her own. Good riddance to that leaky roof, I say. And the garden! Don't even get me started on the garden. Still, Northamptonshire… it's a good move. Closer to you, which is the main thing. Exactly. And she’ll be near a decent hospital. Remember when she had that bout of pneumonia last winter? Scared the life out of me. Don’t remind me. Thought we were going to lose her, honestly. Being near the hospital  is  important. Though ironically, I'm the one needing check-ups now. This dodgy knee… the doctor says it's just wear and tear. Fifty-eight years of walking, apparently. You need to take it easy, Dad. No more gardening marathons. Honestly, you push yourself too hard. Easy for you to say, teaching posh kids how to properly use a semicolon. Not exactly strenuous, is it? Hey! It’s surprisingly draining, thank you very much. You wouldn’t believe the grammatical horrors I witness on a daily basis. One student genuinely thought “literally” could replace every other adverb.  Literally!  It’s a linguistic catastrophe. Good grief. Sounds like the world’s gone mad. Still, you've always been good with words. Always top of the class. Remember that time you won the essay competition in sixth form? About… what was it? The impact of post-structuralism on modern poetry. Thrilling stuff, I know. Won me a £50 book token. Spent it all on Penguin classics, naturally. Of course you did. Always a bookworm. Speaking of spending… Have you had a chance to look at those mortgage rates again?

… honestly, I just think Auntie Brenda will be happier if she’s not right next to Uncle George. Last year was a  disaster . He kept talking over her about his gout, and she just glared at him the whole evening. It wasn't festive. Oh, God, yes. The gout saga. You're right, definitely separate them. So, Brenda by me then? That feels…safe. And George… maybe at the end of the table, near David and Sarah? They’re good at redirecting. Perfect. Absolutely perfect. David’s a magician when it comes to gently changing the subject. Now, about the menu. I was thinking roast beef, standard for Mum, she always enjoys that, but I’m worried about getting a good cut. Remember last time? It was… chewy. Ooh, yeah, it wasn’t the best, was it? We could try that fishmonger in Stamford? Old Man Hemmings? He’s pricey, but his quality is amazing. They always have really good, properly aged beef. Stamford’s a bit of a trek, isn’t it? I was hoping to pick it up Saturday morning while I'm doing the weekly shop. There’s that new butcher over by the bypass…I’ve heard mixed reviews. Hmm. Maybe risk it then? Or we could do salmon. Mum likes salmon, doesn't she? It’s easier to get right, less chance of a rubbery disaster. And quicker to cook. Thinking about everything else… have you remembered candles? She loves those little scented ones. Candles, yes! Lavender, her favourite. I’ve got a box in the utility room. Oh, and speaking of utility rooms, I spent ages yesterday rearranging the cupboards. It was a nightmare. You wouldn’t believe how many tins of peaches she’s hoarding! Mum and her peaches! It’s a mystery. Is she… is she remembering things okay? I popped round on Tuesday and she asked me three times what I did. It's just... a bit more frequent now, isn’t it? It is. It’s the little things. She called me by my sister's name this morning. And she keeps forgetting where she put her glasses – which are usually on her head. It's… unsettling. The doctor said it's likely early stages, you know… dementia. Oh, blimey. That’s… that's tough. Is she… aware? Not fully, I don’t think. She gets frustrated, confused. Mostly, she just attributes it to being "a bit forgetful with age."

… honestly, it feels like someone’s been digging around with a rusty spoon in me gob. It's just  throbbing . Oh, still bad then? I thought you said it was easing up yesterday. That sounds absolutely horrific, honestly. Are you still swilling the salt water about? Aye, religiously. But it's not touchin' it. I reckon they’ve messed me about properly with those wisdom teeth. Two out, one impacted, and the other… well, the dentist said it's just a bit of a weirdo and might not come down at all. Honestly, the whole mouth feels… hollow. Like there's just  holes  where teeth used to be. Holes? That sounds… disconcerting. Is it affecting your eating much? You barely touched your crêpe earlier. Nah, can’t really manage much, to be fair. Anything chewy is a no-go. Soup’s me best friend at the moment. And honestly, I miss a good roast dinner, like you wouldn't believe. Proper Yorkshire puddings too. You know, the ones Mum makes… Oh god, Mum’s Yorkshire puddings  are  legendary. She’d be horrified to hear you’re living on soup. She’d be on the first train here with a Tupperware box. Speaking of parents, have you told them about the dentist? They’ll be frantic. I texted Dad. He just sent back a load of worried-face emojis and asked if I’d remembered to take the painkillers. Typical. Mum will ring. She  always  rings when I have anything remotely resembling a problem. Which, to be fair, feels like every other week these days. That’s Mum for you! Overprotective to a fault. But you know she loves you. So, how long are you thinking of staying here in France for? Uni starts back pretty soon, doesn't it? That’s the stressin’ bit, innit? I'm supposed to be back in Doncaster on the 24th. But with this mouth… I don't fancy a five-hour train journey with it feelin’ like this. I’m thinking of maybe asking for an extension, or at least seein’ if I can do the first week online. I reckon you should. No point putting yourself through that if you’re genuinely still in pain. And honestly, you deserve a bit of a slow return, considering. You’ve been properly stressed with all the uni stuff  and  now this. It’s not just the uni, it’s… everything.

…and honestly, the lactose-free Victoria sponge was a disaster. It just  didn’t  rise properly. I think I needed a different raising agent. Still, better to test it now than when we've got Auntie Maureen coming for tea, eh? Can we make cookies instead? Chocolate chip ones? Yeah! And can we use the little chess men as money when we play shop? The kings are worth loads! The chess men as money? That’s ambitious, Leo. Very ambitious. Alright, alright, we can consider the chess men. But first, cookies. Agreed. And yes, chocolate chip is a perfectly acceptable alternative to a failed Victoria sponge. More importantly, though – we were talking about acts of kindness. Remember? For Chinese New Year? Oh yeah! Like giving Mrs. Higgins her mail when it’s raining? I did that last week! You  did ! That was lovely, Poppy. A very thoughtful thing to do. And Leo, what were you thinking of? I dunno… maybe… building a birdhouse for the garden? Grandad showed me how, sort of. It was really wobbly. A birdhouse! Brilliant! That’s a fantastic idea. It’s a bit cold for putting it up  right now  maybe, but we can definitely make a start on it this weekend. We could even decorate it. What about something for Mr. Patel at the shop? He's always so cheerful. We could draw him a picture! A really, really colourful one with dragons on it! Because it's Chinese New Year! That's a  wonderful  idea, Poppy. He’d absolutely love that. See? These are all brilliant, simple things. It doesn’t have to be huge gestures. It’s the thought that counts. Mum, can I have purple hair like that lady we saw in town? Oh, here we go. Leo. We've discussed this. Purple hair is… a commitment. And probably not something your Year Three teacher would appreciate. But it looked cool! And she had glitter! I want glitter hair too! Pink glitter! Right. Okay. Glitter hair is maybe a bit easier to negotiate. We’ll stick to hair clips for now, yes? Purple hair is definitely off the table. Though… I was thinking of maybe having a little demi-permanent colour myself. Something subtle. Perhaps a deep aubergine? Aubergine? That’s a vegetable color! It is, isn’t it? It's a posh way of saying dark purple. But don’t tell your father, he’ll have a fit.

…and honestly, Mum, the dent’s not  that  bad. It’s just… a little scrape. Old Mr. Henderson barely tapped the back of the Fiesta. He was so apologetic, practically in tears! He said he mistook the accelerator for the brake. Classic. A ‘little scrape’ that requires a trip to the body shop, darling. And Mr. Henderson, bless his soul, is nearly eighty. It’s a miracle no one was hurt. You were lucky. Really lucky. I was picturing the worst when the police called. I know, I know. But I was mostly thinking about the theatre trip tonight! I was  really  looking forward to seeing Alice in Wonderland. Is it still on? Yes, it’s still on. I’ve already confirmed with Mrs. Davies that she’s still picking up Leo. Though perhaps a slightly less… eventful evening is what we all need. Did you notice a bruise forming on your neck? I was worried you might have whiplash. Honestly, Mum, you worry too much. It just stung for a bit. Speaking of Alice, do you think they'll do the scene with the Cheshire Cat properly? I read the book again last week, and it's even weirder than I remembered. They usually do a good job at the theatre. It’s a small, local production, but the director’s quite inventive. It reminds me of that hideous costume you wanted to wear for your Year 7 play – the one with all the glitter? Don't remind me! I thought I would be the most amazing Queen of Hearts, but apparently it was ‘health and safety’ and ‘too much plastic’. Still, I found some amazing tutorials on YouTube for stage makeup. You wouldn’t believe what you can do with eyeliner these days. The internet. A blessing and a curse. I saw something on there the other day about reclaiming scars. Apparently, people are getting tattoos  over  their scars to make them less visible. Really? Like, actual scarring? I got that scratch from climbing the rocks by the beach last summer, remember? It’s still faintly visible. I thought it looked kind of cool, like a battle wound. It  was  a bit dramatic, chasing after that rogue frisbee. It reminded me of when I was your age. I fell out of a tree trying to rescue a kitten. Ended up with a broken wrist and a much more noticeable scar.

…and honestly, Harold, I was up half the night thinking about it all. These people from Cheshire – lovely really, quite frantic – phoned me after the meeting last night about the solar farm. Exactly the same issues as we had with the turbines. They haven't done their homework, you see. Assuming 'green' equals 'good' without looking at the impact assessment properly. It’s a common mistake, Margaret. A very common one. They get caught up in the rhetoric. “Save the planet!” wonderful sentiment, perfectly valid, but it doesn’t preclude needing to actually  look  at where they’re proposing to put a field of solar panels, does it? Ramsgate’s got its share of development headaches, believe me. Not turbines, thankfully, but the relentless house building…it’s suffocating. Suffocating is right. Though wind farms…they’re a different beast. Visual impact, noise…and the land use! When we were fighting the one near Glossop, it wasn’t just about nimbyism, you understand. It was a genuine concern about the visual intrusion on the Peak District. We had to get some serious landscape architects involved, showing the cumulative effect. Exactly! That’s what I was trying to explain to them last night. They were relying on emotive arguments about birds and bees, which are valid, of course, but the planning committee needs  facts . They need demonstrable evidence of negative impact. And frankly, the local council…well, they’re mostly swayed by the developers anyway. Money talks, Harold, it always does. It wouldn't surprise me if there was a bit of back scratching somewhere along the line. Oh, undoubtedly. And it’s not even necessarily bribery, necessarily. It’s access. The developers get to meet with the planners, wine and dine them, present their case in a slick, professional manner. These local protest groups? They’re usually just well-meaning amateurs up against a well-oiled machine. That’s why proper research is critical. Getting hold of the planning history for similar applications, understanding the council policies… And the appeal process. Don't underestimate that. Once it goes to appeal, you’re dealing with a disinterested inspector who needs convincing. We nearly lost ours at Glossop because we hadn’t prepared a robust rebuttal to the developer’s transport assessment. Cost us a fortune to commission an independent one, but it turned things around. It’s just…frustrating, isn't it? All the government bluster about clean energy, pouring money into subsidies for these things, but comparatively peanuts for  research .

…and honestly, the roundabout at the end of Pershore Road? Utter chaos. You need to be bold, Sarah,  bold . That’s what young drivers lack these days. Too polite. They let everyone else barge in. Dad, you say ‘bold’, I hear ‘aggressive’. And Mum, honestly, you're not helping! I'm already nervous about the test next week. Now, now, both of you. Your father just means you need to assert yourself a little. He's right about that roundabout, it’s a pig. Though it’s calmed down a bit since they put the cameras up. Still, don’t go thinking you can just sail through. Exactly! Assertive, that’s the word. Not aggressive. Though some of those drivers  are  asking for it. Remember old Mr. Henderson from the village? Used to drive his Morris Minor like he was on a Sunday afternoon drive… even on the M1! Oh, Dad, you and your stories. That was before my time, you’ve told me that one a dozen times. But seriously, insurance is a nightmare. I got a quote today and nearly choked on my tea. They want almost as much for a year as the car cost! It’s the age, love. That's always the biggest factor. And being a new driver. It’ll come down, though, once you've got a year’s no-claims bonus. Did you try comparing websites? Confused.com, MoneySuperMarket… that sort of thing? I did, Mum, exhaustively! It seems adding my Dad as a named driver brings it down a little, but he’d barely drive it. I’d be happy to be a named driver, just for the discount. Though I haven’t driven anything since retiring, truth be told. My eyes aren’t what they used to be. Still, insurance companies like to see a more experienced head attached to it. Good idea, dear. Speaking of things needing attention, have you two given any more thought to that little cottage in Cornwall? I saw an advert, quite reasonable. It'd be lovely for a week, just the three of us. Away from everything. Cornwall sounds amazing, Mum! Though September might be better, once I've passed and can actually drive down there! And if the insurance ever becomes vaguely affordable. September's a good shout. Less crowded. Though September can be a bit drizzly. We had a dreadful holiday in Torquay one September… rained for ten days solid.

… honestly, Dad, it’s just  bonkers  trying to park in Brighton now. They've put those new cycle lanes in, which is good, I suppose, but it’s just squeezed everything else. I spent twenty minutes circling yesterday looking for a space near the pier. Twenty minutes! And then it was barely big enough to get out of the car. Brighton, eh? Always a bit of a kerfuffle down there, innit? Never understood the appeal, myself. Too many…  people . Though, mind you, Gillingham ain’t exactly quiet anymore either. Used to be able to leave your door open in the fifties, you know. Nobody batted an eyelid. I think you're romanticising a  bit , Dad. Even in the fifties there were probably dodgy characters about. But yeah, it's definitely changed. Did you see that post on Facebook about the council wanting to charge residents for parking permits even  on  their own driveways? It’s a joke! Facebook… you and that phone. Always glued to it. All those notifications popping up. Drives me mad just watching you. I turn ‘em all off, I do. Less stress, see? It's how I keep up with things! And it’s not  always  stress, it’s good for keeping in touch with people. Anyway, back to the parking… It feels like they're just squeezing money out of everyone. It’s like these politicians… all talk, no action, and always a way to make things harder for ordinary people. Politicians. Don't even get me started. All the same. Promises, promises. Never did a day's honest work in their lives. Back in my day, you had to  graft . I tried being self-employed, you know. Delivering papers. Didn’t last long. Too much reliance on the weather. Always raining. You’ve told me that story! Several times. Sounds… grim. It was! Proper grim. And then trying to get the benefits… the Disability Living Allowance… Took ages, and they treated you like a criminal. Least I had Mum to sort things out. She was a fighter, your Mum. Speaking of sorting things out, you eaten enough? There’s still some of that quiche left. I’m good, thanks. It was lovely. You’re getting really good at quiche, actually. Better than me! I tried to make a shepherd’s pie last week, and it was… an experience. Well, you’re too busy studying to worry about cooking.

… honestly, the sheer  audacity  of Professor Davies to suggest Hamlet’s inaction is purely down to melancholia. It’s a power play, Ben, a calculated stalling tactic! He just doesn’t want to admit the play is riddled with political intrigue. Oh, Davies. Always needing to be contrarian. You’d think after thirty years of lecturing Shakespeare he’d loosen up a bit. Though, to be fair, you  are  arguing a pretty niche point. Most undergrads just want to know if Ophelia was mad or just… well, tragically manipulated. Niche? It’s fundamental! It’s the whole tension of the piece! Anyway, he marked down my essay for “lacking nuance”. Nuance! I gave him nuance by the bucketload. The man actively rewards performative ambiguity. Sounds about right. You’re getting good at the academic sarcasm though, I’ll give you that. It’s a valuable skill. Like learning to… I don’t know, perfectly slice a golf ball into a bunker. Utterly useless in most situations, but incredibly satisfying when you nail it. You playing again this weekend? Still convinced you’re going to “win” at it? Last time I saw you, you were battling a rogue gorse bush and muttering about the unfairness of physics. Look, winning isn’t the point. It’s the… the  attempt  to win. The striving! And okay, the gorse bush was a low point. Very prickly. Besides, I think I’ve finally gotten the hang of my seven iron. Speaking of striving… how’s the bar work going? Still getting shouted at for pouring the wrong Guinness head? Don’t remind me. Old Man Hemmings, the owner, is convinced I’m intentionally sabotaging his perfectly calibrated pouring system. He keeps calling me “Young Pritchard” as if my surname is some kind of insult. Pritchard? Is that a family thing? Sounds… substantial. It’s Welsh, apparently. One of my great-grandparents hailed from somewhere near Cardiff. Everyone just calls me 'Rich'. Pritchard feels…formal. And Hemmings uses it with  maximum  disapproval. Honestly, I think he just likes wielding power. He’s got this whole ‘stern publican’ aesthetic down. It’s terrifying. Sounds like Davies in a different uniform. Actually, thinking about surnames… my nan always used to call me “Batesy” – a diminutive of Bates, obviously. Mortifying when she’d shout it across a garden centre. “Batesy, don’t wander off!” It just… stuck. 'Batesy'! That’s brilliant!

… honestly, it’s just relentless at the moment. This tech conference next month? Absolute chaos. They wanted a medieval banquet  and  a virtual reality showcase, same night. Like, how do you even…? And the client keeps changing their mind about the catering. One minute it’s all vegan, next they’re after a full Yorkshire pudding spread. It’s a nightmare, it really is. A medieval banquet? Seriously? Sounds fancy. Though, a Yorkshire pudding spread  is  the way to go, innit? Beats all that rabbit food. What’s it paying like though, if it’s that stressful? Good money, thankfully. That’s the only thing keeping me going. It’s a big contract for the company. But honestly, I’m dreaming of a job where I don't have to actively quell existential crises over centrepieces. You lot having a chilled one, work-wise? Chilled is…a strong word. Production’s up, which is good, but everyone’s just running around like headless chickens. We’re trying to launch this new product line and the supply chain’s been a mess. It’s spreadsheets and fire-fighting, basically. Want another glass? This Pinot’s actually pretty decent. Oh, go on then. Don’t mind if I do. Cheers. So, fire-fighting then, eh? Sounds familiar. At least you’re not dealing with knights and dragons. What about you, Liam? Still doing the building work? Yeah, still at it. New site out near Barton. Long days, but the money’s alright. It’s graft, right? Keeps me fit. Though my back’s singing a different tune most evenings. I'm thinking of trying to get onto a bricklaying course, see if I can level up a bit. That’s a brilliant idea, Liam! Proper skilled trade, bricklaying. You could earn good money. Definitely. My dad always said a trade is a good thing to have under your belt. Speaking of belts… I’ve been trying this new diet. Cutting out carbs. It’s awful. I miss bread so much. Cutting out carbs?! What for? You look alright to me. I’m more of a ‘see food, eat food’ kind of bloke. I need me chips. It’s just… I saw a picture of myself last week and thought, ‘right, something’s gotta give’. It’s ridiculous, isn't it? Being bothered about that sort of thing. But I'm starting to feel a bit better, even if I’m constantly hungry.

…Honestly, the reception’s a bit dodgy, isn’t it? Keeps breaking up. You alright, Margaret? Can you ‘ear me proper now?      Yes, Arthur, lovely and clear now. Just a little glitch, dear. You were saying about the eclipse? Did you manage to get a good look?      Aye, saw a fair bit of it. Not as dramatic as they made out on the telly, mind. Still, put a right gloom over things for a bit. Reminded me of November, that did.      It were a bit underwhelming, I’ll grant you. All that fuss. Still, fascinatin’ thinkin’ about the cosmos, innit? Black holes and all that… where did it all  begin ? Makes your ‘ead spin.      Oh, don’t start on the cosmos, Arthur! You and your black holes! Though, I did see a lovely painting programme the other day, all about nebulae. Beautiful colours.      Nebulae, eh? Sounds a bit…foreign. I was watchin’ that programme about house prices. Still bonkers, they are. Makes you wonder where folks find the money.      Bonkers is right, George. Makes you glad you’re settled, doesn't it? Speak of settled… have you two given any more thought to movin’ closer? Being near us would be a proper help, you know.      We’ve talked about it, Arthur. We’ve talked about it. It's not as simple as packin’ a bag, is it? Especially with…well, with things as they are. And the cost of it all!      And honestly, Arthur, your garden’s lovely, but it's a lot of work! Look at you, showing off all your plants on Skype! Speaking of which, have you renewed your TV licence?      Oh, blast. Nearly forgot. Must do that today. Always slips my mind. Right, I’m just giving you a quick tour round the back… see, I've finally got the bamboo under control. It was takin’ over! Looks a bit neater now, don't it?      Looks alright. Though bamboo's a bit…invasive, innit? Just keeps spreadin’. Like gossip.      Oh, George! Always the pragmatist. It  is  rather pretty, Arthur. And what about the neighbours? Have they finally finished with that fencing?      They’re still at it. Bit of a palaver, honestly. Old Mrs. Higgins is convinced they’re creepin’ onto her land by an inch. Says she’s got it measured! Honestly, the things people worry about.      Sounds like a right carry-on. Ours are alright, thankfully.

… honestly, I still can’t believe you’ve never been to Durham. Never! It’s  right  there, practically on your doorstep when you were at uni in York. I know, I know! It feels like a glaring omission now you mention it. We were always so focused on, you know, York itself, Leeds for nights out… Durham just never… registered. It’s not like I was deliberately avoiding it. Avoiding it?! It’s beautiful! The cathedral, the castle… the river. Honestly, pet, you’ve missed a treat. It's not some bustling metropolis, mind, it's proper quaint. Unlike, say, Manchester. Now  that's  a city. Manchester’s alright. Bit… much, sometimes. Too spread out. Durham sounds nice, though. Is it easy to get to on public transport? Because, admit it, my driving is… questionable after a long day at work. Easy peasy. There’s a train straight from York, takes about half an hour. Though, you'd probably want to drive, really. Then we could go out to Beamish afterwards. Have you heard of Beamish? The open-air museum? Beamish… vaguely. Something about Victorian shops and trams? Sounds a bit… twee. Twee?! No! It’s brilliant! They’ve got a whole reconstructed 1900s town. Proper immersive. And they do a cracking fish and chips. Better than that place we went to in Harpenden, that’s for sure. What  was  that place? 'The Golden Fryer'? Sounded promising, tasted like cardboard. Okay, okay, you've made your point about the chippy. It wasn’t  that  bad. It’s just… Harpenden's not exactly a food mecca, is it? More Waitrose and chain pubs than authentic cuisine. Exactly! That’s why we need to get you up North more often. Proper grub, proper history and… proper people. Not that I'm biased, obviously. Of course not. So, Durham then. We should go. Maybe next weekend? We could look at some of those old houses you were talking about, the ones with the wonky windows? Aye, lovely houses. The architecture up there is amazing. All stone and character, nothing like those new builds they’re chucking up everywhere. I saw one near Sunderland the other day, honestly looked like a Lego brick. No soul. It’s the same down here. They’re building these estates with no thought for anything other than maximising space. No gardens, no driveways, just rows and rows of identical boxes.

…and honestly, it weren’t a robin at all, tha knows. I was  sure  it was a robin, clear as owt, but Martha, she’s got ears like a bat, pointed out the song was too complex. Turned out to be a wren, little thing, makin’ a right racket for its size. Oh, they do, don’t they? Full of themselves, those wrens. I had one nesting in an old boot last year. A boot! Can you imagine? Though, I do find identifying them by ear trickier than you think. I’m more of a visual person, I suppose. Aye, I’m alright at the ear bit. Years of walkin’ t’moors helps, I reckon. Gets y’ tuned in. Though I’m relyin’ more and more on that app now, tha knows, the one wi’ the bird sounds. Makes me feel a bit daft, but it’s handy. Makes a body wonder how we ever managed afore. Speaking o’ handy, I’ve finally chucked that awful alarm clock. Really? The one that sounded like a strangled cat? Oh, good riddance. What have you replaced it with? Just my mobile, gently vibratin’. Much kinder on the nerves. And t’birds! They start singin’ early, practically force me awake naturally. Though, I tell you what, feedin’ them lot is a commitment. I’m through a right bag o’ seed every week. It is, isn’t it? I’ve reduced mine a bit, actually. I read something about making them overly reliant, and I felt a bit guilty. I still put out a little for the blue tits, though. They’re my favourites. Speaking of guilt… I had the dentist yesterday. Oh dear. Not a pleasant experience, is it? Any bother? Just the usual poking and prodding. And a lecture about flossing. Honestly, at my age, they should just be grateful I still  have  teeth to floss. Though, I did have a bit of a fright this morning. Had a nosebleed, out of nowhere. Oh, bless yer! That’s nasty. Are you alright now? Probably just dry air, this time o’ year. Yes, it stopped quickly enough. Just a bit unsettling. Makes you realise how…fragile things are, doesn't it? Reminds me of old Mrs. Higgins down the road. She's not been well at all. Apparently, it's somethin’ to do with her throat. Oh, no. Poor thing. Heard she were a bit poorly.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of perfectly curated lives on Instagram is exhausting. Little Bethany from school was showing me her mother’s holiday photos – Maldives, private villa, daily spa treatments. It’s just…not real, is it? It feels deliberately misleading. Oh, absolutely. It’s a performance. I see it all the time in my work, actually. People presenting this incredibly glossy version of themselves, particularly post-separation. ‘Look how well I’m coping! Look how much fun I’m having!’ when underneath, they’re utterly heartbroken. It’s damaging. I try to gently point it out to clients, but it’s hard to break through that need for outward validation. It is. It’s the comparison game, isn’t it? It feels especially pointed now, you know, thinking about… everything. It’s been three years since the last IVF cycle, and realistically, it’s not going to happen. I’m starting to accept that. Oh, Sarah, I’m so sorry. That’s…that’s really tough. I remember how much you wanted this. Honestly, you were so strong going through it all. Do you feel… at peace with it now, or is it still a raw wound? Raw is a good word. It’s less about  wanting  a child now and more about mourning the future I’d imagined. Honestly, the hardest part is seeing everyone else. Everyone’s popping out babies, or already has teenagers… even Mark’s sister just had twins! It’s lovely for them, genuinely, but… it stings. It must do. Have you thought about… other options? Adoption, perhaps? Or are you leaning more towards exploring life as a single person? I’ve thought about adoption, yes. But the process feels… daunting. And truthfully, a bit lonely. Single parenthood is incredible, I know, but I always pictured doing this  with  someone. Sounds silly, doesn’t it? I’m even thinking about a complete change. I’ve always secretly wanted to write. Write? Really? What kind of thing? I don't know! Maybe a novel? I've been doing this creative writing course online, and it’s unlocked something. I’ve got this half-formed idea about a woman who leaves everything behind to run a small pottery studio in Cornwall. Total escapism, I suppose. Honestly, it's more fulfilling than marking Year 9 essays these days. Actually, I'm considering reducing my hours at school. That sounds fantastic!

…and honestly, the sheer volume of marking is just  relentless . They keep adding things to the curriculum, expecting us to be miracle workers, but not giving us the time to actually, you know,  teach  properly, let alone assess everything. Honestly, sometimes I feel like a glorified data entry clerk. Tell me about it, love. Though my days of marking are thankfully behind me. Thirty years I spent at the comprehensive, trying to wrestle teenagers into understanding sentence structure. Felt much the same, I did. More paperwork than pedagogy some days. Though, back then it wasn't all about targets and Ofsted, was it? More about just… getting ‘em to read a decent book. Exactly! It’s become so performative. It's not about fostering a love of learning anymore, it's about hitting those percentages. It's exhausting. You were at a comprehensive in Birmingham all that time then? Aye, North Birmingham. A real mixed bag, that one. Wonderful kids, mostly. Challenging, certainly. My wife, bless her, she was a primary school teacher. Now  that  was a tough gig. Little ‘uns with all sorts of needs, not enough support… She retired early, she did. The strain took its toll. How’s your mum, by the way? I haven't seen her since the street party last summer. She’s…alright. A bit achy, you know, getting older. She keeps telling me I need to find a ‘nice local boy’ and settle down. It’s relentless! She means well, of course, but the pressure! And then she worries about the crime around here. She saw someone trying to jimmy a neighbour’s back door last week. Honestly, scared the life out of her. Oh, that’s not good at all. It  has  gotten worse, hasn’t it? Used to be you could leave your door unlocked, practically. Now… well, you hear stories. It’s a shame. Used to be a strong community spirit, but everyone’s so… guarded now. That's the effect of things, I suppose. It is. And it worries me. I mean, I love Birmingham, I really do. But it feels like things are slipping. Politically, I’m just so fed up with it all. It feels like nobody is listening to teachers, nobody is investing in education, and nobody is addressing the underlying causes of this… everything. Politics. Don't get me started. I’ve lost faith, I have.

…Aye, but tha's missin’ the point, innit? It weren't  just  a pie, like. It were a proper Yorkshire pud, all fluffy and massive, drownin’ in gravy. Coulda fed a small family, that pie. Seriously, I reckon I ate about half of it meself. Right, and I suppose you’re claiming this is standard fare down in Leeds then, Dave? ‘Cos the pies I get in Sunderland are… well, they’re pies. Solid. Functional. No fluffy clouds o’ Yorkshire pudding involved. Honestly, you two sound like you're arguing over national treasures. It was a pie. A  good  pie, presumably? I had a rather decent sausage roll from Greggs earlier, which is probably more culturally significant than most people realise. Leo, always the pragmatist. Though I confess, a well-executed sausage roll  is  a thing of beauty. But back to pies… I reckon the quality of pastry is the key. Flaky, buttery… none of that shortcrust rubbish. See! David gets it! Pastry’s crucial. And it has to be proper beef and onion, not that chicken and mushroom muck. My grandma used to make ‘em, proper old school. She’d be turnin’ in her grave if she knew folk were puttin’ fruit in ‘em. Fruit in a pie? Now  that’s  a crime. Though I did accidentally eat a pecan pie once thinking it was a steak and kidney… that was a confusing experience. Changed the subject, eh? Anyone fancy sticking something on? I’m thinking 80s. Proper synth-pop. Ooh, 80s is a good shout. Though I’m partial to a bit of early Kraftwerk if we're going down the synth route. Always loved their minimalist stuff. Bit different from the Depeche Modes and New Orders, mind. Kraftwerk’s brilliant. Very… precise. Though honestly, after a week of analysing bridge stress reports, I sometimes crave something a bit chaotic. Like The Cure. Moody, angsty… relatable. The Cure? A bit gloomy for me, that. I’m more of a Stone Roses man, myself. Madchester vibes, y’know? Summat to get ya movin’. Gets me thinkin' about bein' back up North, in a proper club. Stone Roses are decent. Though I've been on a bit of a Blondie kick lately. Debbie Harry’s just… iconic. And the instrumentals are surprisingly complex. Anyone seen anything good at the cinema lately? I've been meaning to catch that new Wes Anderson. Anderson?

… honestly, the membership's gone up  again  at PureGym. It’s ridiculous. Like, I get it, inflation and all that, but another tenner a month? I’m starting to think I need to go back to just running, even though my knees complain. Tenner?! Seriously? Southport’s gyms aren’t  that  bad, thankfully. I’m using the one at the leisure centre mostly, it’s a bit dated but functional. And cheaper. Though I do miss having proper squat racks. You lifting heavy at the moment, then? Oh, don’t even get me started on gym prices. It’s daylight robbery. I cancelled mine ages ago. I tried doing yoga at home, but… the cat kept walking across my mat. It lost all zen pretty quickly. Actually, that reminds me – anyone fancy trying that new climbing place? I saw it advertised, near Mill Road. Climbing? Sounds…intense. I’m more of a weights guy, myself. Building up endurance for gaming marathons, you know? Though, yeah, gym prices  are  a joke. I'm lucky, my company has a deal with a place in town, otherwise I'd be bankrupt. Speaking of endurance, anyone been following the weather? Looks like we’re in for another week of drizzle. Perfect gaming weather, but awful for anything else. Drizzle is putting it mildly, mate. It’s been biblical. I was thinking of trying to get away for a weekend, even just to the coast. Anywhere but here. But the forecast's grim everywhere. Southport, Sarah, is it usually like this? Usually? It’s Southport! We  specialise  in grey skies and bracing winds. Although, admittedly, this has been a bit relentless even for us. Honestly, a weekend away sounds amazing. Maybe further afield? I was looking at cheap flights to Barcelona a while back, it was surprisingly affordable. Barcelona sounds incredible! Too good to be true probably. I was thinking more realistically, maybe a campsite in the Peak District? A bit of walking, a bit of…avoiding the rain. I need a break from editing manuscripts, it’s all murder mysteries and gloomy castles at the moment. Makes you feel a bit down, you know? Peak District in this weather… ambition. Although, a good murder mystery  is  perfect reading for a rainy weekend. I'm pretty much glued to my PS5 most evenings currently, working on level design for the new update. It's taking ages, the boss keeps changing his mind.

Honestly, bloody awful defending. You’d think they’d have learned  something  after last week. It's just… predictable, innit? Always leaving space for the winger to run into. Predictable is putting it mildly, love. It’s practically begging to be exploited. And the commentator’s going on about ‘grit’ and ‘determination’. Grit doesn’t stop a through ball, does it? No, it really doesn’t. It just makes the inevitable humiliation a bit more… determined. Remember when we went to that Sunderland game against Norwich a few years back?  That  was a masterclass in determined humiliation. Oh, don’t remind me. The entire stadium seemed to collectively sigh every time they got the ball. Though, to be fair, the pie  was  good. The pie was the highlight, yeah. Honestly, you'd get better football watching a kids' league. Still, at least it's something to do. So, are you making any headway with the data analysis? You were looking a bit… stressed yesterday. It’s…slow going. I think I'm approaching it from the wrong angle. All these regression models, and I’m just not getting the significant correlations I need. It’s incredibly frustrating. Feels like I’m staring at spreadsheets for hours and achieving nothing. Ugh, that sounds awful. You need a proper break. We should actually  do  something over Easter, not just…exist. I was thinking maybe that little hiking trail near Grantchester? We could pack a picnic. That sounds… lovely, actually. Really lovely. A bit of fresh air, away from the screen. I’ve been meaning to see those meadows in bloom. It'd be nice to do something that doesn't involve staring at numbers. How's your work going, by the way? Still buried under reports? Sadly, yes. The new project on consumer behaviour is a beast. Honestly, the amount of qualitative data is insane. Transcribing interviews is starting to feel like my entire existence. It's fascinating stuff, don’t get me wrong, but it’s a serious slog. It always is, isn't it? That’s research for you. All glamorous theory and then, like, ninety percent tedious data entry. Have you seen anything good recently? Needed a good distraction from the reports. I watched ‘Past Lives’ the other day. Proper tearjerker, that one. Have you heard of it? I’ve seen some buzz about it. Greta Lee, right? I’m always a bit hesitant with the really emotionally heavy films, to be honest.

…Ah, Jaysus, look at this one, Mary. Leo at four, covered head to toe in mud at that funfair in Youghal. He was  delighted  with himself, wasn’t he? Absolutely covered. Remember how your sister, Aisling, nearly had a fit trying to get him cleaned up?      Oh, I do! He looked like a little swamp monster. And he was so proud of it! He wouldn't let anyone near him with a towel. Honestly, that fair was chaos. I was convinced we'd lose him in the crowd at least three times. Leo, darling, you were a menace!      Mum! You always exaggerate. It was fun. And I didn't  nearly  get lost. Just… momentarily misplaced.      Momentarily misplaced? He was halfway to the dodgems before we realised! It's good to see those old photos, though. Brings it all back. Speaking of bringing things back, how did the London Marathon go, Mam? I meant to ask yesterday.      Ach, it was a grand spectacle. Not running it, mind you! Though I did volunteer at one of the water stations. A young man I knew from the church was running it, poor soul. He was absolutely knackered by mile 20. But he finished! Said seeing the crowds kept him going. It's a beautiful city, London, even with all the hustle and bustle.      It  is  a busy place. I haven’t been back since… well, since before Leo was born, I think. I always meant to take him to a show, maybe in the West End. He's getting to an age where he might appreciate something like that now.      I’d like that, actually. I’d be up for seeing something. Anything that isn’t a superhero movie.      Fair enough. There’s a new cinema opened up in Blackpool, right on the promenade. Been meaning to drag Mary there. Actually, talking about trips… remember that time we tried to go to Iceland? The blizzard nearly stranded us in Reykjavik.      Oh god, don't remind me! That was terrifying. Everything was closed, the roads were impassable… we spent three days huddled in that tiny guesthouse, eating nothing but Skyr.      Skyr for breakfast, lunch, and dinner! I thought I’d turn into a carton of the stuff. Still, the Northern Lights were spectacular, weren’t they? Worth almost freezing for.      Iceland… it’s a wondrous place. Reminds me of the Highlands of Scotland, in a way.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of emails I get now about “disruptive innovation” and “synergy” just makes me want to scream. It’s all buzzwords, isn’t it? Reminds me of my dad trying to understand what ‘the internet’  was  in the nineties. He kept calling it ‘the information superhighway’. Oh, your dad was a delight. Always a few steps behind the tech, bless him. Mine thought email was a passing fad. Said letters were  proper . Though, he did get rather addicted to solitaire on the computer eventually. Solitaire! That's a good one. We used to play patience with a proper pack of cards, you know. Real cards, not on a screen. Used to spread them all out on the kitchen table. And always with a little pot for the winnings - usually a biscuit. A biscuit pot, that’s lovely! It’s funny the things you remember. Thinking of games, did you two ever play ‘Conkers’? I was  terrible  at it. Always got my conker smashed to smithereens within five seconds. Oh,  Conkers ! Absolutely! Horrendous for the fingernails, though. Mum used to insist on varnishing them for extra durability. It didn’t help much. And the arguments about ‘cheating’ – wasn't there always someone who soaked their conker in something? Vinegar! That’s it! Old Man Hemmings’ grandson used to soak his in vinegar for days. No one could crack  that  conker. Scandalous! We told on him, of course. It wasn’t fair. The lengths we went to! It's a small world, isn’t it? I was thinking about Old Man Hemmings just last week. Apparently his granddaughter, Sarah, is now a solicitor in Cambridge. I read it in the local paper. No way! Good for her. Small world indeed. Speaking of small worlds, I ran into Brenda from accounts at the supermarket yesterday. She’s taken up crocheting! Said it calms her. Crocheting! Mum was a master. She made the most beautiful blankets. She tried to teach me, but I’m all thumbs. I have more success with a Kindle than a crochet hook, frankly. Have you tried eBooks, Doreen? Oh no, dear. I like a proper book. Smell of the paper, the feel of it in your hands. Can't beat it. Though I do enjoy listening to audiobooks sometimes, when my eyes get tired. I’m reading a lovely historical novel at the moment, set in Norfolk.

…and honestly, Doreen, I still reckon they’re charging too much for a loaf. Two pound fifty! For  bread ! Back in my day, you got a proper bloomer for, oh, sixpence maybe? Less even. Though things were different then, weren’t they? Sixpence bought you a bit more, that’s for sure. You and your prices, Arthur. Always going on about the price of things. It  is  a bit steep, I grant you, but well, everything's gone up. You know that. It’s not just the bread. Petrol, electric…everything. Aye, I know, I know. Still feels a bit…wrong, doesn’t it? Seems like folks work harder and harder just to stand still. Remember Old Man Hemmings down the road? Used to run the greengrocer’s. Worked his fingers to the bone, he did. But he always managed, always had a good spread on the table, even durin’ the war. He did. A lovely man. Always gave the children a little apple when we went with our mothers. Kindness, that’s what’s missing these days, Arthur. Not just money. Everyone’s so rushed, so busy lookin’ after themselves… Maybe you’re right. Though I tell you what  is  rushin’ me, it’s this blooming hip. Gets worse every day, it does. Tried that cream the doctor gave me, but it’s like rubbin’ water on a duck’s back. Oh, dear. Still playing up, is it? Have you been doin’ your exercises? Mrs. Peterson was saying hers helped no end. Though she’s a bit of a whizz, that one. Always active. Still does water aerobics, can you believe it? At her age! Water aerobics! Sounds like torture to me. No, I ‘aven’t been keepin’ up with ‘em. Too much bother, really. And frankly, they don't feel like they're doin’ any good. It's just… achin’. It reminds me of when I fell out of that tree when I were a lad. Climbin’ for birds’ nests, I was. Stupid thing to do, lookin’ back. You always were a bit of a daredevil. Your mother used to tell me stories. Always getting into mischief. Though she loved you fiercely, she did. Even when you'd come home with mud all over your face and a scraped knee. She did. Best mother a boy could ask for. Miss her, I do. And your mum, too. She made a lovely cup of tea.

… honestly, little Timmy tried to tell me a ladybird was a ‘flying biscuit’ yesterday. A  flying biscuit ! Where do they even get these ideas? It’s adorable, but… a flying biscuit. Oh my god, that’s brilliant! Kids are just… unfiltered, aren’t they? My Year 2s were convinced slugs were ‘slippery noodles’ last week. It makes marking their writing so much more entertaining, though. Are you still enjoying teaching Year 1? Slippery noodles! That’s  much  better than flying biscuit, if I’m honest. Though Timmy wins points for creativity. You two are killing me. How is it going, Maisie? Still battling glitter and glue sticks? Battling is putting it mildly! It’s chaos, glorious chaos. It’s rewarding, yeah, but I spent half of break time yesterday picking bits of sparkly purple stuff out of my hair. Honestly, I think I’m slowly becoming one with the classroom. Did you manage to get that new curriculum sorted, Chloe? You were stressed about it last time we met. Yeah, mostly. It’s a beast. The phonics screening check is looming, which is terrifying for everyone involved. Honestly, the pressure they put on six-year-olds… Anyway, I’m trying not to think about it. What about you, Isla? How's the copywriting world treating you? Still churning out catchy slogans and pretending you understand marketing jargon? You know me too well. It’s… fine. It pays the bills. Currently working on copy for garden gnomes.  Garden gnomes . Honestly, my degree didn’t prepare me for this. My mum keeps asking when I’m going to use my English degree for something ‘substantial’. Oh, mums. Mine’s been on about me finding a ‘nice doctor’ ever since I finished Sixth Form. As if that’s just a readily available commodity! Speaking of things mums put pressure on… has anyone started thinking about Christmas presents yet? I’m already panicking. Don’t even  mention  Christmas. I haven’t even recovered from my birthday! Liam’s family are notoriously difficult to buy for. Last year, his aunt Mildred gave me a knitted tea cosy with a picture of his childhood hamster on it. No way! That’s… spectacularly bad. Liam’s a good egg, though. Is everything okay with you two? You've seemed a bit quiet about things lately. It’s okay, just… work is stressful for both of us, you know?

…Honestly, the bins are a disgrace, aren’t they? I mean, I’ve lived in Salzkotten – a perfectly tidy little town in Germany – and even  there  we had more respect for public spaces. You wouldn’t catch anyone leaving black bags just…propped up against the wall like that.      Tell me about it, Dr. Schmidt. It’s always been bad around here, but it’s got worse since the council cut back on collections. People just don't care, do they? It attracts rats, you know. Proper big ‘uns.      Yeah, I’ve seen a few scuttling about on my way to work. It’s a bit grim. Not the best first impression when people are coming to the surgery, is it?      Rats? Like, Peter Pettigrew rats?      Not quite, lad. Though I suppose they  are  rather sneaky creatures. No, these aren’t animagi, thankfully. Just…normal, everyday rats. Though probably bigger than the ones Remus Lupin dealt with.      He’s hooked on those books, that one. Reads ‘em cover to cover. Good for him, I say. Keeps him out of trouble. Though, talking of trouble…did you hear about old Mrs. Davies getting her purse snatched yesterday? Right on Upper Parliament Street.      No, that's awful! Is she alright? She’s a lovely woman, always has a kind word.      Shaken up, mostly. Lost a good bit of money, though. It’s getting like that now, isn’t it? You can’t walk anywhere without looking over your shoulder. Different to when I was a girl.      It is worrying. My mum was saying the other day she’s scared to let my little brother go to the park on his own anymore. It’s all this…everything going on in the world. You hear things on the news, about places like… well, you know… and it makes you think it could happen anywhere.      ISIS, you mean? It’s a disturbing reality, absolutely. Though I think sensationalizing it doesn't help. This neighbourhood has its problems, yes - petty crime, fly-tipping – but equating it to international terrorism is…a stretch, wouldn’t you say? It’s more likely to be someone needing to buy a fix, to be honest.      My Dad says that’s why there’s so many needles around. He works down by the docks, and he says he sees ‘em all the time.      It’s a sad state of affairs, isn’t it?

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork for gluten-free requests now is astonishing. It wasn’t like this even five years ago, was it? Little Timmy can’t have wheat, little Daisy's allergic to nuts, now young Alfie's discovered he  feels  better without dairy! Where does it end? Oh, you’re telling me! It's the same at Berkeley.
