Though my nephew, bless him, went to university, got a degree in…English Literature, I think it was…and ended up working in a call centre. Like you, Kevin. Full circle, eh? Don't remind me! Though, to be fair, it pays the bills. And I can have a good moan about customers all day. Gets it off my chest. Honestly, some of the stories you hear. It's interesting, though, isn't it? The disconnect between academic study and practical application. I've been thinking about linguistics – how language actually  works  - and it's completely different to just teaching grammar rules.

… honestly, the level of basic grammar some of my online students have is  shocking . I mean, I’m not expecting Oxbridge level, but ‘me and him went to the shops’? It’s just… pervasive. It’s like nobody's being taught proper sentence construction anymore. Tell me about it! I’m battling similar things with my young learners in Kraków. Though it’s more about getting them to understand prepositions of place, rather than basic subject-verb agreement. Still frustrating though. You’d think after years of school… It's probably the influence of how people  speak  now, isn't it? Everything’s so colloquial. Absolutely. And social media, the texting… it’s all contributing to the erosion of proper language. Though, I do wonder if I'm just becoming a grumpy old woman. It’s been a while since I had a ‘proper’ job, hasn’t it? Feels like another lifetime. Don’t be silly! You're not grumpy. Just… observant. And fiercely protective of the English language, which is admirable. It's just different now. Speaking of lifetimes ago… how's the pension pot looking? Seriously, are we  ever  going to be able to retire comfortably? Don't even  start  me on pensions. It’s a disaster. I barely contributed anything, frankly, and now it feels like a cruel joke. I relied on… well, you know. And now… TEFL’ing a few hours a week barely touches the sides. It's a bit pathetic, really. I suppose I should look into getting the car’s MOT done, at least. Another expense. Right? I’m still paying off my student loan, even though I finished my Masters five years ago! It's outrageous. And the interest rates! It's like a permanent debt sentence. It did give me the chance to come and teach here though, so… swings and roundabouts. Poland's been good to me, so far. That's good. I always thought you’d flourish abroad. You always were the adventurous one. I considered teaching in Spain years ago, before... everything. Too much effort now, I think. I'm quite happy pottering around Cambridge when I’m not glued to a laptop screen. Although, Tarnow is lovely. This bistro is really charming. It is. And the food's great. So, we’re agreed then? We’ll drive back towards Kraków tomorrow morning? I was thinking we could stop at that castle near Olkusz?

… honestly, I’m still leaning Human Sciences. It just feels… broader, you know? Less pigeonholed than straight Maths. Dad's still on about how a maths degree is ‘a guaranteed ticket’, whatever  that  means. He keeps going on about actuarial science, it sounds…dull. Guaranteed ticket to spreadsheets and early grey hairs, more like! My old man’s the same with the Maths push, purely because his mate's son got some fancy job after doing it. But you’re right, Human Sciences sounds way more interesting. What bits are you most keen on? The psychology side? Yeah, and the sociology. Understanding  why  people do things, not just calculating probabilities. Plus, I'm actually decent at the essays. Maths essays…that’s a special kind of torture. How’s the application going for you then? Still dead set on Warwick? Pretty much. Sent off the UCAS stuff last week, feeling pretty relieved, actually. Just waiting now. Mum’s already started looking at student kitchens, which is slightly terrifying. She's got this whole vision of me becoming some culinary genius. Oh god, mums. Mine’s started talking about laundry schedules. Laundry schedules! I’m going to be living it up at uni, not running a domestic service. Speaking of which… are you still up for a pint after this? Just to celebrate getting the application done? Definitely. Although, ironically, my mum's also threatened to cut me off if she hears I'm already "experimenting" with alcohol before even getting in. She's a bit…strict. What are you having? Thinking about a proper pint of proper lager, not that fizzy stuff. Same. Cider’s alright, but it always feels a bit… sticky. I’m thinking a proper German lager, something with a bit of heft. You wouldn't believe what Ben tried to order last week – some weird fruit thing. Looked like bubblegum. Ben? Seriously? He’s usually got a fairly solid taste. Though, I did see him attempting to cook last weekend. Apparently, pasta carbonara involves ketchup.  Ketchup ?! That’s a crime against Italy. Honestly, his cooking skills are a danger to public health. Remember when he tried to make brownies and nearly set the kitchen on fire? How could I forget? The smoke alarm was going off for a good half hour. Anyway, enough about Ben's culinary disasters. Rugby's back on properly this weekend, right? You still playing?

…and that’s why National Insurance contributions, even though they  feel  like another tax, are actually building up your state pension. It's a system, see? Not always a  fair  system, mind you, but a system nonetheless. You've been paying into it since you started work, haven't you? Yeah, definitely. It all feels a bit opaque though, Dad. Like… where  does  it all go? I know it’s for pensions and the NHS, but beyond that… it's hard to see. Especially with all the talk about tax cuts now. Opaque is a good word for it. Deliberately so, I often think. They want it confusing. Makes it harder for folk to hold ‘em accountable. As for where it goes… well, a good chunk goes on debt servicing, for starters. All the borrowing during Covid, that's still biting us. And then there's the big stuff – Defence, Education, Transport. Though whether the money is  well  spent… that’s another matter entirely. So, these tax cuts… the ones they're proposing? Are they actually a good thing? Because it feels like they’re cutting things that really matter to give… well, to give more to people who already have more. That’s a very astute observation, love. It’s almost always regressive, these things. They talk about stimulating the economy, getting money flowing, but it’s usually trickle-down economics, isn’t it? And that rarely trickles down to those who need it most. When I was doing your mother’s tax returns –complicated, she had a bit of income from the garden, you know – I used to see how much the higher earners were sheltering their money. Tax loopholes, offshore accounts… it’s all perfectly legal, apparently, but it doesn’t  feel  right. It doesn’t. And it feels like every time there’s a crisis, it’s always the public services that take the hit. Schools, hospitals… my friend Sarah, she’s a nurse, and she’s absolutely exhausted. They're constantly short-staffed and under-resourced. Aye, it’s the same story everywhere. They can always find money for vanity projects, though. High Speed Rail, for example. Wonderful if you’re travelling from London to Birmingham in a hurry, perhaps, but what about fixing the potholes on the backroads? What about supporting local businesses? It’s all about priorities, isn’t it? And their priorities aren’t always aligned with what people  need .

… honestly, it’s just  constant  fire-fighting, Mum. Like, one minute I'm scheduling a stakeholder meeting, the next I'm untangling a spreadsheet someone's completely messed up. And then Brenda from marketing needs help with… I don't even remember what Brenda needed help with now. It’s all a blur. Sounds awfully busy, love. That’s what happens when you’re the ‘go-to’ person, isn’t it? Everyone thinks you can fix everything. Reminds me a bit of being an Exams Manager, actually. Always someone needing a last-minute favour, a misunderstanding needing clarifying… though spreadsheets weren’t usually the problem, it was invigilator rotas! It's more than just busy, though. It's… pointless sometimes. We've had three different people managing this project  this year . Each one has a completely different idea of what we're trying to achieve. It’s exhausting reinventing the wheel every three months. Three? Goodness me. That  is  chaotic. Is there anyone above you you can talk to about it? Someone who can actually, you know,  manage  the management? Mark. My line manager. He’s… well, he’s nice. But he’s more worried about looking good in meetings than actually helping us. He’ll say things like “We need to synergise and leverage our core competencies,” which basically means “do more with less.” It’s infuriating. Oh, that’s corporate-speak for a headache, alright. Sounds like your Mark needs a good Norfolk talking-to. We’re quite direct, you know. No beating around the bush. I can imagine! Seriously though, I'm starting to dread Mondays. And it’s not even the work itself, it's the lack of… direction. How are things with your new colleague, Sarah? You mentioned she was joining the exams team? Oh, she's lovely. A bit green, bless her, just finished her degree. She's learning the ropes quickly though. She reminds me of you when you first started out, all bright-eyed and bushy-tailed. Though you weren’t quite as… cynical then! Time and project management, Mum. They’ll do that to you. Anyway, Sarah sounds good. It’s nice to hear you’ve got someone decent on the team. It's just... it feels like everyone's stressed at school these days, right? All the pressure on the kids, the constant changes to the curriculum... It is, it really is.

…Aye, well, that’s what I mean about that Sharon. Always gotta one-up ya, doesn’t she? Said  her  nephew got an internship at Google. Google! Like it’s fallin’ off trees down there. Makes you wonder, doesn’t it? Whether it’s all true, or just a bit of embellishment for the book club. Oh, Grandad, you and Sharon. It’s a running battle. She’s just proud, you know? And Google  do  have internship programmes. Lots of them. It's competitive, though. Very competitive. My firm takes on a few each year, the applications are… intense. And they're not necessarily looking for the brightest, but the ones who can  sell  themselves. Sell themselves? What’s that got to do with anything? It’s about bein’ good at yer job! When I were applyin’ for labs, it were your qualifications that mattered, not how charming ya were. Different world, eh? Speaking o’ applying… any news on that job, love? Not yet. Sent off another three yesterday. It’s… frustrating. There’s loads of ‘entry level’ positions wanting three years’ experience. And everyone wants you to be proficient in seven different software packages. I practically built a corpus from scratch for uni, that should count for something! It’s a nightmare, isn't it? The gap between education and the actual job market. I’m lucky, engineering’s still fairly in demand. Though even  I  had to do a lot of networking. You having any luck with LinkedIn? LinkedIn is… exhausting. It’s all people bragging about their promotions and posting inspirational quotes. I did connect with a few people from the course, though. One fella pointed me towards a position at a museum, actually. Using corpus linguistics to analyse historical texts. Sounds right up your street, that. Better than fiddlin’ about with computers all day, anyway. Still, I don't understand all that computer stuff. I had an iPod, aye, one of the early ones. Lost it on holiday in Spain. Full o’ Vera Lynn, it were. Vera Lynn on an iPod. That's a… contrast. My Nan had one of those. She mostly used it for audiobooks. Grandad, you and your Vera Lynn! We need to update your playlist. I can make you one. Maybe some Elbow? Or The Futureheads? Proper Sunderland bands. The Futureheads? Aren’t they that scruffy lot? I saw ‘em on the telly once.

… honestly, the sheer  volume  of acronyms they threw around at that conference was ridiculous. I felt like I needed a PhD in Educational Jargon just to understand the coffee break conversations! Did you have that at all, Chloe? Oh, God, yes, absolutely! It’s always the way, isn’t it? Like they think if they make it sound complicated enough, it  must  be good pedagogy. I swear, half the time I just nodded and smiled and hoped nobody asked me to elaborate. Though yours sounds worse. Was it the TESOL one in Birmingham? It was. And it was…intense. I mean, good content, some really interesting workshops on using tech in the classroom – which I’m always up for, obviously – but it was the whole  vibe . Everyone trying to prove how ‘progressive’ they were. Lots of talk about decolonising the curriculum, which is fine, important even, but it felt… performative, you know? Like people were ticking boxes. I get what you mean. I went to one last month, smaller, just regional, focused on KS3. Similar. Everyone vying to be the most ‘student-centred’ and ‘inclusive’. It’s exhausting! I ended up spending most of the social event strategically avoiding anyone who started a sentence with “Actually, in my experience…” Oh, brilliant. That’s the signal to head for the buffet, isn't it? Honestly, I just needed a pasty and a quiet corner. Teaching teenagers Italian to tourists is stressful enough without having to absorb all that educational theory at warp speed. You’re lucky dealing with older students, aren't you? It has its moments! Though ‘lucky’ isn’t necessarily the word I’d use when Mr. Henderson decides he’s suddenly going to write a novel based on  Beowulf  and wants me to proofread it  during  his lesson. Seriously, I had to subtly steer him back to grammar exercises. He's a retired naval officer, bless him, set in his ways. Oh, goodness me. That's… a situation. At least Italian tourists are usually just grateful you can help them order the right pizza. Although, last week I had a man insist that ‘prosciutto’ was spelt with a ‘k’. It was a battle of wills I didn’t need. Oh, the linguistic battles! They’re endless. Did you catch anything genuinely useful at the conference, though? Anything you think you'll actually implement? I did. There was a really interesting session on using collaborative writing tools online.

… honestly, I just don’t  get  the obsession with these fitness influencers. All that posing and protein powder. It feels…performative, doesn’t it? Like it's less about actual health and more about getting 'likes.' Oh, absolutely. It’s exhausting just  watching  it. I’ve got a few students who are completely glued to it, trying to emulate these impossible bodies. It’s a bit worrying, actually. I try to steer them towards actually enjoying movement, you know? Like, “Have you considered hiking? Or just a really long walk with some good music?” Exactly! A long walk is bliss. I used to walk miles when I lived in Cambridge, just pottering along the Backs. Though, admittedly, that was fuelled by a potent combination of boredom and excellent coffee. This journey… well, it’s the most exercise I’ve had in months. Though, mostly it’s just operating the campervan. It's surprisingly physical, you know? It is! And navigating these Polish roads is definitely a workout for the brain. Did you see that sign back there? I  think  it said Rzeszów was that way, but honestly, Polish road signage is a whole other level of cryptic. Cryptic is a good word. I practically needed a Rosetta Stone. Honestly, I'm relying entirely on your superior navigation skills. I’m terrible with directions. Always have been. Remember that time in the Lake District… Oh god, don’t remind me! We ended up on a sheep farm! I thought your Aunt Mildred would never let us live it down. She’s still convinced you intentionally led us astray to “experience rural life.” It wasn’t intentional! I just… misread the map. And Mildred  always  assumes the worst. Speaking of which, have you been reading anything good? I’ve been trying to get through this historical novel, but it’s terribly dense. All lords and ladies and endless descriptions of tapestries. I just finished "Convenience Store Woman" by Sayaka Murata. It's brilliant. Really unsettling, but brilliant. It’s a short read, which is good because I’ve not had a lot of time. Being a proper teacher now, I'm exhausted by the end of the day. The lesson planning is relentless. Sometimes I miss just being a TEFL assistant, you know? Less responsibility. I can imagine. Though, frankly, I'm suspicious of  that  much responsibility at your age. It sounds dreadful!

…and that’s why I’m telling ya, the sheer  engineering  of the pyramids, it wasn’t just slaves draggin’ stones. There was a level of understanding of, well, everything – mathematics, astronomy, even likely tectonics, knowing how to build on shifting ground. It’s mind-boggling. More mind-boggling than figuring out this new server migration, I tell ya. Well, that's saying something! You’ve been wrestling with that server for weeks. But yes, the pyramids. I did watch a documentary on that recently, and it’s really shifting the narrative, isn’t it? Less about brute force, more about ingenious planning and probably some lost technologies. It's all tied into, I suppose, this obsessive human drive for… longevity. For leaving a mark. Exactly! It’s the same drive that makes us obsessed with telomeres and anti-ageing now. Trying to cheat death, like. Though I’m more worried about my knees giving out before I reach a respectable age, to be honest. All that kayaking last summer didn’t do ‘em any favours. Oh, don’t complain! You  loved  the kayaking. Little Leo was fascinated watching you paddle out into the bay. He’s still saying “Papa boat!” It’s so sweet, and a little heartbreaking, actually, thinking about how quickly time goes. He had that speech delay, remember? It feels like only yesterday we were chasing assessments and therapies… Aye, I remember. Tough time that was. He’s flying now though, isn’t he? A little whirlwind. And the speech therapist was right – it wasn’t necessarily a ‘delay’ but just…a different pace. He processes things differently. You know, it makes you wonder about how we define ‘normal’ sometimes. Like, looking at historical figures - some are labelled ‘eccentrics’ or even ‘mad’, but maybe they just wired differently, like some folks on the autism spectrum. Think of some of the ‘icons’ – brilliant, but…singular. That’s a good point. It's easy to pathologise what’s just…divergence. It's something I’ve thought about a lot, being a full-time Mum and seeing how Leo learns and interacts. It's completely changed my perspective. Back in my twenties, I was so focused on career, on ‘achieving’. Now… now it’s more about understanding. And wondering what on earth we're leaving for him to inherit. All this talk about global warming… Don't get me started on that.

...Honestly, Dad, I just think it's daft spending eighty quid on a highchair. Eighty! For a baby to… well, you know,  sit  in. There’s some perfectly good ones on Facebook Marketplace for like, twenty, thirty max. And they're practically the same thing.      Now, now, Lily. Your Mum’s got her heart set on this one. It's adjustable, see? Grows with ‘im. And it’s got that wipe-clean leatherette. Doesn't want little sticky fingers all over a fabric one.      It's a good point, Lily, about the Marketplace though. We should definitely check there for things. This whole baby thing is unexpectedly…expensive. We’re already looking at new car seats and cots. It adds up so quickly.      Told ya! Seriously, Mum, even the sunglasses you were looking at… seventy-five quid for  baby  sunglasses? He’s six months old! He’ll probably try to eat them!      He’s gotta protect his eyes, petal! Bright sun reflecting off the sea, you know. Don't want ‘im squintin’ all the time.      Your father is right about protecting his eyes. It’s about prevention. But Lily has a point about being sensible with money. We booked that new Italian place for Saturday, though, didn’t we? That’s… not exactly cheap.      Oh, yeah! Luca’s? That’s proper fancy. I’m looking forward to that. Still, could've gone to Nando's and saved a fortune. Though I suppose it's nice to do something… different.      Different is good. Your Mum and I haven’t been out for a proper meal just the two of us since… well, since before you started sixth form, I reckon.      And we’ve been trying to get that coffee machine sorted for months. Did you manage to find one with a milk frother, Geoff? The one I liked was on offer, but it sold out.      Aye, I did. Found one at Currys. Got a voucher off, too. Ten quid. Every little helps, eh? Although, Lily, you were on about vouchers earlier… those Boots ones? Have you used them all up yet? We could use them for baby wipes or something.      Nearly. I’ve got a couple left. I was saving them for makeup, but… wipes are probably more important. Honestly, this whole situation makes me think about Brexit again. All these supply chain issues…      Oh, here we go…      I’m serious!

…and honestly, Mrs. Higgins actually  waved  at me this morning. Waved! Usually it's just a sort of pursed-lip acknowledgement, you know? Like I've offended her begonias. No way! Mrs. Higgins waving? That  is  a Christmas miracle. Maybe the tree did it. It's looking proper festive, isn’t it? You’ve outdone yourself this year, Mum. Oh, it’s alright. Bit too big for the living room, actually. Nearly took out the angel. Honestly, I was thinking, did I go overboard? It felt…necessary, though, didn't it? After last year. Not having much of a Christmas. Definitely necessary. Last year was a bit bleak. And it looks lovely. It's a proper, full one. Reminds me of the ones you used to drag home from the farm when I was little, smelling of pine. Oh, those were the days. Your father would complain about the needles  everywhere  for months. Still, he'd help me decorate. Speaking of which, have you booked anything with Tom for your birthday? It’s next week already! I’ve been meaning to! He’s being all secretive. Said he's got a surprise planned. Something about ‘experiencing a bit of German culture’. Which is…confusing. I’m hoping it’s not lederhosen. Lederhosen?! Oh, goodness me! Well, you know Tom. Always a bit…extra. German culture, though. Interesting. He's been reading up on it hasn't he? Something about his grandad fighting there in the war? Yeah, that’s what sparked it. He got really into researching his family history, and it led him down a German rabbit hole. Apparently, his grandad was stationed near Cologne. He’s suddenly obsessed with the Rhine. It’s all a bit much. It’s nice he’s taking an interest in history, though. My great-uncle Albert was over there too…the First World War. Didn’t talk about it much, ever. Just…very quiet. These nails need a good file. They're dreadful. I keep meaning to have them done. You should! Treat yourself. They’d look pretty with a bit of sparkle, especially with Christmas coming. I could book you an appointment at that new place in town? The one I use. Oh, you’re sweet, love. Maybe. I’m just…a bit stretched with work at the moment. Old Mr. Peterson’s been poorly again, and young Emily’s just had her third child.

…and honestly, the estate agent didn’t mention  anything  about the nursery. Like, at all. I knew it was a residential area, obviously, but right next door? That’s… a lot of screaming. Not ideal when I'm trying to mark essays, is it? Oh, bless him, trying to find peace and quiet. It’ll be background noise, won’t it? You get used to it. My nan lived near a primary school for years. Said it kept her young, hearing all the kids. Nan's are built different, love. I need  silence . This is supposed to be my sanctuary. Anyway, internet. That’s the next big thing. I’ve phoned BT, they said engineer’s coming on Thursday. Thursday! That's three days without decent internet. How am I supposed to lesson plan? Three days? Crikey. That  is  rough. Can’t you tether from your phone? It'll eat your data, but... desperate times. I’ll hotspot you if you’re really stuck. Tempting, very tempting. But my data isn't fantastic either. Right, okay, diversion tactics. Let’s talk about more pressing issues. Food. We’ve got… biscuits. That's it, isn’t it? Biscuits are a perfectly acceptable food group, thank you very much. Although, I did grab a few bits from the shop on the way. There’s pasta, and a jar of pesto. And some really nice tomatoes - they're doing proper vine ones at the moment. Perfect for a simple pasta dish tonight. Pesto sounds amazing. I feel like I haven’t actually  cooked  properly in weeks. Just living on toast and takeaway. Speaking of which, any recommendations for nearby takeaways? I’m going to need a backup plan for those internet-less nights. There’s that Indian place on the high street, ‘Spice Paradise’. It’s pretty good, slightly overpriced, but good. And there's a decent fish and chips shop too, although maybe not the healthiest option. We should really get a proper shop done tomorrow. And sort the rubbish situation. Do you know what day collection is? No clue. I found a leaflet somewhere, I think. It was buried under a mountain of ‘important documents’ – which mostly turned out to be old receipts. Honestly, this unpacking is a nightmare. I need to get organised. And… …I need to go for a cigarette. Already? We’ve literally just arrived. Stress, darling,  stress . It's a very stressful unpacking process.

…and honestly, the carbonara was  almost  worth the train fare just to get here. Almost. Peterborough isn’t exactly a culinary hotspot, is it? Though Bills is alright, it’s reliable. You’re so dramatic, Chloe! It’s perfectly decent. And you know I’m sticking with the halloumi and harissa burger – I’ve already decided. It's been a  week . Needed some spice. How was the train, at least? Any delays? Relatively smooth actually, surprisingly. Bit crowded, but got a seat. Honestly, it’s just… good to be out of Southampton for a bit. Work’s been manic. This project’s just spiralling. The client keeps changing their mind about the colour scheme, it's infuriating! Oh, tell me about it. Placement life is… an experience. I’m mostly just making endless cups of tea and trying to look like I know what I’m doing in meetings. It’s marketing, apparently, but it feels a lot like glorified admin right now. At least  your  project has colour schemes to fight about. True. Though I'd trade colour schemes for fewer emails any day. Speaking of things to fight about, how are Mum and Dad? Did Dad finally manage to fix the leaky tap in the bathroom, or is the kitchen still doubling as a drip-catching zone? You know my Dad. It’s ‘almost fixed’ apparently. He’s been saying that for three weeks. Mum’s driving him mad about it. She’s threatening to call a plumber. She’s been really busy with Auntie Priya’s anniversary, organising everything. Are your parents okay? Last I heard your Mum was a bit under the weather? She’s much better, thanks. Just a nasty cold. She’s back to her gardening now, which is a good sign. She practically lives in the greenhouse. Dad’s just… Dad. Still obsessed with cricket. He was trying to explain the finer points of leg spin to me last time I was home. I just nodded and pretended to understand. Bless him. Ours are planning a trip to India next month. First time back for Mum in, like, twenty years. I’m so excited for her, but slightly anxious. It's going to be a culture shock. Oh, wow! That's amazing. That’s a big trip. Will you be going with them? Sadly, no. Work, unfortunately. I’ve already asked, but it’s a non-starter.

… honestly, it’s just  different  up there. People are more… upfront, y’know? Less of this Cambridge polite nodding and hoping you’ll just go away. In Sunderland, if someone disagrees with you, they’ll  tell  you. Straight to your face. And usually with a bit of colour. Colour, eh? Sounds… bracing. I’m used to Birmingham passive-aggression, which is a whole different beast. It’s like a carefully constructed performance of politeness masking total disdain. Less shouting, more eyebrow-raising. Exactly! No performance. Just… blunt. My gran, bless her, she once told a postman his trousers were too tight. Right there on the doorstep. Didn’t even offer him a stamp. Oh, that’s brilliant! You've got to admire that kind of honesty. It's a world away from the academic circles I swim in. Everyone’s so careful about how they phrase things, terrified of causing offence. It’s exhausting. How’s the research going, anyway? Still wrangling data on… what was it, behavioural economics and consumer choices? Still wrangling. It's alright. Pretty dry, truthfully. More spreadsheets than revolutionary insights at the moment. I’m starting to think I spend more time cleaning data than actually analysing it. Honestly, sometimes I miss just… being a student and reading about interesting stuff. The responsibility of  managing  it all, deadlines, budgets… it’s a bit much. I get that. The PhD is a lonely slog, but at least it's  my  lonely slog. I can mess things up entirely without letting anyone else down. Although, my supervisor did give me 'the look' this morning when I admitted I’d spent the previous afternoon listening to The Smiths and re-organising my record collection instead of, you know, writing. Oh, relatable. The Smiths are a valid research activity, in my opinion. What are you wearing at the moment, anyway? That jacket is… interesting. This old thing? It's a vintage find. Got it in a charity shop near Digbeth. It's comfortable. And it hides a multitude of sins. You always look so… put together, even when we’re just down the pub. This is ‘put together’? This is me trying to be comfy and hide the fact I haven’t slept properly in about a week. I got this jumper on ASOS, actually. It’s ethically sourced, apparently. Trying to be a responsible consumer, you know? It’s a losing battle, given what I research, but I try.

…Aye, but like, Mr. Sunak’s just keepin’ things the same, innit? More of the same promises, no real change. It’s all just… words, Gran. Words and posh suits. Oh, lad, you and your politics. Always been a keen one for arguin’, haven’t you? Reminds me of your grandad, bless ‘is soul. Though he was more Labour through and through. Called the Conservatives ‘toffee-nosed’. Well, he had a point, didn’t he? They just don’t  get  it, d’ya know? Like, my mates’ families are really struggling with the cost of living. Mam's workin' all hours and it’s still tight. And they're talkin' about tax cuts for the rich? It’s mental. Aye, it’s a difficult time for a lot o’ folk. I remember back in the seventies, things were bad then too. Strikes everywhere, power cuts… Your grandad was a miner, you know. Always said the government didn't care about the working man. Though, mind you, Thatcher changed things drastically. Not always for the better, in my opinion. So, you didn’t like her then? Mam says she said things got better under her, but… Better for  some , lad. Better for those who already had. She broke the unions, she sold off the industries… it felt like they were deliberately trying to dismantle everything my generation had built. My brother worked at the steelworks in Billingham. Lost his job when they closed it down. Never really recovered, poor soul. Wow. I just learn about it all in school, but it doesn’t feel… real, y’know? Like, dates and names and stuff. You actually  lived  through it. Oh, aye. Lived it and breathed it. And it’s comin’ around again, in a different way. This talk of austerity… they've been sayin’ that for years, and who suffers? Not the MPs with their allowances, that’s for sure. Exactly! They're all gettin’ pay rises while nurses are usin’ food banks. It's a joke. Old Mr. Henderson, the history teacher, he says it’s all cycles – boom and bust, Tory and Labour, recession and recovery. He says history repeats itself. There's truth in that, lad. But that doesn't mean we shouldn’t try to learn from it. Your Mr. Henderson sounds a wise man. But cycles can be broken, you know. It takes people standin’ up and sayin’ enough is enough.

…and honestly, Leo, puttin’ your elbows on the table like that? It’s just… not done, y’know? Your mother and I tried to drum it into you, and now Granny’s lookin’ at you like you’ve sprouted a second head. But it’s comfy. And everyone else is doin’ it. Leo, sweetheart, your dad’s right. It's just polite. Think about it – you wouldn’t lean all over someone else, would you? It’s the same principle. And Granny has very strong opinions on these things. Strong opinions? Och, I just like to see a bit o’ decorum! Back in my day, a wee boy gettin’ his elbows on the table would’ve gotten a sharp rap on the knuckles! Though I wouldn’t dream o’ doin’  that  now. Times have changed. You always did have a way with discipline, Mary. Though I think a gentle reminder is sufficient these days. Anyway, did you lot see that blood moon last night? Absolutely spectacular. Orange as a pumpkin. Yeah! It was wicked cool! I took loads of pictures. I’m gonna put one on my Insta. Did you, now? That's nice. It  was  beautiful. Though I was mostly too worried about little Alfie sleeping through it all. He’s been teething something awful. Poor wee fella. That’s why you deserve a proper sit-down meal, instead of chasing him around all day. Which brings me to…family dinners. We should be doing these more often, don’t you think? Before Leo’s off gallivantin’ with his friends every weekend. Hey! I’m not gallivanting! I’m… socialising. Socialising is just a fancy word for gallivanting, lad. Don’t think I don’t know. But your Da’s right. These meals… they’re important. It’s when we all catch up. Remember when you were little, Leo, and we used to come to Fitzgerald’s Park after dinner? I remember. And you used to tell me stories about the fairies in the trees. Ah, well, a bit of imagination never hurt anyone. There  are  fairies, you know. They just prefer those who believe. Granny’s got a gift for storytelling, that’s for sure. It’s also why she’s brilliant at babysitting. Honestly, I don’t know what I’d do without her sometimes. Having a few hours to myself to just… breathe. She’s a lifesaver, truly.

…and honestly, the whole thing with the Scottish referendum all those years ago, it still rankles. All that energy, all that debate… and for what? Seems to me they’ve just kicked the can further down the road, haven’t they? Another independence push is inevitable, isn’t it? It’s exhausting. More exhausting than marking twenty essays on the symbolism of  Great Expectations , and that’s saying something. You and your Dickens. Aye, it is a bit of a mess, that Scotland business. Though, I always thought they had a point, to be fair. We really do tend to London-centric down here, don’t we? Still, a split Britain… doesn’t bear thinking about, does it? Though, frankly, with the state of things, sometimes you wonder. Precisely. Though I suspect it’s more a symptom than the disease itself. Speaking of things that don't bear thinking about, young Tim, the chap interviewing for the Head of History position… utterly dreadful. Arrived fifteen minutes late, blaming ‘traffic,’ which, at ten in the morning on a Tuesday in Brighton…! And then, completely lacked any real grasp of the curriculum changes. Just spouted a lot of buzzwords about ‘student-led learning’ and ‘decolonising the syllabus’ without actually knowing  what  to decolonise. Sounds a right charlatan. You’ve seen a few come and go, haven't you, in all your years at BHAS? . I remember old Mr. Hemmings, now  he  was a historian. Knew everything. Could talk for England, he could. Used to buy his fish and chips from Miller’s down on the seafront, regular as clockwork. Miller’s! Good lord, that takes me back. Hemmings was a character, absolutely. But this Tim… it’s worrying. The Governors seem keen on ‘fresh ideas’ but I’m thinking ‘lack of experience’ and ‘incompetence’. It’s young Sarah Miller – you remember my colleague, Sarah? – she was the one who pointed out he hadn't even mentioned the new Edexcel specifications. Absolutely vital! Sarah’s a sharp one, that girl. Always has been. Good head on her shoulders. Reminds me a bit of my daughter, actually. She finally got that promotion she was after, you know. Marketing Director at that tech firm in London. She’s doing brilliantly, honestly. Though, she's always working. Doesn't seem to have a moment to breathe. Says it’s ‘dynamic’. I just call it stressful. Oh, that’s wonderful news about Emily!

… honestly, Dad, you wouldn’t  believe  the price of a decent paintbrush these days. It’s gone mental. Nearly ten quid for a synthetic sable! Ten!      Oh, don't get me started on prices, Aaron. Did you see the price of lettuce at Tesco this morning? Absolute robbery. I swear they weigh it in gold dust now.      You're telling me. Everything’s just…creeping up. It's making thinking about getting a flat properly feel miles off, even with the extra tutoring work. The tuition fees alone were a killer.      Aye, well, that’s the world we live in now, isn't it? Everything's going up, and wages...well, they just don’t keep pace. Still, we managed, didn’t we? Remember when a loaf of bread was, what, 60p?      Proper nostalgia right there, Dad. But seriously, 60p! I can barely afford a pasty for that now. Speaking of which, fancy stopping somewhere for lunch? I’m starving. Maybe that little cafe near St Neots, Ann? The one with the good sausage rolls?      Oh, that’s a lovely idea! They  do  do a cracking sausage roll. Though, I’m trying to be good, you know? Got to think about the pension, and all that. Less sausage rolls, more… well, sensible salads.      Sensible salads, eh? You always were a sensible one, Ann. Me? I'm all about the indulgence. Though, thinking about pensions…makes you realise how quickly time flies. Seems like yesterday I was chasing you lot around the garden.      It does, doesn’t it? It’s weird. I was telling one of my students the other day about board games we used to play, like Monopoly, and they had  no  idea. They were all glued to their phones. Honestly, the attention spans these days…      Phones, yeah. It's all screens. You wouldn’t catch old Mr. Henderson down the street without his paper and a good crossword. He’s got a voice like gravel, that man, though. Sounds like he’s swallowed a bag of rocks.      Oh, Mr. Henderson! Lovely man, but you’re right about the voice. It carries for miles. Reminds me of old Mr. Davies, the butcher back in Crayford, where your dad grew up. He had a booming voice, shouting the prices. You could hear him down the whole street!      That’s right! Good old Davies. Knew everyone’s order before they even walked in.

…Honestly, Grandad, I’m telling you, roundabouts are  designed  to confuse tourists. Every time we get one near the airport, it’s carnage. And you, driving in Manchester traffic after… well, after not for a while, it's a bit much, innit?      Carnage, she says! I’ve seen carnage, lass. Didn't involve roundabouts. Involved V2 rockets, mostly. Though Manchester traffic  is  a different beast altogether. Used to be trams, you know. Proper trams. Much more civilised.      He’s not wrong about the trams. I was reading about Manchester’s transport history actually, prepping for a project. Apparently, they cleared a huge amount of Victorian infrastructure to make way for cars. Bit shortsighted, really.      See? Ben agrees. Grandad, you were a BT engineer, not a demolition expert. Stick to remembering how to fix a phone line, not navigating a multi-lane roundabout. And honestly, the sheep! We've seen, like, five flocks already.      Sheep are important. They keep the grass down. My father, he used to farm a bit, in Cheshire. Lovely Dorset Horns they were. Never understood why folk think they're daft. Proper intelligent creatures, sheep. More intelligent than some politicians, certainly.      Fair point. Though I suppose intelligence is relative. My grandparents had a goat once. It ate the washing off the line. Twice.      Oh, brilliant! See, Grandad, animals are unpredictable. Like driving. It's all about being prepared for the unexpected. And potentially, stopping before you end up in a ditch with a bewildered sheep staring at you.      A ditch? I’ve been driving for eighty years, girl. I’ve never ended up in a ditch. Though I did once reverse into a haystack. That wasn’t my finest hour. A farmer was  not  amused. He kept muttering about “city folk” and “not knowing a tractor from a teacup”.      You and your stories! Honestly. That’s why I’m driving. You just tell the stories. And try not to backseat drive.      So, Grandad, you worked for BT all your life? Before it was even BT, right? Post Office Telecommunications?      That’s the one. Joined straight after the war. Good steady job. Built the network, you know. Literally built it. Climbing poles, stringing cables… it weren't glamorous, but it were necessary. Changed a lot, mind you. Used to be proper switchboards, with ladies plugging in the lines. Now it’s all… wires and boxes and things I don’t understand.

…and honestly, I still think Mrs. Higgins marked down young Timmy O’Malley just because his mother was a bit…forthright, shall we say? A perfectly good solution to the quadratic equation, and she claimed he’d ‘not shown his working’. Absolute poppycock, if you ask me. Though, of course, you couldn’t  say  that at the parents’ evenings.      Oh, teachers. Always a minefield. My Nan used to say the same about Mr. Davies – claimed he had it in for anyone with red hair. Though, looking back, maybe my cousin  was  a bit of a disruptor?      Davies… Now  he  was a character. Used to threaten us with extra homework if we didn’t clean our boots properly. Proper old school. Though I must say, Maureen, you always were a fierce advocate for your students. I remember you battling with the head over funding for the maths club.      Oh, that was nothing. It was a matter of principle! They wanted to spend the money on…what was it? A climbing frame shaped like a pirate ship? Honestly! A proper maths club, nurturing young minds, was far more important. Besides, I had little Aoife in that class, couldn’t let her down. Speaking of Aoife, have you heard anything more about the trip to Australia?      She texted earlier, said she’s finally sorted the visa. She's flying out next Friday. She's a bit nervous, naturally, but mostly just excited to see Liam.      Good, good. It’s a long way to go, but it’ll do her good. She deserves a bit of sunshine after all that…well, you know. It's brilliant she found someone who makes her happy.      It is. And Liam seems a decent sort. A bit quiet, perhaps, but solid. What about you two? Any plans for a little getaway yourselves? After all, you've both earned it.      We were thinking about a weekend in York. I’ve always wanted to see the Minster. And maybe a ghost walk?      York's lovely. Though be warned, those ghost walks are more theatrical than terrifying. You'll get more of a fright from the queues for the Yorkshire pudding! Honestly, have you been keeping up with your walking, David? You promised you'd join me for a stroll around the lake tomorrow.      I’ve been meaning to, Maureen. Just…a bit stiff lately. The weather hasn't helped, all this damp.

…and honestly, Mrs. Davies just kept circling back to the fractions. She said Leo’s understanding is… “developing,” which is teacher-speak for ‘completely lost,’ isn't it? Developing means he needs more help. Like with my reading last year. I’m good at fractions. I can share my biscuits perfectly. See? You  are  a sharing superstar, Freddie. That's lovely. But fractions on paper are a bit different, darling. Leo, did you feel like you understood the fractions during the lesson? Not really. They’re… wiggly numbers. And Mrs. Davies talks really fast when she explains them. Wiggly numbers, that’s a good way to put it. Right. Okay. We'll do some extra practice tonight. Maybe after your book club tomorrow? Speaking of which, World Book Day is looming. Have you decided who you’re going as yet? I'm gonna be the Gruffalo! I’ve got the claws already! I’m thinking Matilda. I love Matilda. She’s really clever and she makes Miss Trunchbull get in trouble. Brilliant choices, both of you! We need to get the costumes sorted. Right, back to maths for a minute… I was thinking of getting you both that online program, MathsWhizz. It’s quite good, and it adapts to their level. It’s not a replacement for actually  doing  things with me, of course. Is it like a game? It has game-like elements, yeah. It’s not Minecraft, but it's better than staring at worksheets. Now, finish your dinner, both of you. It's getting cold. This roast chicken is lovely, isn't it? Your Dad did a great job. It’s really good. Can we go to the circus after school on Friday? The one in Cambridge? Hmm, let me check with your Dad. He's got that meeting, hasn't he? We’d have to be quick. It's a bit of a rush. Please? Please, please,  please ? They have lions! And acrobats! And probably clowns! Alright, alright. I'll ask. No promises, though. Speaking of things that are… a bit odd. Uncle David told me the most  bizarre  story at the weekend. Uncle David always tells weird stories. You’re not wrong. He was reading about forensic anthropology, apparently. And he was talking about how they can sometimes determine what someone ate before they died just from the bones. And then he went on this whole tangent about… what cooked human flesh smells like.

…and honestly, the fella at the curtain shop, young Mikey, he was telling me about his summer job. Working his way through college, ye know? Seems a world away from when I was his age, hammering away at code all summer for pocket money. Though, truth be told, I wasn’t exactly  enjoying  hammering away at code then either! It’s good they’re getting experience, though, isn’t it? Even if it’s just selling curtains. Little Leo just tries to ‘help’ by untangling everything. It’s more hindrance than help, bless him. Speaking of little ones, have we finalised anything for Oisin’s party? It’s creeping up fast. Dinosaurs! I want dinosaurs! And cake! Always dinosaurs with Oisin, aren’t there? Bless his heart. He’s a wee character, that boy. Though, I must say, the way he puts sentences together… it’s a bit… unique. Not wrong, just… a different rhythm. Like a wee Irish poem sometimes. Ah, he gets it from his mother’s side, that one. A bit of the poetic streak. Though I swear he’s inventing words half the time. And don’t even get me started on his grammar if he’s half asleep. Still, keeps us entertained. Right, party. I reckon we can go with the community hall again? Eileen at the hall is a saint. The hall is good. But last time, remember the chair situation? Half of them were wonky. And we need to get a bouncy castle booked  now , or we’ll be out of luck. They go like hot cakes. I’ll give Eileen a ring tomorrow. And a bouncy castle, noted. Right, priorities. Party, settled . Now, are we still on for the rugby next weekend? I’ve got tickets, decent enough seats. Oh, I’d love to! It’s been ages since I’ve been to a proper match. Though, you know, I’m starting to feel like the designated driver these days. It's a burden I appear to carry for the family! I can’t, unfortunately. Leo’s teething is hideous at the moment. I’m on full nappy duty and comfort patrol. But you two go and enjoy! Maybe I’ll catch a replay on the telly. Shame. You're missin' out. Though, knowing my luck, it'll be pourin’ rain. It's Ireland, after all. Speaking of things drainin’ the good out of ya, I’m trying to get my head around being treasurer for the garage owners’ association now.

…Aye, but that's the thing, isn’t it? ‘Hygge’. It's  everywhere  now. Like, suddenly everyone needs to be all cosy with candles and blankets. It feels… manufactured, dunnit? Back home, we just  were  cosy. It was just… life. No need to give it a fancy Danish name. You’re right, it's become a bit of a buzzword. My mum’s gone full hygge. The living room looks like a woodland creature’s set up shop. But it's not a bad thing, is it? Just people trying to find a bit of comfort, especially with everything going on. It feels like a linguistic appropriation, though. Like taking something genuinely cultural and sanitising it for mass consumption. Similar to how everyone's suddenly "mindful" now. Proper mindfulness takes work, this is just… scented candles. Exactly! Proper mindfulness is sitting in freezing cold meditation, not a lavender diffuser. And it's not just that, it messes with word games, too. We were trying to do a 'describe a feeling with one foreign word' thing and it just became everyone shouting ‘Hygge!’ It’s useless. Okay, that’s fair. It’s ruined the game. We need a new challenge. Anyone got any ideas? I'm completely drawing a blank. I've been staring at engineering blueprints all day. My brain's fried. We could try ‘palindromes’. But not just simple ones. Ones with phrases. Trying to think of a good, clever one… “Madam, I’m Adam” is a bit… done. Oh, aye, palindromes! Good shout. What about, "Was it a cat I saw?" Bit classic, but gets the gears turning. I always liked those. Though, proper long ones are a nightmare. Remember that one about Napoleon? Vaguely. Something about a soldier… it was ridiculously long, and nobody could remember the whole thing. It took like, a full ten minutes to recite. "Able was I ere I saw Elba." That's the one! Supposedly Napoleon said it. It's a bit… constructed, though. Doesn't quite  feel  natural, does it? Nah, it's a bit forced. Like someone’s actively trying to be clever. I prefer ones that just… happen. Like, you're talking and suddenly realise you've said something backwards. You know, that’s a really good point. So, kind of like accidental poetry? Speaking of which, have you guys seen that new poetry slam night at The Eagle? I’ve heard about it.

… honestly, I just needed a solid four hours. A proper kip. Uni’s draining me, Liam. Draining me dry. I swear, if Professor Davies gives us another essay on post-structuralism I’m gonna scream. Post-structuralism, eh? Sounds… cheery. You alright for the Henderson gig on Saturday though? You said you were feeling rough last week. Yeah, yeah, I’ll be there. Caffeine and sheer willpower, that’s the plan. Though I’m predicting a lot of leaning against walls. Are you still obsessed with that new band, ‘Static Bloom’? They’re a bit… much for me. All that synth and moody lighting. Obsessed is a strong word. Appreciative. They're different, alright? It's a nice change from all the indie landfill, isn’t it? You just like things a bit… straightforward, don't ya? Like The Smiths. Always The Smiths with you. Hey! The Smiths are classics. Timeless. You can’t argue with Morrissey. Plus, they remind me of uni, back in first year. Remember that awful fresher’s party where we both ended up singing “This Charming Man” at the top of our lungs? Oh god, don’t remind me. I think I nearly lost my voice. And old man Peterson from down the hall gave us a right telling off. He thought we were vandalising the building with noise. He was a grumpy sod, Peterson. Speaking of grumpy, have you seen Sarah lately? I haven’t bumped into her since… well, since everything with Ben. Nah. She’s been pretty quiet. Last I heard, she was holed up with her mum in Lymm. Said she needed a bit of space. It’s awful, isn’t it? He was a right… well, you know. Yeah. I still can't believe he did that. She deserves better than being strung along. Remember all her photos of them at Gulliver’s World? She was proper smitten. I've got one somewhere on my phone...  scrolls through her phone  Oh god, here it is. Look at her face, she's beaming! Oh,  no . That’s… intense. The matching Gulliver’s World hats. That’s a commitment. A serious commitment! She was so proud. And look at Ben’s face, he looks positively miserable. Maybe it was a warning sign? Hindsight’s a beautiful thing, isn’t it? Don't go digging up old photos, you'll just depress us both.

… honestly, I just think Mr. Henderson was being deliberately obtuse. He kept focusing on the  potential  for increased traffic, as if anyone's actually going to drive all the way to Oldfield Road just to… look at a slightly nicer extension. It's ridiculous. You were brilliant though, honestly. The way you pulled apart his points about light pollution… using the existing streetlamps as a counter-example? Peak Sarah. Oh, please. It was basic logic. And he clearly hadn’t  read  the full application. He asked about the height again, after I’d explicitly stated it adhered to the permitted development guidelines. It felt like a performance. Council planning committees often  are  a performance, darling. A lot of posturing for the local newsletter. Did Mrs. Davies seem receptive at least? She’s usually the reasonable one. She did. She asked good questions, about the landscaping, the tree preservation order… she seemed genuinely concerned with the aesthetics, which is fine, I anticipated that. I think she’s leaning towards approval. It's Henderson I’m worried about. He has a reputation for being…difficult. Right. And if we don’t get this through now, we’re stuck with that wonky shed for another six months, aren't we? The offers are starting to trickle in, but people are factoring in the work needed. Exactly! And honestly, thinking about having to deal with another six months of that shed… it physically pains me. It clashes horribly with everything. It’s like a beige carbuncle on a perfectly good garden. Dramatic as ever. But you’re right. The estate agent said a cleared garden with approved plans for the extension would add at least ten grand to the asking price. Ten grand! That’s a decent chunk towards the deposit on the cottage. It is. And that cottage… oh, Liam, imagine. A proper Aga, a rambling garden… and no beige carbuncles. This application is crucial. Are you sure you've drafted the revised email to the solicitor, clarifying the position with the access road? Done. Sent it this morning. Re-emphasised that the shared access is perfectly legal, and that Henderson's squawking about it is just…well, Henderson being Henderson. I even copied in the council's legal advisor, just for good measure. Good. Cover all bases is the motto. I've been going over the sales particulars again. Should we mention the potential for a loft conversion?

… honestly, I just don’t  get  why he insists on mowing his lawn at 7am on a Sunday. Seven! It's barbaric. Did you see him out there, looking all smug? Oh, Mr. Henderson? Yeah, I saw the orange hi-vis jacket. He’s always been a bit…enthusiastic, hasn’t he? Reminds me of Uncle Barry and his gardening. Though Barry at least waited ‘til nine. Nine is still early! It’s supposed to be a lie-in. Honestly, it’s like he wants to actively ruin everyone’s weekend. Speaking of ruining things, did you see what Sarah posted on Instagram? Let me guess – another picture of her ridiculously perfect holiday? She’s already in the Maldives, isn't she? Honestly, the filter usage is criminal. Worse. She’s with  Mark .  Mark ? Mark from sixth form? The one who used to wear those awful shell suits and try to impress everyone by doing terrible magic tricks? The very same. Apparently, he’s a “successful entrepreneur” now. Who knew? Honestly, the glow-up is…substantial. It’s just… weird. Remember how awful he was to Emily Carter? Oh god, yes. The poetry incident. Still makes me cringe. Serves her right, though, doesn’t it? Always going for the bad boys. What’s he doing in the Maldives with her anyway? No idea! She just captioned it “Making memories ✨” Ugh. I need more coffee. Right, I was thinking, we haven’t done anything fun in ages. What about that new art exhibition at the gallery? The one with the… massive knitted sculptures? Oh, that sounds brilliant! When is it on? I need a distraction from paperwork and… well, everything else at work, to be honest. Been a rough couple of weeks. Old Mrs. Davies was really distressed yesterday. It's draining. Oh, no, that sounds awful. You’re a saint, you are. It’s next Saturday, apparently. We could grab lunch afterwards? That little Italian place on the high street is quite nice. Perfect. Definitely. We need a proper catch-up. Have you been watching anything good lately? I’ve been trying to avoid screens, but I did cave and watch that new thriller on Netflix. It was… underwhelming. I've been obsessed with that documentary about competitive hot dog eating. It's completely bizarre, but I can’t look away. And I finally got around to watching  Paddington 2 .

…No, seriously, I’m tellin’ ya, that advert for the washing powder is  criminal . “Sparkling whites after just one wash!” It’s all smoke and mirrors, innit? Me nan used to say the best bleach was sunshine, and she weren’t wrong. Look at our whites, they’ve seen better days, haven't they? They’re alright. You worry too much, Liam. And sunshine's a bit unreliable in November, love. Besides, you were the one who volunteered to do the washing. I know, I know, I volunteered in a moment of weakness. Thinking I could wrestle it into submission. But honestly, the pressure they put on people with all that advertising… It's manipulative. It's like NLP, yeah? Subliminal stuff. You’re learnin’ all about that with your work, aren't ya? A bit. It’s not  exactly  the same, but the principles are similar. Anchoring, framing… they definitely use those in advertising. Though usually it’s less sophisticated than what we use in therapy. We’re trying to help people, not sell them overpriced detergent. Fair enough. Speaking of overpriced, have you seen the price of a new mobile phone? I swear, they’re practically jewels now. And everyone’s gotta have the latest one. I saw old Mrs. Higgins at the car boot sale last week, tryna sell her perfectly good iPhone 8. Said she needed the 15 'cos her granddaughter told her to. Oh, bless her. That car boot sale was mental. I got that amazing vase for a quid. You were too busy haggling over a rusty spanner, weren’t you? It was a  good  spanner! Potential to fix the car, see? Speaking of the car, I need to get petrol. And maybe we should actually plan something for this week, besides endless telly and avoiding housework? You and your spanners. Alright, let's plan. I've got that session with Mr. Davies on Tuesday, the one with… the literacy issues. Actually, it's fascinating. He’s a really bright bloke, but dyslexic, and it’s affected his confidence massively. It makes me think about how much we take reading and writing for granted. It’s a real barrier, you know? Yeah, I can imagine. It's a pain even trying to decipher some of the online shopping descriptions. Half the time I end up ordering the wrong thing. Was lookin' at trainers yesterday, ended up with… well, let's just say they were a  lot  brighter than I expected.

…and honestly, the estate agent was  awful . Didn’t even bother to point out the damp patch in the bedroom – I spotted it myself! It’s all about getting numbers through the door, isn’t it? No actual service. It's just… exhausting, isn’t it? The whole house hunting process. Tell me about it. We’re still saving, massively. Birmingham’s gone  mental , property-wise. It feels like you need a winning lottery ticket just to get a foot on the ladder. We’re looking in Solihull, hoping for something a bit quieter, but even there… Yeah, it’s bonkers. I keep saying to Sarah, we should just move further out. But then you’re adding commute time, and that’s a whole other headache. Plus, I  like  being able to cycle to the BBC Mailbox. It’s a perk, even if it's a slightly stressful cycle sometimes. I’m with you on the cycling. Though London cycling is a whole different level of terrifying. My flat is decent enough, but I'm starting to outgrow it. Tidying is becoming a strategic operation rather than a cleaning regime, you know? On a completely different note, has anyone tried that new ramen place, 'Koko'? Ooh, Koko! Aye, went last week. Properly good. Though, be warned, the portions are massive. I couldn’t finish mine. Proper belly-buster. And their playlist was spot on – loads of that Japanese city pop stuff. Japanese city pop? Interesting. I’ve been getting really into discovering music through TikTok, actually. Which sounds dreadful, I know, being a language teacher, all about nuanced communication. But honestly, it’s a brilliant way to find new artists. Keeps me feeling, well, young-ish. Don’t be ashamed! I use Spotify’s algorithm religiously. It's frighteningly accurate. It knows me better than I know myself sometimes. Though, it did put me onto some… questionable extreme metal last week. Algorithm glitch, I assume. Speaking of algorithms, I’m working on a piece about the impact of social media on… well, everything. It’s a rabbit hole. Honestly, trying to stay on top of it all is full-time work. And the fact-checking! It's relentless. Preach. I’m wading through misinformation daily. Makes you despair sometimes. I’ve been recommending this app to sources though, Otter.ai. It transcribes interviews brilliantly. Saved me  hours  of notetaking. Otter.ai? Ooh, I need that!

…and honestly, the whole estate was just fields then, David! Fields! You wouldn't recognise it now. We moved here in ‘68, just after Michael and I were married, and it was all very rural. Not like Almondsbury at all, even then, but a good compromise between your Ramsgate and Manchester, I suppose. ‘68, you say? I remember driving through here for my interview at the grammar school. Absolutely no idea where anything  was . Just…green. I kept getting lost, asking directions. Everyone said, “Oh, you’ll get used to the roundabouts.” They weren’t kidding! I’d come from a little town where a roundabout was two cars politely circling a flowerbed. Roundabouts! Tell me about it. I was a nervous wreck trying to navigate the M62 to get to Manchester Uni in the first place, never mind anything local. But coming down here… the school board had put me up in a little guesthouse near the city centre initially. Dreadful place, smelled persistently of cabbage. Cabbage? You were lucky! When  I  came down for my interview at the hospital back in ‘63, they put me in a boarding house run by a woman who insisted on knowing the marital status of every guest, and then offering advice accordingly. She asked me, bright as a button, if I was “looking for a nice girl.” I was already engaged, you understand! Oh, bless you! That’s dreadful. We had a real struggle finding a house. It wasn't a buyer's market, not at all. There simply weren’t many houses available, and when there were, they were… well, let's just say they needed a lot of love. That’s an understatement. The first place I looked at was practically falling down. Damp, no central heating, and a garden full of weeds. Of course, back then, you didn’t get mortgages like you do now. We rented for a good five years before we could even think about buying. Found a little semi-detached near the park. Perfectly serviceable. I was lucky. The university had a few tied cottages, slightly dilapidated, but rent was subsidized. Met Margaret – my wife – actually at a faculty drinks evening. She was in the history department. She'd already secured a proper house, though, a lovely Victorian terrace. We moved in together a couple of years later. I bought straight away, thankfully. Though “bought” is a generous term.

…and honestly, the whole thing with the gallery, it wasn’t  about  the money, not really. Though a bit more would've been lovely, mind you! It was about finding the right piece, the thing that spoke to someone. Old things, they have stories, don’t they? Far more than anything churned out today, all plastic and… well, nothingness. Did you ever have a thing for antiques, dear? You said you were in speech therapy, didn’t you? That’s a world away from chipped teacups and faded watercolours. A world away, indeed! Though surprisingly, stories were quite central to my work too. Unlocking them, rather than unearthing them. I was a speech and language therapist, mostly with children. Trying to help them  find  their voices, you know? Sometimes, a child with a difficult start just needed someone to patiently listen for the story trying to get out. Though chipped teacups do sound a lot less stressful. What sort of art did you specialise in, then? You said you were an artist yourself? Oh, landscapes mostly. Somerset landscapes, naturally. The light here, it's…particular. All those rolling hills, and the levels, of course. I tried portraits once, ghastly business. People are rarely as interesting as they think they are, if you ask me. But a field of wheat shimmering in the sun…that's a story in itself. Though I wasn’t much good at  selling  my own, you understand. Always better at spotting it in others. What was your childhood like, in Australia? It sounds terribly exotic to an old Somerset girl like me. I grew up right here, in Well, practically never left the county until I was nearly thirty. Exotic isn't quite the word, I think. It was hot. Very, very hot. And vast. Sydney’s changed a lot since I was a girl, but even then, it wasn't quaint like this. More…brash, perhaps. My father was a doctor, a proper country doctor, driving all over the New South Wales countryside. Mum was a teacher. We had a garden, filled with hibiscus and bougainvillea – nothing like your Somerset roses, I imagine. I spent a lot of time climbing trees and making up stories. Probably why I ended up helping other people with theirs! Were your parents local here? Oh yes, proper West Country folk. My father was a farmer, you see. A dairy farm. Not a glamorous life, but honest work.

… honestly, I still think a full sleeve is a bit… much, yeah? Like, you’ve got the hummingbird already – that’s brilliant, proper delicate. But wrapping your whole arm? It’s a commitment, innit? Oh, don’t be such a fuddy-duddy, Leo. It’s  art . And honestly, after spending all day kneading dough and dealing with demanding customers, a bit of vibrant colour on my arm sounds pretty bloody good. Plus, the artist does amazing botanical work. It’ll flow from the hummingbird. Wild roses, trailing ivy… Roses and ivy. Right. Sounds… prickly. Just saying, regret is a powerful thing, especially when it’s permanently inked onto your skin. Remember old man Hemmings at uni? The dragon that looked suspiciously like a lizard after a year? Okay, okay, fair point. Hemmings was a disaster. But  this  is different. It’s planned. I’ve been sketching designs for months. Speaking of planning, you alright with the risotto? I've got the stock simmering. Yeah, risotto’s good. Bit fancy for a Tuesday, but… who am I to complain when you’re making the effort? Smells nice already. So, how’s the bakery been? Slow now it’s almost December? Surprisingly busy. Everyone's getting their Christmas orders in. Shortbread, mince pies…the usual. Old Mrs. Peterson wants six different types of Christmas pudding this year. Six! The woman's a legend.      Alright, you lot! Smells amazing in here. What culinary delights are you conjuring up? Risotto, Chloe! Come and warm up. It's freezing out there. Leo’s questioning my life choices regarding future tattoos while I’m trying to feed us. Oh, tattoos? Leo, you’re always judging. Honestly. Anyway, Christmas is looming. Have you two even  thought  about decorations? I'm already stressed about the cafe. I want it completely transformed! Decorations? Not really. I was thinking maybe a small tree. Low effort, maximum impact. A  small  tree? Leo! That's…that’s just sad. We need tinsel, fairy lights, a massive inflatable snowman…the works! I've been looking at those candy cane arches online. Properly gaudy, but in a good way. Candy cane arches? Chloe, you’re ambitious. Is the cafe big enough for a candy cane arch  and  customers? We'll make it work! I’m thinking of doing a gingerbread latte special, and maybe those little snowman cookies… the ones with the chocolate button eyes. What do you reckon?

… honestly, Mum, the whole thing’s just a bit overwhelming, innit? Like, finishing the thesis is one thing – a massive thing, yeah – but then  what ? Everyone else seems to have a plan. Internship lined up, jobs applied for… I’m just… orbiting. Orbiting is alright, darling. A bit of orbiting is perfectly sensible. You’ve just spent three years completely immersed in 18th-century poetry. Don’t feel you need to have life sorted before the ink’s dry on the dissertation. Easier said than done. Old Man Hemmings keeps going on about ‘career trajectory’ and ‘leveraging my skills’. Sounds like he thinks I should be selling insurance, not analysing Blake. Hemmings always was a bit… pragmatic. He's a good academic, just not one for flights of fancy. Look, realistically, you  will  need to think about money. Though, speaking of which, your Aunt Carol was asking about you. She says the market’s a bit mad, but she thinks that little terraced place in Tooting Bec might be coming up. Tooting Bec? Seriously? With all due respect, Mum, I’ve just spent three years living in glorified quads. I’m aiming for slightly more than a postage stamp garden. Don’t dismiss it out of hand! It’s got potential, and it's  London . And it’s affordable, which is a massive bonus. We could help with a deposit… I appreciate that, really. But I don't want to be reliant on you forever. Plus, honestly, the idea of being stuck in South London immediately after Cambridge feels…limiting. I was thinking, maybe, even just for a bit, look at opportunities further afield? Further afield? Like where? Don't tell me you're thinking of America. No, no, not America. Just… maybe Oxford? A few of the colleges have post-doc opportunities, even for someone straight out of undergrad. It'd be a continuation of research, keep the brain ticking… and it’s not  too  far. Oxford… That’s… interesting. I hadn’t considered that. It would be a bit… awkward, wouldn’t it? After choosing Cambridge. Your father would have something to say. Dad’s been pretty quiet about the whole thesis thing, to be fair. He mostly just asks if I'm eating enough. And honestly, it’s not about ‘choosing’ a side, is it? It’s about what’s best for my research. The Bodleian is a serious draw, you know.

…and honestly, the sheer volume of paperwork for ethical clearance these days is  ridiculous . It's not like we're going in wielding shovels, it's linguistic data collection! Though, I suppose any kind of research with people needs to be carefully considered. Absolutely. It’s a different landscape to when Professor Ainsworth was doing his fieldwork, isn’t it? I was reading his notes on the Syrian excavations… the level of detail, but almost no mention of consultation with local communities beyond, you know, paying for labour. Well, dear girl, things  were  different back then. In ‘68, when we were digging at the village site near Oswestry – a Roman settlement, seemingly unremarkable, but yielded a fascinating inscription – we just… got on with it. Permission from the landowner, a nod from the local vicar, and we were away. No committees, no impact assessments. Right. Though, thinking about that Oswestry site, did you find much evidence of the pre-Roman inhabitants? I remember hearing something about a Brittonic language presence in Shropshire. A little. Some pottery shards suggestive of Iron Age craftsmanship, a few postholes. But nothing conclusive about the language. It’s infuriating, isn’t it? Trying to reconstruct vocabularies based on place names and Roman inscriptions. You get glimpses, fragments, but a complete picture… elusive. Much more rewarding, ironically, was later work in Oman. Oman? That's a massive jump geographically! It is, isn’t it? But the Arab cultural history is just breathtaking. We were documenting dialects in the Dhofar region, before much of it became accessible. I used to give lectures on it – rather dry stuff, admittedly, comparing the phonetic features of Shilh dialects to classical Arabic. The students weren't always thrilled. I can imagine! Lectures comparing phonetic features aren't exactly Friday night entertainment. I’m doing a fair bit of work with tonal languages at the moment, actually. Specifically, Mandarin Chinese. The challenges of accurately transcribing tones… it's mind-boggling. Oh, wow. That  is  tricky. We had a visiting scholar from Peking University last year, and even  she  struggled with some of the regional pronunciations during her presentations. Chinese! Fascinating. The writing system alone is a lifetime’s study. Reminds me of my encounter with a young archaeologist in Syria. He’d been to China and kept trying to draw parallels between the development of cuneiform and early Chinese characters. Bold theory, but… tenuous, shall we say?

… honestly, the deadline's just looming, yeah? Dissertation’s a beast. And Professor Davies keeps changing his mind about what he  actually  wants. It's driving me round the bend, innit. Oh, tell me about it. Deadlines. Though mine are usually ‘get 50 sourdough loaves proofed and ready by 6am’. Different pressure, same stress, I reckon. Though, at least with bread, if it doesn’t work, you can generally just…try again. Can’t exactly rewrite a whole chapter the night before submission, can you? You two and your stresses. Mine's keeping Brenda, my barista, from spontaneously deciding to go backpacking in Nepal. She's a lovely girl, but utterly unreliable. Honestly, running a café is 90% people management and 10% coffee. Sounds… intense. Though, from my side of things, managing a film crew feels remarkably similar, just with more expensive equipment at stake. I was just showing someone a viral video earlier – a bloke trying to explain quantum physics using biscuit tins. Got millions of views. Pure gold. Biscuit tins? Seriously? The internet’s gone properly mental, hasn’t it? Still, beats scrolling through LinkedIn looking at jobs I’m completely unqualified for. Saw one the other day, said ‘dynamic marketing strategist’. What even  is  that? Sounds like fancy talk for someone who can make a TikTok. Honestly, half these job descriptions are written in code. It’s a wonder anyone gets hired. I mean, I left uni with a history degree, ended up covered in flour, and I’m perfectly happy, but it wasn’t exactly the plan. Well, that’s the thing, innit? The plan. Remember all those careers advisors pushing us towards these ‘respectable’ professions? My brother, bless him, was convinced he  had  to be a lawyer. Lasted six months. Now he's a carpenter. Happier than he’s ever been. It's a class thing, I think, a lot of it. My parents pushed the ‘good degree, good job’ narrative hard. Anything less was…discouraging. I felt the same pressure. Although, honestly, watching films and taking photos feels a lot more…me than, say, corporate law ever would. Definitely. My nan was always banging on about a ‘secure’ job. Anything with a pension, apparently. Doesn't really compute when you're looking at zero-hour contracts and the gig economy. Plus, I was diagnosed with dyslexia quite late, actually. Secondary school. Suddenly a lot of the pressure made a bit more sense, but the damage was done, you know?

… honestly, the sheer  audacity  of it all. Saying they’re “streamlining” the NHS. Streamlining into oblivion, more like. It’s just… infuriating, isn’t it? Especially after everything everyone went through the last few years. It is. Though, knowing the current government, ‘streamlining’ is code for ‘privatisation by stealth’. They’ve been circling it for years. Remember the polyclinic fiasco back in… oh, 2009? Same playbook, different decade. Exactly! And it’s always framed as being ‘better value for money’. Better value for  whom , I ask you? Certainly not the patients waiting six months for a hip replacement. Or the nurses working double shifts. Honestly, Mum was telling me about her friend’s experience trying to get a doctor’s appointment… it’s a postcode lottery now. Mum’s friend Brenda? Poor woman. She always has something going on. It just feels like they’re deliberately eroding public services, bit by bit. And then they wonder why everyone’s stressed and miserable. Did you see that article about the rise in anxiety amongst young people? Shocking figures. Speaking of stressed, did you manage to look at those pension forecasts I sent over? I’m starting to get properly worried, actually. They’re… not brilliant. I did, briefly. Need to give them a proper look, I admit. Too much Sky News earlier, frankly. But first impressions weren't good. We really need to bump up the contributions, don't we? Even though it feels like throwing money into a black hole right now. It does. And it’s frustrating because we  are  both working, we’re both lecturers, we’re not exactly living lavishly… yet it feels like we’re falling further behind. The cost of everything is just insane. Have you noticed how much the weekly shop costs now? Don’t even. I went for milk and bread yesterday, and came out having spent nearly fifteen quid. Fifteen! For a few basic groceries. It’s daylight robbery. And the energy bills… Honestly, I’m half tempted to just wear three jumpers all winter. We're practically there already! Honestly, I saw that new series on Netflix, “The Diplomat”. It's actually quite good. A decent bit of escapism from all this. Although, even  that  felt strangely relevant with all the geopolitical tension going on. I've heard good things. We should watch it. Though, if I’m being honest, I’ve been falling down a YouTube rabbit hole of miniature train sets.

…and honestly, the sheer  volume  of choice is exhausting. I mean, when I used to do the weekly shop, it was Sainsbury's, a quick scan of the produce, and done. Now, Elsie keeps sending me links to these artisan cheese websites! Artisan! As if a bit of cheddar isn't perfectly good enough. Gran, Elsie's just trying to broaden your horizons. She knows you like cheese! And honestly, some of those cheeses  are  amazing. I tried a Lincolnshire Poacher last week, it was incredible. Lincolnshire Poacher, eh? Good stuff, that. Though nothing beats a decent Red Leicester, if you ask me. Brings me back to school dinners, it does. Used to swap my semolina for a bit of Leicester with young Timmy Higgins. Rascal, that boy. Semolina! Don't even  mention  semolina. That was a culinary crime. Though, thinking about school dinners… remember those awful reformed meat things? They always smelled faintly of sadness. Oh god, yes! And the grey, watery gravy… I think I actively avoided the school canteen most days. So, Dad, did you ever manage to get the bird feeder sorted? The sparrows were looking particularly hopeful this morning. Nearly. The blasted thing’s a fiendish contraption, all different screws and bits. I’ve got the main structure up, but attaching the seed dispenser’s proving tricky. All these new materials… in my day, you just nailed things together and hoped for the best. Modern life, isn't it? All complexities and instructions. Remember when we took the children to Cornwall, David? That inflatable boat nearly broke you. You were wrestling with it for a good hour! Don't remind me. Little devils they were, wanting to be out on the water immediately. And the wind! Blew that thing halfway to France, I swear. Elsie was brilliant, though, calming everyone down with pasties. Cornwall was amazing. I’d love to go back. Though, maybe somewhere a bit warmer next time. I was watching a documentary about the Galapagos Islands last night - the wildlife there is just stunning. Galapagos! Oh, posh. Elsie's always on at me to book a 'proper' holiday. She keeps showing me pictures of luxury cruises. As if! I'm perfectly happy with a week in Bournemouth.
